passages.title: The revealed Book: follow it without anxiety
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the doorway to Sūrat al-Aʿrāf: Allah presents the Qur'an to His Messenger ﷺ, steadies his heart against any tightness over carrying it, and then turns to the world with a single command — follow what your Lord has sent down, and take no protectors in place of Him. What binds the passage together is the movement of revelation itself: the Book comes down (ayah 1–2), the bearer of the Book is reassured (ayah 2), and the recipients of the Book are told what to do with it (ayah 3).

## The opening letters

The sūrah begins with *Alif-Lām-Mīm-Ṣād* — four Arabic letters recited on their own. Letters like these open a number of sūrahs of the Qur'an, and Ibn Kathir does not re-open the discussion here; he simply refers the reader back to his earlier explanation of these letters at the beginning of other sūrahs. What follows immediately is the word *kitāb*, "a Book."

## Where this sūrah is heading

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān gives a helpful aerial view before descending into the verses. Most of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, it observes, revolves around two great themes: *Maʿād* — the Return to the Hereafter — and *Risālah* — Prophethood. The theme of the Return dominates roughly the first six sections, and then, from the eighth to the twenty-first sections, the sūrah unfolds a long, detailed account of the past prophets, the events of their communities, their reward and punishment, and the punishment that overtook them.

## "Let not your breast be narrow because of it"

In ayah 2, Allah addresses His Messenger ﷺ directly: this is a Book sent down *to you* — so let there be no *ḥaraj* in your *ṣadr* (breast, chest) on account of it. *Ḥaraj* means narrowness, constraint, a tightness of the heart. The scholars read this consolation in more than one way, and the readings complement rather than compete:

**No doubt.** According to Mujahid, Qatadah, and As-Suddi — early authorities cited by Ibn Kathir — the meaning is: let there be no *doubt* in your heart about this Book. It is from your Lord; receive it with a settled chest.

**No hesitation in conveying it.** A second reading, which Ibn Kathir also records, is: do not hesitate to convey the Qur'an and to warn with it. Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's word elsewhere, "Therefore be patient as did the Messengers of strong will" (46:35) — delivering revelation to a resistant people takes the patience of the greatest prophets. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān fills in the human texture of this reading, citing what is reported from Abu al-ʿĀliyah (via Mazhari): have no anguish or apprehension in conveying the Qur'an and its injunctions, lest people belie *it* — the message itself — and hurt you. And it draws out the quiet promise folded inside the verse: the same Allah who sent down this Book has also arranged that His Messenger shall remain protected. The One who gave him the burden guarantees the bearer.

**No grief over those who refuse.** Some commentators, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes, understood the constraint differently: it was the pain the Prophet ﷺ felt — out of sheer affectionate concern for people — when they heard the Qur'an and still would not believe. To lift that weight, he is told that his obligation is simply to make the call and convey the message. Once that is done, it is not his responsibility who becomes a Muslim and who does not. The duty is delivery, not results — and so there was no reason for him to be anxious.

The verse then names the Book's double function: *that you may warn thereby* — Ibn Kathir explains, warn the disbelievers with it — *and a reminder to the believers*. One and the same Book lands differently on different hearts: for the disbelievers it is a warning; for the believers, a reminder.

## Ayah 3: the command to the world

Having steadied the Messenger ﷺ, Allah — in Ibn Kathir's phrase — "then said to the world": **Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord.** Ibn Kathir unpacks the command: follow and imitate the unlettered Prophet ﷺ, who brought you a Book that was revealed *for you*, from the Lord and Master of everything. The Book came through the Prophet ﷺ, but — as Ibn Kathir's wording makes plain — it was revealed for those it addresses.

Then the negative half of the command: **and do not follow, besides Him, any awliyāʼ** — protectors, as the translation renders it: figures taken as guardians and guides in place of Allah. Ibn Kathir states its meaning plainly: do not disregard what the Messenger ﷺ brought you and follow something else, for then you would be deviating from Allah's judgment to the decision of someone else. That is the real weight of the verse: following is exclusive. To set any other authority above or alongside the revelation — any person, system, or inherited way whose word overrides the Book — is to swap Allah's judgment for a creature's opinion.

## "Little do you remember"

The passage closes with a gentle rebuke: *qalīlan mā tadhakkarūn* — how little you take reminder! Ibn Kathir hears in this the same note the Qur'an sounds elsewhere, and he gathers the parallel verses: "And most of mankind will not believe even if you desire it eagerly" (12:103); "And if you obey most of those on the earth, they will mislead you far away from Allah's path" (6:116); "And most of them believe not in Allah except that they attribute partners unto Him" (12:106). The lesson threaded through these verses: the majority is not the measure of truth. Most people forget, most people follow the crowd — which is precisely why the command of ayah 3 anchors the believer to the revelation rather than to popular opinion.

## Living this passage

Two takeaways sit on the surface of these ayat. First, the consolation given to the Prophet ﷺ carries a principle for anyone who conveys truth: your duty is to deliver it sincerely and clearly; the outcomes belong to Allah. Anguish over who accepts and who refuses is a weight Allah Himself lifted from His own Messenger — and Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān adds that the Sender of the message also takes charge of protecting its bearer. Second, ayah 3 asks each of us a standing question: when the Book's guidance and some other voice point in different directions, which one do we actually follow? The verse allows only one answer — what has been sent down from your Lord — and warns that taking any protector besides Allah is not a small adjustment but a departure from His judgment. And it ends by telling us why the reminder needs repeating: because remembering is exactly what we do too little of.

passages.title: Destroyed towns and the just weighing of deeds
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a single courtroom scene stretched across time. First the evidence of history: how many settled, secure towns Allah has destroyed for rejecting His messengers (ayat 4–5). Then the hearing on the Day of Resurrection: every nation questioned, and every messenger too, with Allah Himself narrating the full record (ayat 6–7). Then the verdict: the weighing of deeds, in which no soul is wronged by so much as the weight of a speck of dust (ayat 8–9). What binds the six ayat together is one certainty pressed home from three directions — nothing is missed, nothing is forgotten, and the final reckoning is perfectly just.

## The ruined towns: judgment in this world (ayat 4–5)

The passage opens with *wa-kam min qaryah* — "how many societies We have destroyed!", or in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "And a great number of towns We destroyed." Ibn Kathir explains why they were destroyed: "for defying Our Messengers and rejecting them. This behavior led them to earn disgrace in this life, which led them to disgrace in the Hereafter." Worldly ruin, in other words, was not the end of their punishment but its beginning. He connects this to Allah's words elsewhere: "many a township did We destroy while they were given to wrongdoing, so that it lie in ruins (up to this day), and (many) a deserted well and lofty castle!" (22:45) — the deserted wells and lofty castles left lying in ruins.

**The timing is the frightening detail.** The torment came "by night or while they were taking their midday nap." Ibn Kathir observes that both of these "are periods of rest and leisure or heedlessness and amusement" — the times when people feel most secure. He sets beside it the question asked later in this same surah: "Did the people of the towns then feel secure against the coming of Our punishment by night while they were asleep? Or... in the forenoon while they were playing?" (7:97–98), and the ayah asking whether the plotters feel secure that the torment will not seize them "from directions they perceive not" or "in the midst of their going to and from" (16:45–47). The point is that divine punishment does not announce itself; it arrives precisely when people have concluded it is not coming.

**Ayah 5 records the only thing they managed to say.** When the torment struck, "no cry did they utter... but this: 'Verily, we were wrongdoers.'" Ibn Kathir comments: their cry was that "they admitted their sins and that they deserved to be punished." All the arguments, the mockery of the messengers, the confident denial — at the moment of truth it all collapsed into a single sentence of confession. It is the truth, but spoken too late to be of any use.

## The questioning: both sides of the message (ayat 6–7)

Ayah 6 then moves the scene from this world to the Day of Resurrection: "Then surely, We shall question those (people) to whom it (the Book) was sent and verily, We shall question the Messengers." Strikingly, the questioning runs in both directions: the peoples to whom messengers were sent, *and* the messengers themselves. Ibn ʿAbbas, in the report of ʿAli bin Abi Talhah cited by Ibn Kathir, said the questioning will be "about what they conveyed": the nations will be asked how they responded to their messengers, and the messengers will be asked whether they delivered the message. Ibn Kathir links this to the Day when Allah will call out, "What answer gave you to the Messengers?" (28:65), and to the messengers' own answer: "We have no knowledge, verily, only You are the Knower of all that is unseen" (5:109) — even the prophets, on that Day, defer entirely to Allah's knowledge.

**The Prophet ﷺ took this questioning with utter seriousness.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān brings the scene from Sahih Muslim, narrated by Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him): during the address of his Last Hajj, the Prophet ﷺ asked the assembled believers — when you are asked on the Day of Qiyamah whether I conveyed the message of Allah to you, what will you say? They answered: we will say that you conveyed the message, fulfilled the trust of Allah at its best, and wished and did what was most beneficial for the community. And he ﷺ said: "O Allah, You be witness." A narration in the Musnad of Ahmad adds that he ﷺ said Allah will ask him on the Day of Qiyamah whether he conveyed His message, and he will answer that he has — "therefore, all of you should make sure that those who are present do convey my message to those absent." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what "those absent" means: not only people missing from that gathering, but the generations to come — every age must pass the message to the next, "so that all children of Adam to be born right through the day of Qiyamah will have received this message." The questioning of ayah 6 is therefore not a scene we merely watch; every believer is a link in the chain it examines.

**Ayah 7 removes any thought that the questioning is for Allah's information.** "Then surely, We shall narrate unto them (their whole story) with knowledge, and indeed We have not been absent." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The Book will be brought forth on the Day of Resurrection and it will speak, disclosing what they used to do." Ibn Kathir explains "We have not been absent": Allah will inform His servants of everything they said and did, "whether substantial or minor... He witnesses to everything, nothing escapes His observation" — He knows "what the eyes are deluded by and what the hearts conceal," as in the ayah: "Not a leaf falls, but He knows it" (6:59). The questioning is not an investigation. It is the presentation of a case Allah has witnessed in full from the beginning.

## The Balance: the weighing that cannot be unjust (ayat 8–9)

"And the weighing on that Day is *al-ḥaqq*." The commentators bring out two sides of this word. Ibn Kathir reads it as the *true* weighing — perfectly accurate, "for Allah will not wrong anyone," citing: "We shall set up the Balances of justice on the Day of Resurrection, then none will be dealt with unjustly in anything. And if there be the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it" (21:47), and: "Surely, Allah wrongs not even the weight of a speck of dust, but if there is any good (done), He doubles it" (4:40). Notice the asymmetry: not a speck of wrong, but good deeds *doubled* and given "a great reward" from Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads al-ḥaqq as *definite*: the weighing is due and true, "there is no room for doubt in it" — a sentence aimed at the person who cannot imagine how deeds could be weighed at all.

**How can deeds — which have no mass — be weighed?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers the doubt head-on. First, Allah's power is absolute; that we cannot weigh something says nothing about what He can do. Second, even human instruments now weigh what no one once thought weighable — air, electric current, heat. Third, and deeper: Allah can give deeds a real form. The commentary notes many ahadith showing that deeds take shapes in the Barzakh (the state between death and resurrection) and at the Gathering — good deeds as beautified companions in the grave, unpaid Zakah reaching its owner's grave as a poisonous snake saying "I am your wealth, I am your treasure" — and it is recorded in the Sahih that Surahs al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān will come on the Day of Resurrection as two clouds shading those who recited them. The Qurʼan itself says: "what people had done in the world, they would find present there" (18:49).

**What exactly is placed on the scale?** Ibn Kathir surveys three views, each with its evidence. That *the deeds themselves* are weighed, given physical weight by Allah — reported by al-Baghawi from Ibn ʿAbbas. That *the written records* are weighed — as in the hadith of the card (biṭāqah): a man's ninety-nine scrolls of sins, each stretching as far as the sight can reach, are set against a single card bearing *lā ilāha illa Allāh*; he asks, "O Lord! What would this card weigh against these scrolls?" and Allah answers, "You will not be wronged" — then "the scrolls will go up, as the card becomes heavier." At-Tirmidhi recorded similar wording for this hadith and said that it is authentic; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the fuller account through Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, Baihaqi and Hakim, from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar, at the end of which the Prophet ﷺ said: nothing can weigh more than the name of Allah. Or that *the doer himself* is weighed — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a hadith of Abu Hurairah in al-Bukhari and Muslim: on the Day of Qiyamah there will come heavy people whose weight, in the sight of Allah, will not be worth even a mosquito's — and the Prophet ﷺ recited: "We shall assign no weight for them" (18:105); while of the thin-legged ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud he ﷺ said: "By He in Whose Hand is my soul! They are heavier on the Balance than (Mount) Uhud." Ibn Kathir's conclusion — related approvingly in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — is that all of these may truly occur: sometimes deeds are weighed, sometimes the scrolls, sometimes the persons, and the full reality "is known to Allah alone." We are not required to know the mechanics; we are required to know that the weighing is real. This is the sound creedal position: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that the weighing of deeds "stands proved from the Holy Qur'an and is the collective belief of the Muslim Ummah" — the Balance is affirmed as Allah described it, without explaining it away.

**Reconciling the card hadith with the light scales of ayah 9.** If one kalimah — the declaration of faith, *lā ilāha illa Allāh* — outweighs ninety-nine scrolls of sin, how can any believer's scale be light? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits the answer of the scholars of tafsir (from Bayan al-Qurʼan): the weighing at the Gathering will happen twice. A first weighing separates belief from disbelief — there, whoever has the kalimah of faith at all outweighs everything, and is separated from the disbelievers. Then a second weighing sets the believers' good deeds against their sins, and reward or punishment follows accordingly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that where narrations speak of salvation by the kalimah alone despite mountains of sin, this is an exception "beyond the general regulation" — a special manifestation of Allah's grace and mercy, whether directly or through the intercession of a prophet or a righteous servant.

**Ayah 9 names the loss precisely.** Those whose scales are light "have doomed themselves" — *khasirū anfusahum*; in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "they are those who will lose themselves" — and the ayah gives the reason: their wrongful behavior with Allah's ayat. This closes the circle the passage opened: it began with towns destroyed for rejecting the messengers, and ends with souls lost for wronging the revelations those messengers carried.

## What weighs heavy: living under the Balance

Because the scale is real, the sources dwell lovingly on what makes it heavy — and the list is strikingly reachable. The hadith with which Imam al-Bukhari chose to conclude his Sahih, from Abu Hurairah: two words "very light when said but very heavy when weighed on the Scale of Deeds, and with Allah, they are dear" — *Subḥān Allāhi wa bi-ḥamdihi, Subḥān Allāhil-ʿAẓīm*. Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi and Ibn Hibban report from Abu al-Dardaʼ that the Prophet ﷺ said no deed will be heavier than *good morals* on the scale of deeds; and he ﷺ told Abu Dharr of two things not hard for anyone yet heaviest on the scale — good morals, and observing silence, that is, not talking unless necessary. Tabarani reports from Jabir: the *first* deed placed on the scale will be spending on one's family and taking care of their needs. Teaching the faith keeps weighing after death — a hadith describes a man dismayed at his few good deeds when suddenly something like a cloud falls into his pan: the ongoing reward of everyone who acted on what he taught. From Imam Ahmad's Kitab al-Zuhd: Jibril said that all deeds will be weighed except tears shed from the fear of Allah — one such tear extinguishes the wildest fire of Jahannam. And in Abu Dawud, from Abu Hurairah: if a shortfall is found in a servant's *farāʾiḍ* (obligatory acts), Allah will ask whether he has *nawāfil* (voluntary acts) to his credit, and the voluntary will complete the obligatory.

Taken whole, the passage dismantles two illusions. The ruined towns of ayah 4 dismantle the illusion of *security* — that ease and routine mean one is safe from Allah's reckoning. The Balance of ayat 8–9 dismantles the illusion of *insignificance* — that small deeds, small words, small kindnesses do not count. Nothing was ever unwitnessed ("We have not been absent"), and nothing will go unweighed. The believer's response is not dread but attentiveness: to receive the message and pass it on, and to keep dropping into the scale the things the Prophet ﷺ said weigh most.

passages.title: Iblis refuses to bow and vows ambush
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:10–18 — Iblis Refuses to Bow and Vows Ambush

This passage tells the story that stands behind every human struggle with temptation. Allah first reminds mankind of His favour in settling them on the earth (ayah 10), then takes us back to the beginning: the honouring of Adam before the angels, the refusal of Iblis, his expulsion, and his vow to ambush Adam's children on the very road that leads back to Allah (ayat 11–18). Ibn Kathir states the purpose plainly: Allah is informing the Children of Adam "about the honor of their father and the enmity of Shaytan," who still has envy for them and for their father Adam — so they should beware of him and not follow in his footsteps. And notice what brackets the passage: ayah 10 ends, "little thanks do you give," and in ayah 17 Iblis boasts, "You will not find most of them to be thankful." Gratitude is the battleground on which this whole drama is fought.

## The blessing before the battle (ayah 10)

Before introducing the enemy, Allah reminds us whose guests we are. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah made the earth a fixed place for dwelling, placed firm mountains and rivers on it, made homes and allowed people to utilize its benefits, made the clouds work for them to bring rain so they may produce their sustenance, and created the ways and means of earning — commercial activities and the professions. Yet most give little thanks; he cites the ayah, "And if you count the blessings of Allah, never will you be able to count them. Verily, man is indeed a wrongdoer, an ingrate" (14:34).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a striking image: Allah has made this whole earth and what it contains a giant warehouse of human needs and comforts. Science and technology are essentially no more than a trained method of taking out things the Master of the Universe has already created and stored in this warehouse, and using them soundly and beneficially. All of this demands that human beings be grateful to Him at all times — but they are prone to heedlessness, quick to forget the favours of their Creator. So the ayah closes in a mode of complaint: how little you give thanks. Keep that closing note in mind; Iblis will return to it.

## "We created you, then shaped you" (ayah 11)

Ayah 11 addresses all of us in the plural — "We created you, then shaped you" — and then narrates the command given about one man, Adam. Ibn Kathir resolves this: the ayah refers to Adam, but Allah uses the plural because Adam is the father of all mankind; an honour given to the father is an honour given to his descendants. He compares it to Allah telling the Children of Israel who lived in the Prophet's ﷺ time, "We shaded you with clouds and sent down on you manna and the quail" (2:57) — the favour fell on their forefathers in the time of Musa, yet the offspring share in it because those forefathers are their very source.

Ibn Kathir then recalls how the honour was given: after Allah created Adam with His Hands from dried clay of altered mud and made him in the shape of a human being, He blew life into him and ordered the angels to prostrate before him, honouring Allah's glory and magnificence. The angels all heard, obeyed and prostrated. One being present did not.

## The first false argument (ayah 12)

Allah asks Iblis in ayah 12: "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?" Ibn Kathir, following Ibn Jarir, reads this as: what stopped and hindered you from prostrating after I ordered you to do so? Iblis's answer — "I am better than him; You created me from fire, and him You created from clay" — is, in Ibn Kathir's words, an excuse **worse than the crime itself**. Shaytan's reasoning was that he did not obey because he who is better cannot prostrate to he who is less.

Ibn Kathir dismantles the argument at both ends. First, the cursed one looked at the origin of creation and not at the honour bestowed — that Allah created Adam with His Hand and blew life into him. Second, even his claim about the materials was false: clay has the qualities of wisdom, forbearance, patience and assurance; it is where plants grow, flourish, increase and provide good. Fire has the qualities of burning, recklessness and hastiness. And the two natures played out exactly so: the origin of creation directed Shaytan to failure, while the origin of Adam led him to return to Allah with repentance, humbleness, obedience and submission to His command, admitting his error and seeking Allah's forgiveness and pardon. The bundle of his refusal is caught in the name itself: by contradicting the angels he "became *Ablasa* from the mercy" — that is, he lost hope of acquiring Allah's mercy.

On the substance of these origins, Ibn Kathir cites the hadith recorded by Muslim from ʿAishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The angels were created from light, Shaytan from a smokeless flame of fire, while Adam was created from what was described to you."

There is a further lesson the early scholars drew here. Ibn Jarir recorded — in a statement with an authentic chain of narration — that Al-Hasan said of Iblis's fire-versus-clay argument: "Iblis used *qiyās* (analogy), and he was the first one to do so." Ibn Jarir also recorded, again with an authentic chain, that Ibn Sirin said: "The first to use qiyās was Iblis, and would the sun and moon be worshipped if it was not for qiyās?" Qiyās here means analogical comparison — inferring what ought to be from a comparison one has drawn oneself. Shaytan, as Ibn Kathir puts it, made a false comparison when confronted by Allah's command. That is the danger being censured: an inference of one's own set up against an explicit command of Allah — the ground on which the first act of disobedience was argued.

## Cast down by pride (ayah 13)

Allah's sentence in ayah 13 answers arrogance with its precise opposite: "Get down from this; it is not for you to be arrogant here. Get out, for you are of those humiliated and disgraced." Ibn Kathir notes that "get down from this" refers to Paradise according to the scholars of tafsir, or possibly to the particular status Iblis had held in the utmost heights; and that this humiliation was "just recompense for his ill intentions, by giving him the opposite of what he intended" — he intended arrogance and received disgrace.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over a question worth feeling: how could any creature dare to argue in that Presence — the Most August conceivable Presence, whose awe and majesty would not allow even angels and prophets and messengers to breathe? The ʿulamā (scholars), as conveyed from Bayān al-Qurʼān, answer that this itself was a somber and highly cutting manifestation of the divine wrath: because of his rejection, Iblis's view was so obstructed (*hijāb*, a veil) that he became blind to the grandeur and awe of Allah, and irreverence came down to settle on him all over. Insolence before Allah is not boldness; it is a punishment already underway.

## The respite (ayat 14–15)

Then comes an astonishing turn: from under the very wrath of Allah, Iblis makes a request — "Delay my end until the Day they are resurrected" — and in ayah 15 Allah replies, "You are of those respited." Ibn Kathir comments that Allah gave Shaytan what he asked for out of His wisdom, it being His decision and decree that is never prevented or resisted; none can avert His decision.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān examines the grant closely. Iblis asked for respite until *Yawm al-Baʿth*, the Day of Resurrection, when the second Horn is blown and the dead are raised — which, had it been granted as asked, would have meant Iblis remaining alive at the very time when nothing is alive except Allah, the Ever-Living, the Self-Sustaining. But in another ayah Allah says, "till the day of the appointed time" (15:38). The narration of Suddiy reported in Tafsir Ibn Jarir explains: Allah did not give him respite until the Day of Resurrection, but until the day the Horn is blown the first time, when whoever is in the heavens and the earth shall be stunned, and dead. So the prayer was answered — but not completely. Iblis lives until the first blast, dies along with the whole creation when "All that is on it will perish and to remain there shall be the Face of your Lord, full of majesty, bounty and honour" (55:26–27), and when all others are resurrected, he too stands resurrected. Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi in Bayān al-Qurʼān adds that the whole span from the blowing of the first Horn up to the entry into Paradise or Hell is one long day in which different things happen at different times, so that day can be named after whichever event is meant — the day of the Horn, of perishing, of Resurrection, of Recompense. This resolves the apparent differences in wording.

The episode also settles a common puzzle: can the prayer of a disbeliever be answered? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that in this world it can be — even the prayer of the foremost disbeliever, Iblis, was answered — while the ayah "the prayer of the disbelievers is but in vain" (13:14) concerns the Hereafter, not this world.

## The ambush on the straight path (ayat 16–17)

Respite in hand, Iblis does not repent; Ibn Kathir says he "went on in defiance and rebellion." His vow in ayah 16 — "Because You have *aghwaytanī*, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path" — uses a word Ibn ʿAbbās explained as "misguided me." Others rendered his meaning: "As You caused my ruin, I will sit in wait for Your servants whom You will create from the offspring of the one you expelled me for." As for "Your straight path" (*ṣirāṭ mustaqīm*), Ibn Kathir explains it as the path of truth and the way of safety — Iblis vows to misguide people from this path so that they do not worship Allah alone; and Mujahid said that the "straight path" refers to the truth. Note where the ambush is laid: not in the alleys of open evil, but on the very road to Allah. The person already off the path needs no ambush.

The Prophet ﷺ described exactly this, in a hadith Imam Ahmad recorded from Saburah bin Abi Al-Fakih, who heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: Shaytan sat in wait for the son of Adam in all his paths. He sat in the path of Islam — "Would you embrace Islam and abandon your religion and the religion of your forefathers?" — but the son of Adam disobeyed him and embraced Islam. He sat in the path of Hijrah (migration in the cause of Allah) — "Would you migrate and leave your land and sky?" — but he disobeyed him and migrated. He sat in the path of Jihad — "If you fight, you will be killed, your wife will be married and your wealth divided" — but he disobeyed him and performed Jihad. Whoever among them does this and dies, said the Prophet ﷺ, it will be a promise from Allah that He admits him into Paradise.

In ayah 17 Iblis names his directions of attack, and Ibn ʿAbbās (as reported by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah) decodes each one: *from before them* — raising doubts in them concerning their Hereafter; *from behind them* — making them more eager for this life; *from their right* — causing them confusion in the religion; *from their left* — luring them to commit sins. Ibn Kathir sums it up: this covers all paths of good and evil — Shaytan discourages people from the path of good and lures them to the path of evil. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cautions that the four directions are not meant to set up limits but to say "from all sides and directions" — which is why the possibility of his misleading people from above or beneath the feet does not contradict the ayah, nor does the hadith that Shaytan can enter the human body and move through the arteries and veins of blood.

And yet one direction is missing from Iblis's list. Al-Hakam bin Aban said that ʿIkrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning this ayah: "He did not say that he will come from above them, because the mercy descends from above."

Iblis ends: "and You will not find most of them to be thankful" — the thankful being, as Ibn ʿAbbās said in the report of ʿAli bin Abi Talhah, "those who single Him out [in worship]." Ibn Kathir observes that when Shaytan said this it was a guess and an assumption on his part — yet the truth turned out to be the same, for Allah said: "And indeed Iblis did prove true his thought about them, and they followed him, all except a group of true believers. And he had no authority over them, except that We might test him who believes in the Hereafter, from him who is in doubt about it" (34:20–21). Hear the echo of ayah 10: Allah said "little thanks do you give," and Iblis has staked his entire campaign on keeping it that way. Every act of genuine gratitude is a defeat inflicted on him.

Because of this, says Ibn Kathir, there is a hadith that encourages seeking refuge with Allah from the lures of Shaytan from all directions. Imam Ahmad narrated that ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to often recite this supplication in the morning and when the night falls: "O Allah! I ask You for well-being in this life and the Hereafter. O Allah! I ask You for pardon and well-being in my religion, life, family and wealth. O Allah! Cover my errors and reassure me in times of difficulty. O Allah! Protect me from before me, from behind me, from my right, from my left and from above me. I seek refuge with Your greatness from being killed from below me." Waki explained "from below" as referring to earthquakes. Abu Dawud, An-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban and Al-Hakim collected this hadith, and Al-Hakim said, "Its chain is Sahih." The duʿā answers the ambush point for point — and asks protection from above and from below as well, the directions Iblis left unnamed.

## Expelled, despised (ayah 18)

The final word belongs to Allah: "Get out from this, *madhʼūman madḥūrā*." Ibn Kathir says Allah here emphasized His cursing, expelling and banishing of Shaytan from the uppermost heights, and the early authorities pile up the meanings of this pair. Ibn Jarir: *madhʼūm* is the disgraced, and *madḥūr* the distanced — banished and expelled. From Ibn ʿAbbās comes "despised," and in the report of ʿAli bin Abi Talhah, "belittled and despised." As-Suddi said, "hateful and expelled"; Qatadah, "cursed and despised"; Mujahid, "expelled and banished." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (from Bayān al-Qurʼān) notes that in these ayat Shaytan is commanded to leave twice — in ayah 13 and again here — the first saying being, perhaps, a proposal and the other its implementation.

Then the decree that closes the scene: "Whoever of them follows you — surely, I will fill Hell with you all." Ibn Kathir sets beside it the parallel passage: "Go, and whosoever of them follows you, surely, Hell will be the recompense of you all — an ample recompense... But Shaytan promises them nothing but deceit. Verily, My servants — you have no authority over them" (17:63–65). That last line is the passage's hidden mercy: Iblis was given time, but he was never given authority. Hell is not filled with his victims; it is filled with his *followers* — those who chose to walk behind him.

## Living under ambush

What does this ask of us? First, what Ibn Kathir named at the outset: know your enemy — he still envies you and your father Adam — so beware of him and do not follow in his footsteps. Second, guard against his actual method: doubts about the Hereafter, eagerness for this life, confusion in religion, and the lure of sins — and never let a comparison of your own devising talk you out of a clear command of Allah, for that was the first sin ever argued. Third, take the shield the Prophet ﷺ taught: the morning and evening supplication of protection from every side — and above all gratitude, since a thankful servant is precisely the servant Iblis wagered Allah would not find many of.

passages.title: Satan deceives Adam and Eve in Paradise
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat tell the story of humanity's first test as one unbroken drama: Allah settles Adam and his wife in Paradise with a single prohibition; Shayṭān dismantles that prohibition through whispering, false argument and a sworn oath; the couple fall, are exposed, and respond with the words of repentance that define the believer forever; and Allah decrees the descent to earth — the very world we now live in, die in, and will be raised from. What holds the passage together is the contrast between two responses to failure: Iblis's, and Adam's. Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān note that this story was already told in Sūrah al-Baqarah; Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān simply refers the reader back to its detailed commentary there.

## One tree, and a jealous enemy (ayah 19)

In **ayah 19** the generosity comes first: Adam and his wife may dwell in Paradise and, as Ibn Kathir puts it, eat from *all* of its fruits — except one tree. The prohibition is a single point in an ocean of permission, and crossing it would make them "of the wrongdoers."

Ibn Kathir explains what set the tragedy in motion: Shayṭān **envied** them. He saw the favours and fine clothing they were enjoying and "plotted deceitfully, whispering and suggesting treachery," wishing to strip them of it all. The attack was not random malice; it was jealousy seeking to pull others down from a blessing.

## Anatomy of a whisper (ayat 20–21)

**Ayah 20** names the method: *waswasah* — the whisper, the quiet insinuation. And remarkably, the ayah announces Shayṭān's real goal before quoting a word he said: he whispered "in order to expose what was hidden of their private parts." The aim of the temptation was never the reward he promised; it was their humiliation.

Then comes the lie itself, and Ibn Kathir slows down over its wording. Shayṭān said: "Your Lord did not forbid you this tree save you should become angels or become of the immortals." Ibn Kathir reads the Arabic *an takūnā* ("that you become") in the sense of *lest you become* — that is, Shayṭān claimed: "He only forbade it **so that you would not** become angels or live here forever. Eat, and you will gain both." Ibn Kathir supports this reading with parallel Qur'anic usages where the same construction means "lest": "(Thus) does Allah make clear to you (His Law) lest you go astray" [4:176], and "He has affixed into the earth mountains standing firm, lest it should shake with you" [16:15]. He also points to the matching scene in Sūrah Ṭā Hā, where Shayṭān says openly: "O Adam! Shall I lead you to the Tree of Eternity and to a kingdom that will never waste away?" [20:120]. Notice what the lie does: it does not say "disobey your Lord." It keeps Allah in the sentence but reinterprets His command, claiming the prohibition was designed to keep the two of them from a good. The first sin in human history began with a corrupted *explanation* of a divine command.

**Ayah 21** adds the final instrument: *wa-qāsamahumā* — "and he swore to them." Ibn Kathir says this means he swore **by Allah** that he was their sincere well-wisher — arguing, in effect, "I was here before you, so I know this place better than you." Qatādah puts Shayṭān's reasoning into words: "I was created before you, and I have better knowledge than you. Therefore, follow me and I will direct you."

How could such a deception succeed? Ibn Kathir offers a sentence worth memorising: "It is a fact that the believer in Allah might sometimes become the victim of deceit." Shayṭān was willing to swear by Allah while lying — so sincerity of tone is never, by itself, proof of sincere counsel.

## The taste, and what it uncovered (ayah 22)

**Ayah 22** opens with *fa-dallāhumā bi-ghurūr* — "so he brought about their fall through deception," or as Ibn Kathir renders it, "he misled them with deception." The moment they tasted the tree, the threat announced in ayah 20 came true: what had been hidden of their bodies became manifest, and they began covering themselves with the leaves of Paradise.

The early authorities fill in this picture. Wahb bin Munabbih — in a report Ibn Jarir transmits with an authentic chain — said that Adam and Ḥawwāʼ had been covered by a **light**, which kept each from seeing the other's nakedness; when they ate, it was stripped away. Ibn ʿAbbās, in a statement with an authentic chain, said the leaves they reached for were **fig leaves**; Mujāhid adds that they fashioned them "as a dress (or garment)." Set the promise beside the result: Shayṭān had said that eating would bring angelhood and immortality; what it actually brought was the exposure of what had been hidden, and a scramble to cover it with leaves.

Ibn Kathir then relates a vivid scene from Ubayy bin Kaʿb: Adam was a tall man — "about the height of a palm tree" — with thick hair. When he committed his error and saw himself exposed, he fled in fright through Paradise, until a tree caught him by the head. "Release me," he pleaded; it answered, "I will not release you." Then his Lord called to him: "O Adam! Do you run away from Me?" He said: "O Lord! I felt ashamed before You." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Marduwyah collected this through several chains from al-Ḥasan, from Ubayy bin Kaʿb, who narrated it from the Prophet ﷺ; Ibn Kathir notes, however, that relating it to Ubayy himself is more correct. Whatever its final grading, its point is luminous: Adam's instinct after sin was not defiance but shame — and shame before Allah is itself the seed of return.

The ayah closes with the Lord's rebuke, gentle in its form as a question: "Did I not forbid you that tree and tell you: Verily, Shayṭān is an open enemy unto you?" They had been warned of both the tree and the enemy.

## The sentence that saved us (ayah 23)

**Ayah 23** is the hinge of the whole passage — and, in a sense, of human history: "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we shall certainly be of the losers." No excuse, no blaming the deceiver, no theological self-defence. Full ownership ("we have wronged **ourselves**"), and total dependence on two things only: Allah's forgiveness and His mercy. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk bin Muzāḥim said of this plea: "These are the words that Adam received from his Lord" — Allah Himself taught His servant how to come back to Him.

Ibn Kathir preserves, through ʿAbdur-Razzāq from Qatādah, the exchange that reveals the passage's deepest contrast. Adam said: "O Lord! What if I repented and sought forgiveness?" Allah said: "Then I will admit you into Paradise." As for Shayṭān, "he did not ask for forgiveness, but for respite. Each one of them was given what he asked for." Read that last line slowly. Both had disobeyed. One asked for pardon and was promised Paradise; the other asked only for more time — and got exactly that. In that exchange, each was answered according to what he sought, and the difference between the two lay entirely in what each chose to ask. This is the dividing line between the way of Adam and the way of Iblis.

## Down to earth — but not abandoned (ayat 24–25)

**Ayah 24** carries the decree: "Descend, some of you enemies to others." The command *ihbiṭū* ("get down") is in the plural, and Ibn Kathir reports the discussion over who was addressed: Adam, Ḥawwāʼ and Iblis — some scholars adding the snake, others omitting it, "and Allah knows best." The enmity, he says, is primarily between Adam and Iblis; Ḥawwāʼ follows Adam in this, as in the parallel dual command of Sūrah Ṭā Hā, "Get you down, both of you, together" [20:123]. If the snake account is true, it is merely a follower of Iblis.

Here Ibn Kathir gives a valuable methodological aside. Some commentators name the exact spots on earth where each of them landed — but these details come from the *Isrāʼīliyyāt*, the Israelite tales inherited from earlier communities, and "only Allah knows if they are true." His principle deserves quoting: if knowing those locations had benefited people in religion or worldly life, Allah would have mentioned them in His Book and His Messenger ﷺ would have mentioned them too. Silence in revelation is itself a signal that the detail was not needed.

What Allah *does* tell us is what we need: "You will find on earth a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time." Ibn Kathir explains that our earthly residence runs to "known, designated, appointed terms that have been recorded by the Pen, counted by Predestination and written in the First Record." The exile is not chaos; every lifespan on this earth was written before we arrived.

**Ayah 25** then compresses the entire human story into three clauses: "There you will live, there you will die, and from it you will be brought out." Ibn Kathir pairs it with its twin: "Thereof We created you, and into it We shall return you, and from it We shall bring you out once again" [20:55]. The earth is dwelling, grave, and womb of resurrection all at once. On the Day of Resurrection, he writes, Allah will gather the first and last of His creatures and reward or punish each according to his or her deeds. The passage that began in Paradise thus ends by pointing back toward it — the road home runs through this earth, through death, and through the Gathering.

## What the passage asks of us

Three things, each drawn directly from the text. First, know the enemy's method: he rarely says "disobey"; he reinterprets Allah's commands, and he is willing to swear by Allah while lying — so sincerity of tone is never, by itself, proof of sincere counsel. Second, remember what the temptation actually delivered: the promise was angelhood and immortality; the result was exposure and fig leaves. Third, when you fall — and the believer may indeed "become the victim of deceit" — take the door Allah taught Adam: own the wrong, and ask for forgiveness and mercy rather than mere respite. In Qatādah's report, the one who asked for forgiveness was promised Paradise, and the one who asked only for respite received only that.

passages.title: Children of Adam: clothing, modesty, Satan's snares
passages.tafsir:
## The passage as a whole

These five ayat are the sermon that follows the story. The sūrah has just narrated how Iblīs deceived Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, and Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes that the very first fruit of that deception was the loss of their covering: their garment came off and they began screening themselves with leaves. Now Allah turns from the story to its audience — all of humanity. Twice the call goes out, "O Children of Adam": once to teach what clothing really is (ayah 26), and once to warn that the being who stripped our parents is still at work (ayah 27). Ayah 28 then shows the warning being ignored in real time — the Arabs of the Jāhiliyyah circling the Kaʿbah naked, insisting Allah commanded it; ayah 29 states what Allah actually commands; and ayah 30 closes with the sobering result: humanity divided into two parties, with the misguided party convinced it is the guided one. The thread running through it all is Satan's oldest trick — undressing human beings, physically and spiritually — and Allah's remedy for it.

## Ayah 26: what clothing really is

**"We have sent down upon you clothing…"** The verb is striking: *anzalnā*, "We sent down" — the same verb the Qur'an uses for iron (57:25), which is dug out of the earth. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains that this need not mean dropped ready-made from the sky; it means bestowed in a way in which human ingenuity plays no part at the root. No one manufactures cotton or wool into existence: the mother-material of every garment is purely Allah's creative gift, and only the tailoring is ours — and even the way to that craft was shown by Him. Eyes that see reality, the commentary says, see every dress as a gift sent from the heavens.

**Two garments, then a third.** The clothing *yuwārī sawʾātikum* — *yuwārī* is from *muwārāt*, "to cover, conceal," and *sawʾāt* (plural of *sawʾah*) are those parts of the body whose exposure every human being, by nature, feels to be shameful. Ibn Kathir explains the pair in the ayah: *libās* is the clothing that covers the private parts — the essential; *rīsh* is outer adornment used for beautification — the complementary. Ibn Jarir even included furniture and outer clothes under *rīsh*. Allah did not stop at bare necessity; He clothed His servants in beauty and dignity too.

Maʿārif adds two observations. First, the address is to all children of Adam, not Muslims alone — a sharp pointer that covering the body is both a human need and a natural desire, observed without distinction of religion or community. The claim that the first man roamed naked and only "evolved" into dress is, on the Qur'an's telling of Adam's story, patently false: modesty has been with mankind from the very beginning. Second, dress is one of the lines separating man from animal. An animal's covering is naturally made a part of its body, serving protection from the weather or beautification; no elaborate arrangement is made for covering its shame as such — though even there, the commentary observes, particular body parts are so formed and placed that they are not left totally exposed, some screened by a tail, others by other obstructers of view. And coming straight after the account of Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, this mention of dress carries a signal: for human beings, nakedness — the exposure of one's shame before others — is a mark of abject disgrace and indecency at its worst, and an antecedent to all sorts of evils and disorders.

## "And the clothing of taqwā — that is best"

In the well-known reading of the ayah, this is a fresh sentence: everyone knows the two physical garments, but there is a third kind of dress, and it is the best of all. (In another reading, noted in Maʿārif, the word joins to "We sent down," making taqwā a third thing sent down.) What is this garment? Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUrwah ibn Zubayr explained the dress of taqwā — a technical term meaning the fear of Allah that guards a person from sin — as right conduct, good deeds and fear of Allah. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, quoted by Ibn Kathir, put it beautifully: "When one fears Allah, Allah covers his errors. Hence the 'libās of taqwā.'" Just as cloth conceals the body's shame, taqwā conceals a person's weaknesses and moral shortcomings, and delivers him from immediate hardships and ultimate losses.

And the rule works in reverse. Ibn Jarir reports from ʿUthmān al-Ghanī (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ swore by Allah: whatever a person does in secret, Allah wraps that deed around him like a sheet and announces it — its good if it was good, its evil if it was evil — and then he recited this very ayah. The one who abandons taqwā will be exposed no matter how carefully he covers up; the person of taqwā is covered by Allah Himself.

**Dress in the service of taqwā.** Maʿārif draws the threads together: the real purpose of physical dress is to help achieve taqwā, and taqwā should show in how one dresses. Concretely: the parts that must be covered are fully covered; the garment is not so tight that the body looks naked in outline; it carries no flair of pride or arrogance, but reflects modesty and humility; it is not extravagant; men's dress is not feminine nor women's masculine — something odious in Allah's sight; and one does not abandon the established norms of one's community in imitation of others. Maʿārif goes as far as to say that when Satan made his first assault on the human body-cover, the Sharīʿah answered by making the covering of the body the first duty after īmān itself — before even Ṣalāh and Ṣawm. Hence Sayyidnā Fārūq al-Aʿẓam — that is, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) — reports that the Prophet ﷺ taught that whoever wears a new dress should recite: "Praise be to Allah who gave me clothes with which I am to cover the cover-worthy parts of my body and look handsome with it in my life." And he ﷺ also said that a person who wears a new dress and gives the old one away in charity to someone poor and needy comes under the protection and patronage of Allah in all states of his life and death (cited by Ibn Kathir from the Musnad of Ahmad). Both purposes of dress — covering and adornment — appear in that duʿāʾ. The ayah ends: "That is among the signs of Allah, that they may take heed." Clothing itself is an āyah, a sign, if we would only read it.

## Ayah 27: the enemy who sees you

"O Children of Adam, do not let Satan put you to trial as he expelled your parents from Paradise, stripping them of their garment to show them their shame." Ibn Kathir pauses on the sheer depth of this hatred: Iblīs plotted to move Ādam from the dwelling of comfort to the dwelling of hardship and fatigue — this worldly life — and to have his private parts uncovered after they had been hidden. He then cites the parallel ayah: "Will you take him and his offspring as protectors instead of Me, when they are enemies to you? What an evil exchange for the wrongdoers!" (18:50). The enmity is ancient, personal, and permanent; Maʿārif says it must never be lost sight of, in anything we do, under any circumstance.

Then comes the unsettling clause: "he sees you — he and his *qabīl* — from where you do not see them." *Qabīl* means company or group (the same root gives *qabīlah*, tribe). An enemy who watches unseen has every tactical advantage, so the chances of falling to his deception are strong. But the passage immediately drains the fear: "We have made the satans allies of those who do not believe" — implying, as Maʿārif notes, that for believers who keep turning to Allah, Satan's wily web is much too weak, and staying out of it is not difficult at all. Some righteous elders gave the remedy in one line: against an enemy who sees us while we cannot see him, come under the protection of the One who sees him while he cannot see Him.

Maʿārif adds a precise note from Rūḥ al-Maʿānī: the statement that humans cannot see the satans describes the general rule and habit, not an absolute impossibility — as when jinn came to the Prophet ﷺ, asked questions and embraced Islam, which appears in authentic narrations of hadith.

## Ayah 28: the trick still working — the naked ṭawāf

Now the passage shows Satan's project succeeding in the Arabia of the Prophet's ﷺ own day. Mujahid reports that the idolaters used to circle the Kaʿbah naked, saying, "We perform ṭawāf as our mothers gave birth to us." Ibn Kathir fills in the picture: all the Arabs except Quraysh — who were known as al-Ḥums — held that one could not make ṭawāf in clothes in which one had disobeyed Allah. So a pilgrim either borrowed a garment from a man of al-Ḥums, or discarded a brand-new garment after the ṭawāf, never to be worn again — or, lacking either, went round the House naked. Even women did so, usually at night, one of them covering herself with a scrap and chanting that whatever appeared of her, she did not permit to be looked at. Maʿārif observes the tragic absurdity: so devoid of sense had they become that it never occurred to them that circling the House naked was far more contrary to etiquette — and to human dignity itself — than any garment could be.

When challenged, they gave two defences: "We found our fathers doing it," and "Allah has commanded it for us." The Qur'an does not even dignify the first with an answer here. Maʿārif explains why: blind following of ancestors is self-evidently no argument — the forefathers of the world's peoples did contradictory things, so this logic would validate every error on earth at once. The second claim, however, is answered with force, because it is a lie against Allah: "Say: Allah never commands *fāḥishah*." The word — explained in Maʿārif from Mazhari — denotes an evil so extreme that its ugliness is loud and clear to common sense and sound taste; here, by most commentators, it is this very naked ṭawāf. Commanding such a thing is against Allah's wisdom and against His being the Purest of the pure. Then the warning: "Do you say about Allah what you do not know?" To attribute anything to anyone without evidence is effrontery and injustice; to attribute it falsely to Allah is a crime whose magnitude cannot be imagined. (Maʿārif is careful to add that the ijtihād of qualified scholars deducing rulings from the Qur'an's own words does not fall under this verse — that work operates under the authority of the revealed text itself.)

## Ayah 29: what Allah actually commands

Against their invented religion, the Prophet ﷺ is told to declare the real one: "My Lord has commanded *al-qisṭ*" — justice, balance, moderation; conduct that neither falls short of the appointed limits nor exceeds them. Under this one word, says Maʿārif, come all the acts of worship and all the injunctions of the Sharīʿah.

Two specific commands follow, answering exactly the two dimensions the naked ṭawāf corrupted. First, "set your faces aright at every *masjid*" — most commentators take *masjid* here in the sense of *sajdah*, prostration and worship: be correct and properly oriented in every act of worship. It can also mean keeping one's orientation to the Qiblah, and, at its broadest, subordinating everything one says and does to Allah's command with a stance that never wavers. This is the outward, bodily dimension. Second, "call upon Him, making the religion sincerely His" — the inward dimension: worship purified of every partner, even of the hidden shirk (*al-shirk al-khafiyy*) of showing off. Ibn Kathir compresses this into the two conditions without which Allah does not accept any deed: it must be correct — in conformity with the Law the Messengers brought — and it must be free of shirk. Maʿārif draws the lasting lesson: outward obedience without sincerity is not enough, and inward sincerity without following the Sharīʿah is not enough; whoever splits "Sharīʿah" from "Ṭarīqah" (the spiritual path) as though one could suffice without the other has fallen into a gaping error.

**"As He began you, so you shall return."** The scholars differed over this clause, and Ibn Kathir lays out both readings. Mujahid, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatādah took it as the bodily resurrection: He created you from nothing, and after you perish He will bring you back. Ibn Jarir preferred the explanation of ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam — as He created you in the beginning, He will bring you back in the end — supporting it with the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, collected in the Two Sahihs, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "O people, you will be gathered to Allah barefooted, naked and uncircumcised — 'As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it.'" In a passage about clothing, the reminder lands with full weight: we return to Allah as uncovered as we began. Ibn ʿAbbās, in another report, read it with the next ayah: Allah began the sons of Adam as some believers and some disbelievers, and will return them on the Day of Resurrection the same way — which Ibn Kathir supports with the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd recorded by al-Bukhari, that deeds may run one way until "that which was written in the Book takes precedence." And he balances it with the fitrah texts: the hadith of Abu Hurayrah in the Two Sahihs, "Every child is born upon the fitrah — it is his parents who make him a Jew, a Christian or a Zoroastrian," and Muslim's hadith of ʿIyāḍ bin Ḥimār: "Allah says, 'I created My servants ḥunafāʾ (pure monotheists), but the devils came to them and deviated them from their religion.'" Every soul was created able to recognize its Lord and worship Him alone; Satan's whole enterprise, from Eden to the Kaʿbah, is deviation from that original nature — while Allah's decree will certainly come to pass in His creation.

Maʿārif notes one more subtlety: the ayah says *taʿūdūn*, "you will return," rather than "We shall bring you back" — a hint at how effortless the resurrection is for Allah's perfect power. And placing this reminder here has a purpose: it is the living certainty of the Last Day, and of reward and punishment, that makes the difficult easy and the painful bearable — without that gripping awareness, no advice and no law can hold a human being back.

## Ayah 30: error that feels like guidance

The passage ends with the division: "A group He has guided, and a group deserved to be in error — because they took the satans as allies instead of Allah, while they think they are guided." Allah's guidance was open to all; these people turned from it, followed the satans, and were then led to think their sickness was health and their error guidance.

Ibn Jarir draws from this a decisive point of creed: the ayah refutes those who claim that Allah punishes no one for a wrong he sincerely believes in until correct knowledge reaches him and he obstinately rejects it. If sincerity alone excused, there would be no difference between the misguided group — who genuinely believe they are guided — and the group that truly is; yet Allah has distinguished them "in both name and judgement." Maʿārif states it plainly: ignorance of the Sharīʿah is no valid excuse, because Allah gave every person reason to tell true from false, and did not leave us to reason alone — He sent prophets and books that made right and wrong all too clear. The fault of the sincere-but-wrong is that they never honestly compared their inherited way with what the prophets taught. One narrow door of excuse remains: a person who truly strove his utmost in the quest for truth and still failed to find it may be excusable with Allah — as Imam al-Ghazali held in Al-Tafriqah Bayn al-Islam wa al-Zandaqah. But "everyone around me does it" and "it feels right" — the very arguments of the naked ṭawāf — save no one.

## Living it

The passage asks four things of a believer. Treat your clothing as an āyah: wear it to cover, to look decent, and never in pride, extravagance or imitation that strips it of its purpose. Above it, put on the better garment — right conduct and the fear of Allah — knowing that Allah covers the one who fears Him and exposes the one who does not. Treat Satan as a real, watching enemy whose only sufficient answer is to come under the protection of the One who watches him. And accept no religious practice on the strength of custom or feeling alone: Allah commands justice, correct worship and sincerity — and to Him, as we began, we return.

passages.title: Lawful adornment and what Allah truly forbids
passages.tafsir:
# Lawful adornment and what Allah truly forbids (7:31–34)

This passage corrects two mirror-image errors at once: forbidding on yourself what Allah has made lawful, and freely committing what He has actually forbidden. The pagans of Makkah did both — they circled the Kaʿbah naked and starved themselves of good food as acts of "reverence", while indulging in shamelessness, oppression and shirk. Ayat 31–33 untangle that inversion — take your adornment, eat and drink, and know precisely what your Lord *has* prohibited — and ayah 34 seals it with the warning that every community's respite has a fixed end.

## The scene these ayat answer

To feel the force of ayah 31, picture the practice it abolished. Muslim, An-Nasaʾi and Ibn Jarir record (in Ibn Jarir's wording) from Ibn ʿAbbas: "The idolators used to go around the House while naked, both men and women, men in the day and women by night." A woman making tawaf would even say, "Today, a part or all of it will be unveiled, but whatever is exposed of it, I do not allow." They had convinced themselves that stripping off their clothes honoured the House of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the companion custom: during the days of Hajj they would also refuse good food — butter oil, milk, wholesome things — eating only enough to stay alive, treating self-deprivation as worship.

So Allah answered both inventions in a single breath: **"Take your adornment to every masjid, and eat and drink — but do not be extravagant"** (ayah 31). Modesty before Allah is not achieved by nakedness, and devotion is not achieved by refusing His provision.

## "Take your adornment" — what zīnah asks of us

The word choice matters. Allah did not merely say "cover yourselves"; He called clothing **zīnah** — adornment, what looks good on you. Ibn ʿAbbas explained it as wearing "clean, proper clothes that cover the private parts," and said people were commanded to wear their best clothes for every prayer; Mujahid, ʿAtaʾ, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Qatadah and many of the Salaf said the same. Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah and the Sunnah together encourage wearing one's best clothes for prayer — especially Friday and ʿId — along with perfume (for men) and the siwāk, as completions of adornment. He cites the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad — also collected by Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, with At-Tirmidhi grading it "Hasan Sahih" — in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "Wear white clothes, for it is among your best clothes, and also wrap your dead with it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the legal weight. Although the ayah came down about naked tawaf, the scholars of tafsir and law unanimously hold that a ruling revealed about a particular event is not restricted to that event — what counts is the generality of the wording. From that generality the majority of the Sahabah, Tabiʿin and the mujtahid Imams deduced that just as naked tawaf is forbidden, **prayer without proper covering is invalid** — for the Prophet ﷺ said that the tawaf of the House is itself salah, and most commentators understood "masjid" in the ayah to mean the act of prostration itself. Hadith then supplies the detail the Qurʼan states briefly: a man's *satr* (the area that must be concealed) is from the navel to the knees; a woman's is her whole body except the face, palms and feet — and a hadith in Tirmidhi states that an adult woman's salah is not permissible without proper head and body covering. The exemption of a woman's face in prayer, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to add, does not mean she may move freely unveiled before non-mahram men without a valid excuse.

Beyond the obligatory minimum, the word zīnah grounds a further etiquette: since Allah asked for *adornment*, not bare functionality, praying bare-headed or in clothing you would be embarrassed to wear in front of guests — an undershirt alone, a rolled-up sleeve — is *makruh* (disliked). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the logic memorably: if no one would appear before friends like that, how can it be a fitting way to stand before the Master of all the worlds? It records that Hasan رضي الله عنه would wear his best dress for salah, saying: Allah loves beauty, so I dress beautifully for my Lord, for He has said, "Take your adornment to every masjid."

## "Eat and drink, but waste not" — the anatomy of isrāf

The second command is as liberating as it is restraining. Al-Bukhari cites Ibn ʿAbbas: **"Eat what you wish and wear what you wish, as long as you avoid two things: extravagance and arrogance."** Al-Jassas, in Ahkam al-Qurʼan, drew a foundational legal principle from the fact that "eat and drink" names no object: in Arabic diction, omitting the object signals generality — so *everything* edible is lawful unless the Shariʿah itself proves a specific prohibition. Lawfulness is the default; prohibition needs evidence.

The boundary is **isrāf** — literally, crossing the limit — and the sources show it cuts in several directions at once. Ibn Jarir's summary is the sharpest: Allah does not love those who trespass His limits in either direction — "those who go to the extreme over what He has allowed, allow what He has prohibited, or *prohibit what He has allowed*." So eating the haram is isrāf; but so is treating the halal as haram without a valid excuse — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Ibn Kathir, Mazhari and Ruh al-Maʿāni) calls this too "a rebellion against Divine Law and a very grave sin." Overeating past one's need is isrāf; so is under-eating to the point of weakness or death, which the Shariʿah counts as sin. Even being consumed by food — living to eat — is isrāf, as is compulsively gratifying every craving: the Prophet ﷺ said, as reported by Ibn Majah from Anas, "It is also an isrāf that one eats everything one desires."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān condenses all this into eight rulings from this half-ayah: eating as needed is obligatory; everything is halal until proven otherwise; consuming the prohibited is isrāf; declaring the halal to be haram is isrāf and a grave sin; eating beyond fullness is impermissible; eating so little that one cannot fulfil one's duties is isrāf; obsessing over food is isrāf; and one need not have whatever one happens to crave.

**From the Sunnah.** Imam Ahmad recorded — An-Nasaʾi and At-Tirmidhi also collected it, At-Tirmidhi grading it "Hasan" (or "Hasan Sahih") — that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The Son of Adam will not fill a pot worse for himself than his stomach. It is enough for the Son of Adam to eat a few bites that strengthen his spine. If he must have more, then a third for food, a third for drink, and a third for his breathing." ʿUmar al-Faruq رضي الله عنه counselled the same: avoid excess in eating, for it spoils the body, breeds disease and slackens activity — moderation is health. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates (from Ruh al-Maʿāni and Mazhari) the famous exchange in which Harun al-Rashid's Christian physician claimed the Qurʼan contained no medicine, and ʿAli ibn Husayn ibn al-Waqidi replied that Allah placed the whole of medicine in half a verse: "Eat and drink and do not be extravagant" — to which the physician conceded, "Your Book and your Prophet have left no medicine for Galen."

## Ayah 32 — who dared forbid what Allah made beautiful?

Ayah 31 corrected the practice; ayah 32 confronts its premise. **"Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has produced for His servants, and the good things of provision?"** The question is a rebuke: declaring things halal or haram is the sole right of the One who created them. Ibn Kathir says the ayah refutes all who prohibit food, drink or clothing "according to their own understanding, without relying on what Allah has legislated." Living in tattered rags despite having means, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists, is no teaching of Islam.

The lived Sunnah proves it. When his means allowed, the Prophet ﷺ wore the best of dress — one narration mentions a ridāʾ (upper wrap) worth a thousand dirhams. Imam Malik dressed elegantly and would give each day's outfit away to a poor student after a single wearing. The Prophet ﷺ said that when Allah extends His blessing to a servant, He loves to see the effect of that blessing on him — so dressing well within one's means is a form of gratitude, while deliberately wearing worn-out clothes despite ability is a kind of ingratitude. Two cautions guard this: no showing off, and no pride. And where the Prophet ﷺ, ʿUmar and others did wear patched garments, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why: they spent their income on the poor and on the cause of religion, leaving little for themselves, and as leaders they kept a simple bearing so the wealthy would take the lesson and the poor would not feel diminished. The Sufi masters' austerity for beginners follows the same logic — a temporary medicine to break the ego's cravings, not a claim that abandoning good things is itself rewarded.

Then the ayah's remarkable clause: these good things are **"for those who believe in the life of this world, exclusively theirs on the Day of Resurrection."** In this world the table is open to all — the disbeliever eats from it too, for this world is the venue of deeds, not of rewards. But the commentators among the Sahabah and Tabiʿin drew out three complementary meanings: the blessings are by right the believers' even now, others merely sharing in them; for the disbeliever these same blessings become his nemesis in the Hereafter, as Ibn ʿAbbas explained; and worldly enjoyment is always laced with striving, anxiety and fear of loss — only in the Hereafter will the believer taste blessing in absolute purity, with no toil before it and no worry after it. Paradise, Ibn Kathir states plainly, is prohibited to the disbelievers.

## Ayah 33 — what Allah has truly forbidden

Having cleared away the invented prohibitions, ayah 33 gives the real list — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes it covers "almost all kinds of prohibitions and sins," whether of belief or of conduct, against oneself or against the rights of others, precisely because Jahiliyyah society was steeped in every one of them. The ayah names five things:

- **Al-fawāḥish** — shameful, immoral deeds, "what is apparent of them and what is hidden." Imam Ahmad recorded — and it is in the Two Sahihs — that the Prophet ﷺ said: "None is more jealous than Allah, and this is why He prohibited fawāḥish, committed openly or in secret. And none likes praise more than Allah."
- **Ithm** — sin. As-Suddi and Mujahid explain it as disobedience generally; Ibn Kathir refines it as the sin one commits against oneself.
- **Baghy bi-ghayr al-ḥaqq** — transgression without right: oppression, the sins that violate other people's rights. Ibn Kathir pairs the two: ithm is against yourself, baghy is against others, and Allah prohibited both.
- **Shirk** — associating partners with Allah "for which He has sent down no authority."
- **Saying about Allah what you do not know** — lies and inventions in creed, such as claiming a son for Allah.

Of the last two — shirk and forging lies against Allah — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says simply that their being grave sins is quite evident.

Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān exposes the pagans' twofold ignorance — the double error this whole passage has been correcting: they denied themselves the good things Allah had made lawful, and embraced the very things He had forbidden — losing the blessings of this world and of the next together. And it draws a sobering general lesson: excess (*ghuluww*) in religion and self-invented practice (*bidʿah*) habitually make people heedless of religion's actual core, so the harm is double — the innovation is itself a sin, and it crowds out the true religion of Allah and the genuine way of His Prophet ﷺ.

## Ayah 34 — the appointed term

Why, then, do those who invert Allah's law seem to flourish? Ayah 34 answers: **"For every community there is an appointed term; when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor advance it."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains this as Allah's customary way: in His infinite mercy He grants sinners a long rein, giving them time to stop — but the length of that rein is fixed in His knowledge, and when the moment arrives it comes exactly on time. The punishment may descend in this world; if not, it waits just beyond death.

There is a fine linguistic point in "nor advance it." The real thrust of the sentence is that there will be *no delay* once the term arrives; "nor advance it" is added as the natural companion phrase that completes the idiom — like asking a shopkeeper "is that your last price, more or less?" when only the "less" is really meant. The threat is one-directional: the respite will not be extended.

## Living it

The passage leaves a believer with a clear, balanced posture. Dress with dignity — best of all when standing before Allah — covering what must be covered and adding beauty within your means, without display or pride. Receive Allah's provision with gratitude and moderation: neither the indulgence that fills the stomach past need, nor the invented piety that calls His halal haram. Reserve the word "forbidden" for what Allah Himself forbade — indecency, sin, oppression, shirk, and speaking about Him without knowledge. And do not mistake the delay of consequences for their absence: the term is appointed, and it keeps perfect time.

passages.title: Messengers to Adam's children: deniers enter Hell
passages.tafsir:
This passage is Allah's charge to the whole human family — "O Children of Adam" — laying down the terms on which history will run: messengers will come from among you, and every soul will end on one of exactly two paths. The five ayat hold together as a single arc. Ayah 35 states the covenant and the promise; ayah 36 states the threat; ayah 37 follows the deniers from their comfortable lives to the moment the angels seize their souls; and ayat 38–39 follow them further still, into the Fire — the scene Ibn Kathir titles "People of the Fire will dispute and curse each other."

## The address: "O Children of Adam"

This call — yā banī Ādam — speaks to all of Adam's descendants at once, believer and denier alike. In Ibn Kathir's commentary it is read in sequence with the words that come just before it (ayah 34): "every Ummah has its appointed term; when their term comes, neither can they delay it nor can they advance it an hour" — every Ummah meaning, as Ibn Kathir glosses, "each generation and nation," destined for its fixed span. Then, in Ibn Kathir's words, "Allah then warned the Children of Adam that He sent to them Messengers who conveyed to them His Ayat" — His revelations. And in sending them, Ibn Kathir observes, Allah conveyed both good news and warning together; the next two clauses deliver each in turn.

The terms themselves are simple. Messengers will come *minkum* — "from among yourselves" — reciting Allah's Ayat, and everything turns on how each soul receives them.

**The mercy of respite.** On that appointed term of ayah 34, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses an obvious objection head-on: those "basking in the sunshine of the blessings of Allah" while sinning openly should not misread their comfort. It is the customary practice of Allah that He, in His infinite mercy, "keeps granting a long leash to sinners so that they would somehow stop doing what they do" — but the term of that leash stands determined in Allah's ultimate knowledge, and when that time comes, it just comes, "neither too late nor too soon." Sometimes the punishment descends right here in this world; if not, "it waits to receive them soon after their death." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note on the wording: saying the term will be "neither late nor early" is like asking a salesperson, "Is that your last price, more or less?" — the real question is only about the lower price. The real point here is that there will be no delay after the appointed time; "before" is mentioned alongside "late" to bring it closer to common comprehension.

## The two paths (ayat 35–36)

**The path of safety.** "Whosoever has Taqwa and becomes righteous — on them shall be no fear nor shall they grieve." Ibn Kathir explains the pair concretely: it means "abandoning the prohibitions and performing acts of obedience." One is restraint, the other is action; the promise embraces both. And the promise is exactly what the ayah says: no fear, and no grief.

**The path of ruin.** Ayah 36 names the opposite pair: those who *rejected* Allah's Ayat and treated them with *arrogance*. Ibn Kathir's gloss is precise and searching: "their hearts denied the Ayat and they were too arrogant to abide by them." Rejection begins in the heart, and arrogance is what refuses to abide by the truth. For such people the verdict is total: "they are the dwellers of the Fire, they will abide therein forever" — Ibn Kathir adds, "without end to their dwelling in it."

## The portion that runs out (ayah 37)

Ayah 37 opens with a challenge: "Who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or rejects His Ayat?" Ibn Kathir spells it out — none is more unjust. These are the two crimes against revelation: inventing a lie about Allah, and rejecting the Ayat that He has revealed.

Yet these very people often prosper — and Ibn Kathir's own heading for this passage names the paradox: "Idolators enjoy their destined share in this life, but will lose their supporters upon death." What is the "appointed portion" that "will reach them from the Book (of Decrees)"? Ibn Kathir cites the early commentator Muhammad bin Ka'b Al-Qurazi — a view shared by Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam: it refers to each person's *deeds, allotted provisions, and age*. The denier's written share of this world will reach him in full — and then the account closes. Ibn Kathir links this to Allah's words elsewhere: "Verily, those who invent a lie against Allah, will never be successful. (A brief) enjoyment in this world! And then unto Us will be their return, then We shall make them taste the severest torment because they used to disbelieve" (10:69–70), and "We let them enjoy for a little while" (31:23–24).

**The moment of seizure.** Then the ayah moves, without pause, to the deathbed.
