"Our messengers" here, Ibn Kathir explains, are the angel of death and his assistants, who come to capture the idolators' souls to take them to Hellfire. The angels horrify them with a question that is really a sentence: *Where are the so-called partners of Allah whom you used to invoke and worship instead of Him? Call them, so that they save you from what you are suffering.* And the answer: ḍallū ʿannā — "They have vanished and deserted us." Ibn Kathir: we have lost them, and thus we do not hope in their benefit or aid. So "they will bear witness against themselves, that they were disbelievers" — in Ibn Kathir's words, they will admit and proclaim it against themselves.

## Inside the Fire: the cursing of the generations (ayat 38–39)

Ayah 38 opens with Allah's own command to those who, in Ibn Kathir's summary, "associate others with Him, invent lies about Him, and reject His Ayat": *Enter in the company of nations who passed away before you, of men and Jinn, into the Fire.* Ibn Kathir notes the force of "in the company of nations": you enter among your likes, those "similar to you in conduct." Misguidance has a lineage, and in the Fire the whole lineage is reunited.

**Every nation curses its sister.** Each arriving nation curses the one that went before it — "its sister nation," a bitter word, for these were communities bound by the same false path. Ibn Kathir connects this to the words of Al-Khalil, Prophet Ibrahim, peace be upon him: "But on the Day of Resurrection, you shall deny each other" (29:25), and to Sūrat al-Baqarah's scene of the followed declaring themselves innocent of their followers, while the followers wish vainly for one more chance to disown them in return — "Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them. And they will never get out of the Fire" (2:166–167).

**The followers' plea.** When all are gathered together in the Fire, "the last of them" — the nation of followers that enter last — speak against "the first of them." Ibn Kathir explains the ordering: the earlier nations were worse criminals than those who followed them, which is why they entered the Fire first; so their followers complain against them to Allah, because they were the ones who misguided them from the correct path: "Our Lord! These misled us, so give them a double torment of the Fire" — multiply their share of the torment. It is the plea of the imitator: *we only did what they taught us.* Ibn Kathir cites the parallel plea in 33:66–68, where the people of the Fire say, "Our Lord! Verily, we obeyed our chiefs and our great ones, and they misled us from the (right) way. Our Lord! Give them a double torment."

**The answer.** Allah's reply is devastating in its evenness: "For each one there is double (torment), but you know not." Ibn Kathir paraphrases: We did what you asked, and recompensed each according to their deeds. For the misleaders, Allah says elsewhere: "Those who disbelieved and hinder (men) from the path of Allah, for them We will add torment" (16:88); "they shall bear their own loads, and other loads besides their own" (29:13), including "the burdens of those whom they misled without knowledge" (16:25). And yet the followers, too, hear "for each one there is double" — each party recompensed according to its own deeds.

**The leaders' retort (ayah 39).** Then the first speak back to the last — the followed to the followers: "You were not better than us, so taste the torment for what you used to earn." Ibn Kathir records As-Suddi's explanation: *you were led astray as we were led astray.* The closing phrase seals it: the torment is "for what you used to earn" — each party's own earning. Ibn Kathir rounds off the scene with its mirror in Sūrat Sabaʾ (34:32–33), where the arrogant and the weak trade the same accusations — "Nay, but you were criminals" — "Nay, but it was your plotting by night and day" — while each party conceals its own regrets upon beholding the torment: "Are they requited aught except what they used to do?"

## What the passage asks of us

Read as a whole, the passage dismantles the two great excuses a soul might carry to the grave.

The first excuse is *time*: nothing has happened to me, so nothing will. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's commentary on the appointed term answers that prosperity in sin is not acquittal but respite — a mercy extended so that the sinner "would somehow stop" — and when the determined time comes, it comes neither too late nor too soon. Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 37 completes the picture: the idolators enjoy their destined share in this life — deeds, provisions, and age all reach them from the Book of Decrees — and then the angels arrive, and the so-called partners have vanished and deserted them.

The second excuse is *company*: everyone around me believed this; my teachers, my elders, my society. Ayat 38–39 answer that this defence will be made — at the top of the followers' voices — and will not save them. The plea against the misleaders is granted, "for each one there is double," yet each is recompensed according to their deeds, and the retort still lands: "taste the torment for what you used to earn."

Against both stands the quiet offer of ayah 35, still open: Taqwa and righteousness — in Ibn Kathir's words, abandoning the prohibitions and performing acts of obedience — and the result is the only security that matters: no fear, and no grief.

passages.title: Heaven's gates closed; the believers' Paradise
passages.tafsir:
# The Two Endings (7:40–43)

This passage is the settling of accounts for the pledge described just before it (ayat 35–37): every human being, before entering this world, pledged that when Allah's prophets came with guidance they would listen and obey. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that these four ayat now show what became of the two groups who answered that pledge differently — ayat 40–41 the deniers and criminals, ayat 42–43 the believers who kept it. What holds the passage together is its perfect symmetry: a gate that will never open against a door made easy to enter; a bed of fire against rivers flowing beneath; souls thrown back down against hearts washed clean. The whole passage is really the story of two doors.

## The sealed gate (ayat 40–41)

Allah says of those who denied His signs and were arrogant towards them: *"for them the gates of the heavens will not be opened."* Ibn Kathir records two explanations from the early authorities, both traced to Ibn ʿAbbās:

**Their deeds and supplications will not ascend.** This is the view of Mujahid, Saʿid bin Jubayr and Ibn ʿAbbās. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Al-Bahr Al-Muhit) spells out what this means: their prayers go unanswered, and their deeds are barred from reaching *ʿIlliyyīn* — the place named in Surah Al-Mutaffifin (83:18–21) where the deeds of Allah's righteous servants are kept preserved. Maʿārif points to another ayah in this connection: one's good words are taken up to Allah, and one's good deeds carry them there. The denier's rise nowhere.

**Their souls will not be admitted.** This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās by Ad-Dahhak, and also held by As-Suddi and others: at death, the doors of the heavens are shut in the face of the disbeliever's soul.

Ibn Jurayj combined the two: the gates open neither for their deeds nor for their souls — and Ibn Kathir notes that this explanation gathers both meanings together, and Allah knows best.

In support of the second meaning, Ibn Kathir cites from Ibn Jarir a portion of a hadith of al-Barāʾ, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ described the capturing of the soul of the *fājir* — the wicked sinner or disbeliever. The angels ascend with it, and no gathering of angels does it pass but they ask, "Whose wicked soul is this?" It is answered, "The soul of so-and-so," using the worst names he was called in this life. When they reach the lower heaven, they ask that its door be opened for the soul — and it is not opened. The Prophet ﷺ then recited this very ayah: *"For them the gates of heaven will not be opened."* Ibn Kathir notes that this is part of a long hadith which was also recorded by Abu Dawud, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a fuller summary of this hadith of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, reported in detail by Abu Dawud, Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Imam Ahmad. The Prophet ﷺ, seated by a grave that was not yet ready at the funeral of an Ansari Companion, described the two deaths. When death comes to a believing servant of Allah, angels with white, radiant faces come down with the shroud and fragrance of heaven; the angel of death addresses his *rūḥ* (spirit, soul): "O soul at peace, come out to receive the forgiveness and pleasure of your Rabb" — and it comes out nice and easy, like water poured from a leather water-bag. Every group of angels the escorts meet on the way asks, "Whose sacred Ruh is it?" — and he is introduced by the name and title by which he was respectfully known in the world. At the first heaven the gate is opened; more angels join, heaven after heaven, as far as the seventh, where Allah commands: write the record of My servant's deeds in ʿIlliyyīn. But when death comes to a disbeliever and denier, angels of dark and terrifying profile descend carrying a coarse piece of ragged rug; his soul is drawn out as if a thorny branch were being pulled through wet wool, and its stench is deadlier than that of a spoiled dead animal. The angels met on the way ask, "Whose evil Ruh is this?" — and he is named by the worst of the names he bore in the world. At the first heaven they ask for the gate to be opened, *and it is not opened.* The command comes to keep his record in *Sijjīn*, where the record of the disobedient is maintained, and his soul is thrown away, returning to the grave.

So the ayah is not an abstraction. It describes a real turning-away at a real door — either of a lifetime of deeds that never arrive, or of a soul refused entry at the very threshold of its journey.

Then the impossibility is stated in everyday terms: *"And they will not enter Paradise until the jamal passes through the eye of the needle."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the wording: *yalij* is from *wulūj*, to enter a narrow opening; *samm* is the eye of a needle; *jamal* is the camel — Ibn Masʿūd said it is the male camel. Mujahid and ʿIkrimah report that Ibn ʿAbbās used to recite it as *jummal* — a thick rope. On either reading the image is the same: the camel is a big animal, and its entry into the eye of a needle is functionally impossible. Maʿārif draws the conclusion plainly — their entry into Paradise is equally impossible, which is a way of saying that their punishment in Hell is everlasting.

And that punishment envelops them completely: *"Theirs will be mihād from the Fire, and over them ghawāsh."* *Mihād* is a place of rest, a bed or floor; *ghawāsh* is the plural of *ghāshiyah*, something that covers — so, as Muhammad bin Kaʿb Al-Qurazi, Ad-Dahhak bin Muzahim and As-Suddi explained, the Fire is beneath them as bedding and above them as coverings. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the terrible eloquence of the image: the bed and the top sheet — the homeliest idiom of rest — will all come from Hell.

Notice, too, the refrain. Ayah 40 closes: *"Thus do We recompense the criminals,"* and ayah 41: *"Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the first refrain seals the deprivation from Paradise, while the second seals the punishment of Hell itself — because it is the more severe of the two.

## The opened door (ayat 42–43)

The scene turns. *"But those who believed and worked righteousness"* — Ibn Kathir notes the pairing: hearts that believed, and limbs and senses that performed good deeds — *"such are the dwellers of Paradise; they will abide therein."*

But between the condition and the reward, Allah inserts a clause of pure mercy: *"We burden no soul beyond its scope."* Why here? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, again citing Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, explains: hearing that Paradise is conditional on good deeds, a person might find it heavy — who can do what is right everywhere, always, in every condition? This clause removes that doubt before it settles. The injunctions of the Shariʿah (the revealed law) are made flexible and easy in every department of life; leaves and concessions are built into every injunction for sickness, weakness, travel and other human needs. Ibn Kathir makes the same point: Allah is telling us that embracing faith and implementing it are *easy*. The gate the deniers found sealed was never a narrow one for those who sought it.

Ayah 43 then gives two portraits of the people of Paradise, and the first is startlingly inward: *"And We shall remove from their breasts any ghill"* — malice, envy, hatred, the residue of old grievances. Before rivers, before dwellings, Allah mentions the purification of hearts. Paradise is not merely a place without pain; it is a company without malice.

The sources describe how this happens. Al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Saʿid Al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that after the believers are saved from the Fire, they will be kept in wait by a bridge (*qanṭarah*) between Paradise and Hellfire, where the transgressions that occurred between them in this world will be judged, until — purified and cleansed — they are given permission to enter Paradise; and he swore, "By He in Whose Hand is my soul," that one of them will be able to find his dwelling in Paradise more surely than he did his home in this world. Tafsir Mazhari — with ʿAllama Al-Suyuti opting for the same view — takes this bridge to be the last part of the Bridge of Sirat, the part closest to Paradise. And in accordance with a hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim, rights are settled there not in money, which no one will possess, but in the currency of deeds: the usurper's good deeds are given to the owner of the right, and when none remain, the sins of the wronged are transferred to the usurper's account. In a hadith, the Prophet ﷺ called the person who did good deeds in his worldly life but remained negligent of the rights of people the greatest pauper — for through that neglect he lost all his good deeds and stood there empty-handed.

Yet Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to add: not everyone must pass through that reckoning. According to what Ibn Kathir and Tafsir Mazhari report, malice may be removed without any settling of scores at all. Some narrations describe a stream after the Sirat whose water removes every mutual malice from the hearts of those who drink; Imam al-Qurtubi reads *"their Lord will give them a pure drink"* (76:21) the same way — that water of Paradise washes all grudges from hearts. As-Suddi, cited by Ibn Kathir, paints the scene at Paradise's very door: a tree with two springs at its trunk — from one they drink, and all hatred is removed from their hearts, for it is the cleansing drink; in the other they bathe, and the brightness of delight radiates from their faces, and ever after they will never be dishevelled or dirty again.

Ibn Kathir preserves a moment that shows how seriously the Companions took this ayah. ʿAli — whose disagreements with fellow Companions had, in this world, reached the limits of war — recited it and said: *I hope that we — ʿUthman, Talhah, Zubayr and I — shall be among those whose hearts will be cleansed of malice before the entry into Paradise.* He did not deny the wounds; he hoped in the ayah that heals them.

The second portrait is the believers' first words on arrival: *"All praise is for Allah who guided us to this; never could we have found guidance had Allah not guided us. The messengers of our Lord came with the truth."* Standing inside everything they ever hoped for, their instinct is not self-congratulation but gratitude — and testimony that the messengers were true.

An-Nasa'i and Ibn Marduwyah (the wording being the latter's) recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: each of the people of Paradise will see his seat in the Fire and say, "Had not Allah guided me!" — and this will cause him to be grateful; and each of the people of the Fire will see his seat in Paradise and say, "Might that Allah had guided me!" — and it will be a cause of anguish for him. This, says Ibn Kathir, explains the announcement that ends the ayah: *"This is the Paradise which you have inherited for what you used to do."* The believers are awarded seats in Paradise that belonged to the people of the Fire — an inheritance.

But how can Paradise be "for what you used to do" when the Prophet ﷺ said — as recorded in the Two Sahihs — "And know that the good deeds of one of you will not admit him into Paradise"? They said, "Not even you, O Allah's Messenger?" He said, "Not even I, unless Allah grants it to me out of His mercy and favor." Ibn Kathir resolves it: by your good deeds you earned Allah's mercy, and thus you entered Paradise and took your designated dwellings — deeds are the means, mercy is what admits. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same from the other side: no one reaches Jannah by personal effort alone, because even the effort itself is not within one's control — it too comes only through the grace and mercy of Allah.

Maʿārif closes with a beautiful observation from Imam Raghib al-Isfahani on why the believers call their arrival "guidance." *Hidāyah* — guidance — is another name for finding the way to reach Allah, and its degrees are many, varied and unending. Its lowest degree is deliverance from disbelief and *shirk* (associating partners with Allah) into faith; and because the stages of nearness to Allah never end, no one can ever claim to be beyond the need of guidance — not even the prophets and messengers of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ himself not only taught his people to say *"Guide us in the straight path"* but kept making that prayer himself. Entry into Paradise is here named as guidance because it is the *last station* of guidance — the end of the road the prayer has been asking for all along.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with three quiet disciplines. Guard what rises: it is good words carried by good deeds that ascend to Allah, so send something up. Trust the ease: the condition for Paradise was fitted to your capacity, with concessions built in for every human weakness — despair over it belongs to the deniers, not to you. And start emptying your heart of *ghill* now: the grudges Allah will one day remove at the qanṭarah are the very ones His righteous servants, like ʿAli, already longed to be rid of — and the rights of people, the hadith warns, are settled in the costly currency of deeds.

passages.title: Exchanges between Paradise, the Fire, and the Heights
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 44–51: Exchanges between Paradise, the Fire, and the Heights

This passage is a sustained conversation across the divide of the Hereafter. Once the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire have reached their final homes, four calls ring out between them — Paradise calls to the Fire (44), a company on the Heights calls to Paradise (46), the Heights call to the Fire (48–49), and finally the Fire calls to Paradise (50). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that although the two abodes "will be far apart from each other in all respects," many verses of the Qur'an confirm that "in between the two places, there will be points from where one could see the other, and engage in an exchange of conversation" — and that such dialogues continue "through almost one section." What binds the ayat together is this exchange of voices, and the strange geography that makes it possible: two abodes utterly separate, yet within earshot of one another.

## The first call: promises proven true (44–45)

The people of Paradise open the exchange: "We have indeed found true what our Lord had promised us; have you also found true what your Lord promised (warned)?" And from the Fire comes the single, devastating answer: "Yes."

Ibn Kathir titles this section "People of Hellfire will feel Anguish upon Anguish", and reads the call as part of how the people of the Fire "will be addressed, chastised and admonished when they take their places in the Fire." He gathers the Qur'an's parallel scenes: in Sūrat as-Sāffāt (37:55–59) a man in Paradise looks down and sees his old disbelieving companion in the midst of the Fire — "By Allah! You have nearly ruined me. Had it not been for the grace of my Lord, I would certainly have been among those brought forth" — and in 52:14–16 the angels themselves admonish the deniers: "This is the Fire which you used to belie. Is this magic or do you not see?"

Ibn Kathir then recalls a moment from the Prophet's ﷺ own life that mirrors this ayah exactly. After the battle of Badr, standing over the well into which the slain leaders of Quraysh had been cast, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called them by name — "O Abu Jahl bin Hisham! O 'Utbah bin Rabi'ah! O Shaybah bin Rabi'ah! Have you found what your Lord promised to be true? I certainly found what my Lord has promised me to be true." When 'Umar asked how he could address people who had become rotten carrion, he ﷺ replied: "By He in Whose Hand is my soul! You do not hear what I am saying better than they do, but they cannot reply." The question of ayah 44 was, in a sense, asked once already in this world.

The exchange is sealed by a herald: "Then a crier will proclaim between them: the curse of Allah is on the wrongdoers" — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, "the curse will reside with the wrongdoers." Ayah 45 then defines who these wrongdoers are by three marks: they hindered people from the path of Allah, they "sought to make Allah's path appear crooked and winding, so that no one would follow it," and they disbelieved in the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir draws the connection between the last mark and everything else: because they denied the Meeting with Allah, "they used to discount the seriousness of the evil deeds and statements that they committed, because they did not fear any reckoning or punishment. Therefore, they were and are indeed the worst people in statement and action." Unbelief in accountability is not one sin among others; it is the sin that unlocks all the others.

## The wall and the Heights (46)

Ayah 46 introduces the passage's most distinctive feature: "And between them will be a (barrier) screen and on Al-A'raf will be men, who would recognize all, by their marks."

**The language.** Ibn Jarir explains that *al-Aʿrāf* is the plural of *ʿurf* — the word Arabs use for any elevated piece of land; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that *ʿurf* refers to the top portion of a thing, distinct and recognizable from a distance. As-Suddi offers a second layer: the place is called al-Aʿrāf "because its residents recognize (*Yaʿrifun*) the people" — the name of the place echoes what its people do. Ibn Jarir identifies this *ḥijāb* (barrier) with the wall Allah describes in Sūrat al-Hadīd: "So a wall (*sūr*) will be put up between them, with a gate therein. Inside it will be mercy, and outside it will be torment" (57:13); As-Suddi says of the barrier, "It is the wall, it is Al-A'raf," and Mujahid says it is "a barrier between Paradise and the Fire, a wall that has a gate." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *sūr* is the word primarily used for the fortified security wall built around a major city — and explains the scene of 57:13: the hypocrites, who had been tailing the Muslims, start behind the believers on the Bridge of Sirāt; a dense darkness overtakes them; they beg for a share of the believers' light and are told "Return behind you, then seek light" — the light of Faith and Righteous Deeds could only be acquired in the world now left behind — and then the wall is made to stand between them. The Aʿrāf, then, is the top portion of that wall — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, there will be people at this place on the day of Resurrection who will be seeing the happenings in Paradise and Hell both, and talking to people on both sides.

**Who stands there?** This is where the commentators linger. The view Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls "sound, weighty and acceptable with the majority" — held by Hudhayfah, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and several of the Salaf (the early generations) and later generations — is that these are people whose good and bad deeds came out exactly equal on the Scale. Ibn Jarir records Hudhayfah's description: "Their evil deeds prevented them from qualifying to enter Paradise, and their good deeds qualified them to avoid the Fire. Therefore, they are stopped there on the wall until Allah judges them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites a narration reported by Ibn Marduwayh from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, in which the Prophet ﷺ, asked about the people of the Aʿrāf, described people who took part in jihad without their parents' pleasure and permission and laid down their lives in the way of Allah — their disobedience to their parents stopped them from entering Paradise, and their martyrdom stopped them from entering the Fire. The two reports do not conflict, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains: the second is simply an *example* of the first — one mighty good deed and one grave sin, and the scale sits level.

## Hope on the wall (46–47)

The men on the Heights greet the people of Paradise: *salāmun ʿalaykum* — "and at that time they will not yet have entered it, but they will hope to enter." Al-Hasan, upon reciting this ayah, said: "By Allah! Allah did not put this hope in their hearts, except for an honor that He intends to bestow on them." Hope planted by Allah is itself a promise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over the greeting: the *salām* is the blessed legacy of the Prophet ﷺ — a way of his Sunnah offered in this world, said to the dead while visiting their graves, and, as the Qur'an shows at 13:24 and 39:73, the form of greeting on the plain of Resurrection and in Paradise as well. The people of the Aʿrāf greet with the very words the angels will use when they receive the people of Paradise.

But their state is delicate. In ayah 47, when their eyes are turned toward the people of the Fire, they cry out: "Our Lord! Place us not with the people who are wrongdoers." Ibn 'Abbas explains (as Ad-Dahhak reports): when the people of Al-A'raf look at the people of the Fire and *recognize* them, they will supplicate. Facing one way, they hope; facing the other, they plead not to share the wrongdoers' fate.

## The Heights address the Fire (48–49)

Then the men of the Aʿrāf call to men in the Fire whom they recognize by their marks — Ibn Kathir says these are some of the chiefs of the idolators — with a question that dismantles a whole worldview: "Of what benefit to you was your gathering, and your arrogance?" Your great numbers and wealth, Ibn Kathir paraphrases, did not save you from Allah's torment; rather, you are dwelling in His torment and punishment.

Ayah 49 delivers the passage's great reversal. "Are they those, of whom you swore that Allah would never show them mercy?" — pointing at the very people the arrogant had despised. 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reports from Ibn 'Abbas that this refers to the people of the Aʿrāf themselves. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn Kathir, relates Ibn 'Abbas's explanation of the scene: when all the questions and answers between the people of the Aʿrāf and the people of Paradise and Hell are over, the Lord of all the worlds Himself will address the people of Hell — they had sworn that the people of the Aʿrāf would not be forgiven their sins and would not be shown mercy — and then, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's phrase, "there comes an immediate declaration of His mercy": the people of the Aʿrāf are told, *"Enter Paradise, no fear shall be on you, nor shall you grieve"* — or, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds it, "You should have no fear of what had happened in the past nor should you have any anxiety about the future." The very people whose scales could not tip them into Paradise enter, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, "because of the grace and mercy of Allah Taʿālā" — and the arrogant, who had sworn by their own judgment of who deserves mercy, must watch it happen. The people of the Aʿrāf are the living proof that mercy belongs to Allah alone, not to human estimations of worth.

## The last call: a plea refused (50–51)

The final call inverts the first. Now it is the people of the Fire who cry out to the people of Paradise: "Pour on us some water or anything that Allah has provided you with." As-Suddi notes that "anything that Allah has provided you with" means food. Sa'id bin Jubayr adds the most piercing detail in the passage: "One of them will call his father or brother, 'I have been burned, so pour some water on me.'" These are not strangers shouting across a wall; they are families torn down the middle. And "the believers will be asked to reply" — the refusal is not the believers' hardness but Allah's decree: "Both Allah has forbidden to the disbelievers" — the food and drink of Paradise, as 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam explains.

Ayah 51 gives the reason, and it is a description worth sitting with: those "who took their religion as amusement and play, and the life of the world deceived them." Ibn Kathir describes them as taking the religion as amusement and play and being deceived by this life and its adornment, rather than working for the Hereafter as Allah commanded.

Then comes the sentence that closes the passage: "So this Day We shall forget them as they forgot their meeting of this Day." Ibn Kathir is careful here, and we must be too: Allah "will treat them as if He has forgotten them. Certainly, nothing escapes Allah's perfect watch and He never forgets anything" — as the Qur'an itself says, "My Lord neither errs nor forgets" (20:52). The "forgetting" is a just recompense, measure for measure: "They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them" (9:67); "Our Ayat came unto you, but you disregarded them, and so this Day, you will be neglected" (20:126); "This Day We will forget you as you forgot the meeting of this Day of yours" (45:34). The early commentators unfold what this abandonment means: Ibn 'Abbas — "Allah will forget the good about them, but not their evil," and "We shall forsake them as they have forsaken the meeting of this Day of theirs"; Mujahid — "We shall leave them in the Fire"; As-Suddi — "We shall leave them from any mercy, just as they left any action on behalf of the meeting on this Day of theirs." Ibn Kathir seals it with what is recorded in the Sahih: Allah will say to the servant on the Day of Resurrection, "Have I not gotten you married? Have I not honored you? Have I not made horses and camels subservient for you and allowed you to become a leader and a master?" He will say, "Yes." Allah will say, "Did you think that you will meet Me?" He will say, "No." Allah the Exalted will say, "Then this Day, I will forget you as you have forgotten Me."

## Why these conversations happen at all

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks the question a thoughtful reader will ask: Paradise and Hell are far apart in every respect — why can their people see and address each other? Its answer: the Qur'an confirms there will be points of access between the two, and these vantage points are themselves part of the recompense. For the people of Hell, these access points "would really be a different kind of punishment": they find themselves being reproached from all sides — with admonition coming even from the angels — and as they see the blessings being enjoyed by the people of Paradise, they burn in rage over what they missed even as they burn in the Fire. For the people of Paradise, seeing the plight of the other side makes them more grateful for the blessings they had the good fortune of having, and those who were once mocked for believing "would have the last laugh at their undoing," as Sūrat al-Mutaffifīn says: "But, on this Day, those who believed will be laughing at the disbelievers. They will be on raised couches watching (the denouement). Would have the disbelievers not been repaid for what they used to do?" (83:34–36).

**What the passage asks of us.** Three things stand out from the sources themselves. First, take the promise and the warning with equal seriousness — the one question that echoes through the whole scene is "did you find it true?", and everyone, on both sides of the wall, answers yes. Second, never treat religion as amusement and play, and never let this world's adornment deceive you out of working for that Day — that is the precise charge read against the people of the Fire in ayah 51. Third, never swear on Allah's behalf about who His mercy will or will not reach. The men on the Heights — whose evil deeds kept them from Paradise and whose good deeds kept them from the Fire — walk through the gate on nothing but His grace and mercy, while those who had confidently mapped out the limits of divine mercy watch from below.

passages.title: The clarified Book and awaiting its fulfilment
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat form a single argument with a simple before-and-after structure. Before the end comes, Allah has already brought "a Book which We have explained in detail with knowledge, a guidance and a mercy to a people who believe"; after that, nothing is left for the deniers to wait for except "the final fulfillment of the event" — the moment the Book's warning actually comes true — and by then the confession they will make will be worthless. The clarified Book now, its fulfilment then, and nothing in between that could excuse anyone.

## Where this passage sits in the sūrah

The ayat just before this passage showed scenes of the Hereafter. Maarif ul Quran, reporting the explanation of Sayyidna ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him), describes the moment of ayah 49: when the questions and answers between the people of al-Aʿrāf (the Heights) and the people of Paradise and Hell are over, the Lord of all the worlds will address the people of Hell and remind them that they had sworn the people of al-Aʿrāf would never be forgiven their sins nor shown mercy. Then comes an immediate declaration of His mercy, as the people of al-Aʿrāf are told: "Enter the Paradise; there is no fear on you, nor shall you grieve."

Having shown us that ending, the sūrah turns back to the present. Ibn Kathir explains the placement: after Allah mentioned the loss the idolators end up with in the Hereafter, He stated that He has indeed sent Prophets and revealed Books in this life, thus leaving them no excuse. The heading over this passage in the compiled Ibn Kathir text sums it up — "The Idolators have no Excuse" — and the commentary cites Allah's own principle elsewhere: "And We never punish until We have sent a Messenger (to give warning)" [17:15]. The first half of the passage closes every escape route before the verdict of the second half falls.

## A Book explained "with knowledge"

The key phrase of ayah 52 is **faṣṣalnāhu ʿalā ʿilm** — "We have explained in detail with knowledge." Ibn Kathir glosses it: "We have perfect knowledge of what We explained in it." The Book's detail flows from the knowledge of its Author, and Ibn Kathir supports this with two parallel ayat: "(This is) a Book, the Ayat whereof are perfected (in every sphere of knowledge), and then explained in detail" [11:1], and "He has sent it down with His Knowledge" [4:166].

Notice to whom and for whom. The Book was brought *to them* — Ibn Kathir opens by saying Allah has left no excuse for the idolators, for He has sent to them the Book that the Messenger ﷺ came with, explained in detail. Yet the ayah names those for whom it becomes "a guidance and a mercy": "a people who believe." The same Book stands before both: for those who believe, guidance and mercy; for those who turn away, in Ibn Kathir's framing, the removal of every excuse.

## Waiting for the fulfilment

This is exactly why the question of ayah 53 lands with such force: "Await they just for the final fulfillment of the event?" The word rendered "final fulfillment" is **taʾwīl** — here, the event the Book spoke of actually arriving. Ibn Kathir reports from **Mujahid and several others** that this refers to what they were promised: the torment, the punishment, the Fire — or Paradise. And from **Ibn ʿAbbas**: "the Day the event is finally fulfilled" is the Day of Resurrection. Since the explanation has already been given in full "with knowledge," the rhetorical question is a rebuke: what exactly are the deniers still waiting for? Not clarification — only confirmation. And confirmation, when it comes, ends the test.

**"Those who neglected it before will say..."** Ibn Kathir is precise about what this neglect means: "those who ignored it in this life and neglected abiding by its implications." These are not people who never received the Book; they are people who had it, knew of it, and chose to live as if it did not bind them.

## The two requests that will be refused

On that Day the neglecters make a full confession — "Verily, the Messengers of our Lord did come with the truth" — the very truth they spent their lives disputing. And then they make two desperate requests.

**First: "Are there any intercessors for us that they might intercede on our behalf?"** — Ibn Kathir explains: so that we are saved from what we ended up in. The bitter irony is spelled out at the end of the ayah: "that which they used to fabricate has gone away from them." Ibn Kathir writes: what they used to worship instead of Allah abandoned them and will not intercede on their behalf, aid them, or save them from their fate. The intercessors they ask for are precisely the fabrications that have vanished.

**Second: "Or could we be sent back, so that we might do (good) deeds other than those (evil) deeds which we used to do?"** — a plea for a second run at life. Ibn Kathir answers it with Allah's own words elsewhere: "If you could but see when they will be held over the (Hell) Fire! They will say: 'Would that we were but sent back! Then we would not deny the Ayat of our Lord, and we would be of the believers!' Nay, it has become manifest to them what they had been concealing before. But if they were returned (to the world), they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden. And indeed they are liars" [6:27–28]. The request sounds like repentance, but the ayah Ibn Kathir cites ends with the divine testimony that even this plea is false: given the world again, they would go back to what they were.

**"Verily, they have lost themselves."** Ibn Kathir's comment is stark: they destroyed themselves by entering the Fire for eternity. Of all the things a person can lose, the ayah names the one loss that cannot be recouped — the self. Trade everything else away and something of you remains to start over; lose yourself, and there is no one left to recover the loss.

## Living it

The passage draws one line through time, and asks each reader where they stand on it. Before the fulfilment, the Book is open, explained in detail, and offered as guidance and mercy; after the fulfilment, the same Book becomes the evidence that removes every excuse. The people described here are not people who never heard — they are, in Ibn Kathir's words, people who "neglected abiding by its implications." That is the warning aimed at us: the danger is not only outright denial but the quieter neglect of a Book we own, honour, and do not live by.

And the passage quietly demolishes two false hopes people carry: that *something else* will step in for them at the end (the intercessors of their own invention), and that there will be *more time* (the return to do better deeds). Neither will be granted. Whatever a person leans on besides Allah "goes away from them" precisely when it is needed most, and the request for a second life is answered with the testimony that it would change nothing. What remains is the present: the Book has been explained in detail with knowledge, it is guidance and mercy *now*, and now is the only time in which believing and acting on it counts.

passages.title: The Creator on the Throne, prayer, reviving rain
passages.tafsir:
This passage is Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's great pause for breath. After long narratives of warning, the sūrah lifts the reader's eyes to the top of existence — the Creator who made the heavens and the earth and rose over the Throne — and then draws one straight line down from that Throne into the believer's daily life. The logic holding ayat 54–58 together is stated by Ibn Kathir himself: after Allah declares that He created the heavens and the earth and that His alone is the creation and the command (ayah 54), He ordains that He be invoked in duʿāʾ, for He is able to do all things (55–56), and He then points to the rain He sends ahead of His mercy — daily proof that the One who revives dead land will raise the dead (57–58). Majesty, then prayer, then resurrection: one argument in three movements.

## The six days — and why not a single instant? (ayah 54)

Allah states that He created the universe in six days. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: the Qurʼan itself says His command is "like the twinkling of an eye" (54:50) and that when He intends a thing He says "Be" and it is (36:82) — so why six days? The commentator Saʿīd ibn Jubayr answered that Divine wisdom demanded gradual creation to teach human beings the lesson of deliberation and perfection in how things are run. Maʿārif supports this with the Prophet's ﷺ teaching that working with deliberation and dignity is from Allah, while hastening is from Shayṭān (cited via Tafsīr Mazharī from al-Bayhaqī's Shuʿab al-Īmān). Haste spoils work and brings remorse; what is done with thought and calm carries barakah — blessing that multiplies its outcome.

A second question: what is a "day" before the sun exists? Maʿārif answers that "day" and "night" as we define them belong to this world; before the universe, Allah may have appointed other signs for them — just as Paradise will have day and night without depending on the sun. So these six days need not equal ours: Mujāhid, Imam Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, and Ibn ʿAbbās (in Ḍaḥḥāk's narration) held that they are days of the next world, each a thousand years. Ibn Kathir records the view that the six days ran from Sunday to Friday, with the whole creation assembled — and Adam created — on Friday; on Saturday no creation took place, for as-Sabt means stoppage. Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Hurayrah the hadith detailing this creation week, ending with Adam, peace be upon him, created after ʿAṣr on Friday, "in the last hour of Friday, between ʿAṣr and the night." Maʿārif adds the breakdown given in Sūrah Fuṣṣilat (41:9–12): the earth in two days, its mountains, rivers and means of sustenance in another two, and the seven heavens in two more — six in all.

## "Then He rose over the Throne"

On the words *thumma istawā ʿalā al-ʿarsh*, both commentaries stop the reader deliberately. Istawā, followed by ʿalā ("over"), literally means to take position on, to be established; al-ʿArsh means the Throne. What does this mean of Allah? Ibn Kathir sets out the way of the righteous predecessors — Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, ath-Thawrī, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, ash-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq ibn Rāhwayh and the scholars of Islam past and present: we accept the apparent meaning of al-Istawā without discussing its true essence, without likening it to the attributes of creation, and without altering or denying it — for "There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearer, the All-Seer" (42:11). He quotes Nuʿaym ibn Ḥammād al-Khuzāʿī, the teacher of Imam al-Bukhārī: whoever likens Allah to His creation has committed kufr, and whoever denies what Allah has described Himself with has also committed kufr — there is no resemblance to creation in anything Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have affirmed of Him.

Maʿārif tells the famous story: someone asked Imam Mālik the meaning of *istawā ʿalā al-ʿarsh*. He paused, then said: everyone knows the meaning of Istawā; its particular nature and reality human reason cannot comprehend; having faith in it is obligatory; and asking about its nature is bidʿah (innovation) — for the Ṣaḥābah never asked the Prophet ﷺ such questions. The great early scholars — Sufyān ath-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah, ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Mubārak — said the verses on Allah's Being and Attributes are to be believed as they have come, exactly as they are, without interpretation. This is the safest, clearest creed: whatever meaning Allah intended is the true one, and we do not manufacture one of our own.

## A universe running on command alone

"He covers the day with night, seeking it rapidly" — darkness and light pursue each other without a moment's delay; when one vanishes the other arrives (Ibn Kathir). The sun, the moon and the stars are *musakhkharāt bi-amrih* — subjected to His command. Maʿārif draws out the wonder with an image from our own experience: every machine humans build wears out, needs adjustment, sits idle for repairs. But these Divinely-made "machines" have run since day one with perfect precision — not a second fast or slow, no wear, no workshop — because they run on no engine and no fuel at all; they function purely under Divine command. Only when the Absolute Master decides to end them will the system disintegrate: that day is Qiyāmah.

Then the general rule: *a-lā lahu al-khalqu wal-amr* — "Surely His is the creation and the command." Khalq is creating; amr is commanding. No one besides Him can create the most insignificant thing, and no one holds command except what He Himself delegates. Mazharī records a subtler reading from Sufi thought: khalq is the domain of matter, amr the domain of the refined non-material — which is why the Qurʼan calls the soul "from the command of my Lord" (17:85). The verse closes with *tabāraka Allāh* — from barakah, meaning increase, permanence, growth; here it carries the sense of being supremely high and ever-sustaining, "Blessed is Allah, the Lord of all the worlds."

Maʿārif states the point of the whole ayah: the Being who brought this universe from nothing and runs it flawlessly will find no difficulty in recreating it on the Day of Qiyāmah — so the reasonable course is to stop denying resurrection and take this Being alone as one's Rabb: Master, Nurturer, the One asked and the One worshipped.

## Then call on Him — humbly and secretly (ayah 55)

If His alone is the creation and the command, then asking belongs to Him alone. Duʿāʾ in Arabic means calling on someone to fulfil a need, and it also carries the wider sense of remembrance and worship; the early authorities read the verse both ways (Maʿārif): ask Allah alone for your needs, and keep your dhikr and worship for Him alone.

Two words carry the whole etiquette. *Taḍarruʿ* is a felt admission of inability — coming before Allah weak, helpless, stripped of pride and self-regard; Ibn Jarīr explains it as obeying Him in humility. *Khufyah* means secretly, privately; Ibn Jarīr: with humbleness in the heart and certainty of His Oneness, not supplicating loudly to show off. Maʿārif presses the point that duʿāʾ is *asked*, not *read*: words mechanically recited, with the heart absent, are not yet duʿāʾ at all — though Allah in His mercy may still accept even lifeless words.

Why quietly? Maʿārif gives three reasons: loud duʿāʾ makes humility hard to maintain, opens the door to showing off, and betrays forgetfulness of who is being addressed. It is recorded in the Two Sahihs from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari that when people raised their voices in supplication, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Take it easy on yourselves. You are not calling one who is deaf or absent; the One you are calling is All-Hearer, Near." The Qurʼan praises the righteous servant "when he called his Lord in a lowered voice" (19:3). Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said there are seventy degrees of difference between a loud duʿāʾ and a quiet one, and described the early righteous elders whose worship no one ever heard — men who memorised the whole Qurʼan, or prayed long into the night, without anyone knowing. The Prophet ﷺ said, in a hadith reported by Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ibn Hibban and al-Baihaqi from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas: "The best dhikr is hidden, and the best sustenance is what suffices." Where the Sunnah itself raises the voice — the adhān, recitation in voiced prayers, the takbīrs, the talbiyah of Ḥajj — voices are raised; everywhere else, quiet is superior.

"Surely He does not love the transgressors (*al-muʿtadīn*)" — from *iʿtidāʾ*, crossing limits. Ibn ʿAbbās said: in duʿāʾ and in everything else. In duʿāʾ, Maʿārif lists its forms: contrived rhyming and stylistic display that kill humility; over-specified demands — ʿAbdullah ibn Mughaffal heard his son ask Allah for "the white castle on the right side of Paradise" and stopped him: ask Allah for Paradise and seek refuge from the Fire, for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, "There will come a people who transgress in supplication and purification" (recorded by Ibn Majah and Abu Dawud with a good chain); praying for harm to the Muslims; and shouting where there is no need. Abu Mijlaz gave as an example asking to reach the rank of the Prophets.

## Do not spoil what He set right — and pray between fear and hope (ayah 56)

"Do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order." Two opposites meet here: *ṣalāḥ*, the state of being right and ordered, and *fasād*, corruption — which Imam Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī defines as anything crossing the limits of moderation, small or great (Maʿārif). Allah set the earth in order in two ways. Physically: a ground neither liquid nor iron-hard, farmable and diggable, served by wind, light, rain and the resources beneath it. Spiritually: by sending messengers and Books, purifying it from kufr and shirk. The verse forbids ruining either.

Maʿārif's most searching teaching is that the two orders are chained together: every outward corruption breeds inward corruption, and every inward corruption — sin, heedlessness, disobedience — eventually surfaces as outward disorder. When human beings disobey their Master, His creation quietly begins to withhold its real service from them: things still work, but they stop delivering the peace and contentment they were made to deliver, which is why an age drowning in comforts and cures is also drowning in anxieties and new diseases. Maʿārif cites Rūmī: the cloud withholds its rain when zakāh is withheld, and from zinā spreads epidemic — and insists this is no poetic fancy but a reality supported by the Qurʼan and hadith; what we see in this world is only a light sample of the ultimate reckoning.

Hence the verse returns immediately to prayer: "and call on Him in fear and hope (*khawfan wa-ṭamaʿan*)" — fearing His severe punishment and the possibility that one's sins block the answer, while hoping fully in His tremendous reward and mercy. Maʿārif calls fear and hope "the two wings of the human soul": carelessness about one's sins is contrary to īmān, and despairing of Allah's mercy is kufr, so the believer flies between the two. Some scholars added (via al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ): let fear dominate during life and health, so obedience does not slacken, and let hope dominate when death comes, when nothing remains but Allah's mercy.

And the closing promise tilts the scales: "Surely the mercy of Allah is near to the *muḥsinīn*" — the doers of good. Hope is the weightier wing, says Maʿārif, for the One being asked is the Lord of the worlds, whose generosity knows no shortage — He could answer the duʿāʾ of the worst offender. The only real obstacle is one's own sins. Matar al-Warraq said, "Earn Allah's promise by obeying Him, for He ordained that His mercy is near to the good-doers" (collected by Ibn Abi Hatim). The Prophet ﷺ described a man who travels far and raises his hands to Allah looking like a faqir — but his food, drink and dress are all ḥarām: how can his duʿāʾ be answered? (Muslim and Tirmidhi, from Abu Hurairah.) And he ﷺ said that a servant's duʿāʾ keeps being answered so long as he does not pray for something sinful or for severing family ties, and does not grow hasty — saying "I have prayed and prayed and it has not been answered," until he despairs and stops (Muslim, Tirmidhi). He ﷺ also taught that when you make duʿāʾ, make it with no doubt in your heart that it will be answered — certainty in His mercy, alongside honest fear of one's own shortcomings.

## The rain that rehearses the resurrection (ayat 57–58)

Ayah 57 brings the argument down from the heavens to the fields. Allah sends the winds *bushran* — as bearers of good news — "before His mercy," and the mercy here is rain (Ibn Kathir). Maʿārif notes the double gift: the cool winds before rain are a pleasure in themselves, and they forewarn people, giving them time to prepare and take cover. Then the winds "carry heavy clouds" — thousands of tons of water riding on the shoulders of the wind, as Maʿārif marvels: a sky-filling vessel with no engine, no fuel, no human labour, moving purely at its Master's will. "We drive it to a dead land": *balad* is a town or habitation — named deliberately, because the rain's purpose is to feed people — and *sauq*, driving, means the clouds are herded to their destination by Divine command. Everyone has seen heavy clouds hang over a parched town and leave without a drop, to empty themselves where their appointed share lies; and the weather bureaus' forecasts fail whenever the Divine command runs contrary to their rules (Maʿārif).

Then the pivot the whole passage has been building toward: "Thus We shall bring forth the dead — so that you may take heed." The land you watched die comes alive before your eyes every season; the One who does that will raise you. Ibn Kathir explains: just as We revive dead land, We shall raise the dead after they have disintegrated — rain will pour for forty days and the corpses will grow in their graves as seeds grow. Maʿārif cites the narration of Abu Hurayrah that the Ṣūr (Horn) will be blown twice: at the first blast the whole world perishes; between the two blasts rain falls throughout, the scattered parts of every dead human and animal reassemble; and at the second blast the souls enter and they rise alive — a narration the major portion of which is found in Al-Bukhari and Muslim, with some portions from Kitab al-Baʿth of Ibn Abi Dawud.

Ayah 58 adds the second, quieter lesson. The rain is common to all, but the land differs: "the good land brings forth its vegetation by the permission of its Lord," easily and abundantly, "and that which is bad brings forth nothing but *nakidan*" — scanty and useless. Both commentaries read this as a parable of hearts. Divine guidance — the Books, the prophets, the teaching of the scholars — falls like rain on every human being alike; but only the receptive heart grows anything from it, while the heart like rock or saline soil clings to error despite clear signs (Maʿārif). Al-Bukhari records from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made exactly this comparison: the guidance and knowledge he was sent with are like abundant rain falling on land — some fertile, absorbing the water and bringing forth pasture in plenty; some hard, holding the water so that people drink and irrigate; and some barren, neither holding water nor growing anything. The first is the one who understands Allah's religion, learns and teaches; the last is the one who does not raise his head to it and does not accept the guidance.

So the passage closes: "Thus do We explain variously the Ayat for a people who give thanks." The signs — cosmic, verbal, and falling from the sky — are given to everyone; their profit is reaped by the grateful, those who recognise the worth of what has rained on them. That is the practice these ayat leave the believer with: know who your Lord is; ask Him quietly, humbly, between fear and hope; keep your earnings clean and do not rush the answer; do not corrupt what He set right; and keep your heart soft soil, so that when His mercy falls, something grows.

passages.title: Noah warns his people; the flood follows
passages.tafsir:
# Nūḥ and His People: The First Confrontation Between Truth and Denial (7:59–64)

With these ayat, Sūrat al-Aʿrāf turns from principle to history. Having established the great themes of the sūrah — the oneness of Allah (tawḥīd), the truth of messengership (risālah), and the reality of the Hereafter — the sūrah now begins, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, a long sequence of prophet-stories running almost to the end of the sūrah, in which each community is invited to these same universal truths, given good news of reward for belief, and warned of the sad end awaiting denial. Nūḥ (peace be upon him) comes first, and his story here is a complete miniature of the whole pattern: the call (ayah 59), the elite's scornful rejection (ayah 60), the messenger's calm and reasoned reply (61–63), and finally the parting of the ways — rescue for the believers, drowning for the deniers (ayah 64). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that these accounts gave later communities the opportunity to learn a lesson from the fate of those before them — and that for the Prophet ﷺ they became a source of comfort, for this is how things have been with all the prophets.

## Why Nūḥ comes first

Ibn Kathir explains that after mentioning Adam at the start of the sūrah, Allah begins the prophet-stories with Nūḥ because he was **the first Messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth after Adam**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the point: Adam (peace be upon him) was indeed the first prophet, but in his time disbelief and disbelievers simply did not exist — his code dealt mostly with settling the land and managing human needs. The confrontation against kufr (disbelief) and shirk (associating partners with Allah) began with Nūḥ. He is, in terms of the mission of prophethood and a code of religious laws, the first rasūl (Messenger) of Allah — and since the whole world after the Flood was repopulated through him and those with him in the Ark, he is even called "the junior Adam."

The sources give a sense of the vast timescale. According to a narration of Ibn ʿAbbās in the Mustadrak of Hakim — the same being reported by Tabarani from a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ narrated by Abū Dharr — there was an interval of ten *qarn* between Adam and Nūḥ, a qarn generally meaning a hundred years. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes his nine-hundred-and-fifty-year-long prophetic struggle, noting the Qurʼan's clear statement that he reached the age of nine hundred and fifty years. And in another narration of Ibn ʿAbbās in the Mustadrak of Hakim, the Prophet ﷺ said that Nūḥ was invested with prophethood at the age of forty and lived sixty years after the Flood. On one detail the scholars differed: Ibn Kathir records, from Muhammad bin Ishaq and other documenters of lineage, a genealogy placing Khanūkh — said by some to be the Prophet Idrīs (peace be upon him) — among Nūḥ's forefathers; yet Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes (citing Al-Bahr Al-Muhit) that the majority of the Companions held that Nūḥ came *before* Idrīs. The matter has been debated, and both views are transmitted.

One more point of precision from the wording of ayah 59: "We sent Nūḥ **to his people**." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from this that his mission was to his own community — a people living in Iraq, outwardly civilized but sunk in shirk — not to all mankind.

## How idol-worship entered the world

Ibn Kathir preserves, from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAbbās and other early commentators, the remarkable account of how shirk first began — and it did not begin with open rebellion against Allah. It began with **love of the righteous, taken too far**. When certain righteous men died, their people built places of worship over their graves and made images of them, intending only to remember their devotion and imitate it. As generations passed, the images became statues; and later still, the statues became gods, bearing the names of those righteous men: Wadd, Suwāʿ, Yaghūth, Yaʿūq and Nasr. When this practice had spread, Allah sent Nūḥ.

This is worth sitting with. The first shirk in history was not manufactured by hatred of Allah but by unchecked veneration — good intentions drifting, over time, into worship of other than Him. That is why Nūḥ's call goes straight to the root.

## The call: three sentences that contain everything (ayah 59)

"O my people! Worship Allah! You have no god other than Him. Indeed I fear for you the torment of a great Day." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (drawing on Tafsīr Kabīr) unpacks this as three moves. The first sentence — *worship Allah* — is the essence of the entire message. The second — *you have no god other than Him* — cuts off the shirk that had spread among them like an epidemic. The third is the warning of the "great Day": this could mean the punishment of the Hereafter — Ibn Kathir explains it as the torment of the Day of Resurrection, for whoever meets Allah while associating others with Him — and it could also mean the punishment of the Flood in this present world. Both senses stand.

Notice also the address: *yā qawmi*, "O **my** people." Nūḥ speaks as one of them, to his own — a warmth his opponents will not return.

## The chiefs answer with contempt (ayah 60)

It is not the common folk who answer first but *al-malaʼ* — a word Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains as the chiefs, headmen and empowered elders of a community; Ibn Kathir describes them as the chiefs, commanders and great ones of his people. Their verdict: "We surely see you in obvious error."

What did they mean? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the sense of their objection: this man is trying to wean us off our ancestral faith, and all this talk of rising on some Last Day, of reward and punishment, is nothing but superstition. Ibn Kathir adds the reason beneath the reason: he was calling them to abandon the idols *they found their forefathers worshipping*.

Then Ibn Kathir makes an observation that reaches far beyond Nūḥ's time: this is the standing attitude of evil people — they genuinely see the righteous as the misguided ones. He cites Allah's words elsewhere: "And when they saw them, they said: Verily, these have indeed gone astray!" (83:32), and the disbelievers' claim that had the faith been any good, the weak and poor would not have reached it before them (46:11). The inversion is total: the man sent by the Lord of the worlds is diagnosed, by the powerful, as the one who has lost his way.

## The reply of a prophet: no anger against anger (ayat 61–62)

Their words were harsh, yet — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān beautifully observes — Nūḥ does not respond on the same wavelength, "not anger against anger." He answers in the simplest possible words, and in doing so leaves a trail for every carrier of daʿwah (the call to Allah), every teacher and reformer after him: "O my people, there is no error in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of all the worlds. I convey to you the messages of my Lord and give you sincere advice, and I know from Allah what you do not know."

Each clause carries weight:

- **"A Messenger from the Lord of all the worlds."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this single expression strikes decisively at shirk: once Allah is understood as Lord of *all* the worlds — Ibn Kathir: Lord and King of all things — no god or goddess of any denomination can stand as an object of worship. Nūḥ is also saying: I am not bound, as you are, by ancestral customs rooted in ignorance; what I tell you comes under the guidance of my Lord.
- **"I convey… and give sincere advice."** His mission brings Allah no benefit and serves no personal interest of Nūḥ's own; it is purely for their good.
- **"I know from Allah what you do not know."** Their doubts about the Last Day, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, arose from lack of awareness; he had been granted certainty in the matter by Allah.

Ibn Kathir draws out the timeless principle: this is **the attribute of a Messenger** — plain yet eloquent conveyance, sincere counsel, and true knowledge of Allah; no other people can rival the Prophets in this. He then cites what Muslim recorded in his Sahih: on the Day of ʿArafah, when the Companions' gathering was as large as it ever was, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them, "O people! You will be asked about me, so what will you say?" They said, "We testify that you have conveyed and delivered the Message and offered sincere advice." And he kept raising his finger to the sky and lowering it towards them, saying, "O Allah, bear witness! O Allah, bear witness!" What Nūḥ said of himself — *I convey and I sincerely advise* — a vast gathering of Companions testified to on behalf of the final Messenger ﷺ.

## "A man from among you" — why the messenger must be human (ayah 63)

"Do you find it astonishing that a reminder from your Lord should come to you through a man from among you, to warn you, that you may fear Allah, and that you may be shown mercy?" The astonishment answered here is the people's other objection, stated openly in Sūrat al-Muʼminūn (23:24): he is only a man like us — he eats, drinks and sleeps as we do; had Allah wished to send a message, He would have sent angels.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a two-part answer from this ayah. First, prophethood is Allah's exclusive domain: He is the Absolute Master and bestows it on whom He wills; no one may demand otherwise. Second — and this is the deeper point — the very *purpose* of sending a prophet can only be achieved through a human being. The aim is to bring people to believe in and obey Allah, and that requires a living model: someone of their own kind demonstrating that it is entirely possible to worship Allah and keep His commands *while* being subject to every ordinary human need and desire. Had angels brought the call, people would have had a ready excuse — angels feel no hunger or thirst, never sleep, never tire; how could we be like them? A man from among them, walking amongst them as a perfect model of obedience, leaves no excuse. This is why the ayah says "*that he may warn you and that you may fear Allah*": only a warner of your own kind can produce that fear in you.

Ibn Kathir adds the note of mercy: it is no strange thing that Allah sends revelation to a man among you — it is His mercy, kindness and compassion toward you, so that you might avoid His punishment and receive His mercy. The warning itself is a gift.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes this ayah with a sharp observation about human nature: this doubt was never unique to Nūḥ's people. Communities throughout history have balked at a human prophet, and the ignorant in every age refuse to accept the superiority of anyone from their own kind — which is why, even now, people nurse resentment against the men of Allah (awliyāʼ) and the trustworthy scholars *of their own time*, looking down on them precisely because they are contemporaries. It has always been the trademark of the ignorant.

## The flood: rescue and drowning (ayah 64)

"But they rejected him — so We saved him and those with him in the Ark, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. They were indeed a blind people."

The rejection was final: Ibn Kathir notes they insisted on rejecting and opposing him, and only a few believed. Then comes the double decree in a single ayah — *We saved… We drowned*. The full account of the Flood, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, comes in Sūrah Hūd and Sūrah Nūḥ; here the Qurʼan gives only the essence, because the point of the passage is the pattern, not the narrative detail.

Two details from the sources deepen the scene. Zayd ibn Aslam relates (as cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from Ibn Kathir) that when the punishment overtook them, Nūḥ's people were at the very prime of their population and power — the lands and mountains of Iraq were becoming insufficient for their numbers. And herein lies a customary practice of Allah: He grants the disobedient long respite, and His punishment arrives when they stand at the peak of numbers, power and wealth — drunk, so to speak, on their own condition. Security is no proof of safety.

As for those saved, the reports differ. Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Wahb, who said he was told that Ibn ʿAbbās said that eighty men were saved with Nūḥ in the ship, one of them called Jurhum, who spoke Arabic; Ibn Abi Hatim collected this statement, and Ibn Kathir notes that it was also narrated with a continuous chain of narration from Ibn ʿAbbās. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that some narrations give the detail of forty men and forty women, and that the place in Mosul, Iraq, where they came to stay after the Flood became known as *Thamānūn* — "Eighty."

And the closing verdict — "they were indeed a blind people" — Ibn Kathir explains as blindness *to the truth*: unable to recognize it or find their way to it. They had eyes; what they lacked was sight of what mattered. Ibn Kathir then names the law of history this ayah announces: Allah took revenge on His enemies and saved His Messenger and those who believed in him — and this is Allah's Sunnah (His consistent way) with His servants, in this life and the Hereafter: the good end, victory and triumph belong to those who fear Him — "Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers" (40:51).

## What this opening story establishes

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up why this brief account stands at the head of the prophet-stories, and it makes a fitting summary of the whole passage:

1. **One call, always.** The daʿwah of all the past prophets and their basic articles of faith were one — what Nūḥ preached is what every messenger after him preached.
2. **Allah supports His messengers in strikingly wondrous ways** — Nūḥ and those with him faced not the least danger even with a Flood rising as high as mountain peaks around them.
3. **Denying the prophets invites Divine punishment — and the warning is still valid.** The fate that overtook past communities for belying their prophets could overtake their modern counterparts; the wise response is to refuse heedlessness and false security.

For the believer reading today, the passage also quietly teaches *how* to carry truth: speak to people as "my people," answer contempt with clarity rather than anger, convey sincerely with no personal stake, and leave the outcome — rescue and drowning alike — to the Lord of all the worlds.

passages.title: Hud calls 'Ad from arrogance to worship
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the second panel in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf's gallery of the messengers. Having told the story of Nuh (peace be upon him), the sūrah turns to the nation that inherited the earth after the Flood — ʿAd — and to the prophet raised among them, Hud (peace be upon him). The eight ayat form one continuous drama: the call to worship Allah alone (65), the chiefs' contemptuous reply (66), Hud's calm self-defence (67–68), his appeal to Allah's favours upon them (69), their defiant challenge — "bring us what you threaten us with" (70), his announcement that the verdict has already fallen (71), and the sentence carried out: the believers saved, the deniers cut off at the root (72).

## Who were ʿAd?

**A mighty people, richly blessed.** Ibn Kathir cites Muhammad bin Ishaq that the tribe of ʿAd descended from ʿAd, son of Iram, son of ʿAws, son of Sam, son of Nuh — the ancient people Allah describes elsewhere as "Iram of the lofty pillars, the like of which were not created in the land" (89:6–8), and who boasted, "Who is mightier than us in strength?" (41:15). They lived in Yemen, in the region of al-Ahqaf — a name that literally means *sand mounds* — spreading, in Ibn Ishaq's account, between Oman and Hadramawt. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds detail: they comprised thirteen families, their lands were fertile, their gardens abundant, and they built mansions and palaces. They were tall and heavily built — this is exactly what ayah 69's phrase *zādakum fī al-khalqi basṭah*, "increased you amply in stature," refers to. Ibn Kathir notes the same word *basṭah* is used of Talut (Saul), whom Allah "increased abundantly in knowledge and stature" (2:247).

Ibn Kathir also records, from Ibn Jarir, that ʿAli bin Abi Talib described to a man from Hadramawt a red sand mound with Arak and Lote trees — a place ʿAli had never seen but which had been described to him — and said, "There is the grave of Hud, peace be upon him, in its vicinity." Ibn Kathir draws from this the geographical point: ʿAd lived in Yemen, since their prophet was buried there.

**"Their brother Hud."** Why does ayah 65 call Hud their *brother*? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that Hud (peace be upon him) and ʿAd both stood in the fifth generation from Nuh through his son Sam; their family trees converge, making Hud a lineal brother of the tribe. Ibn Kathir adds that Hud was among the noble men and chiefs of ʿAd, "for Allah chose the Messengers from among the best, most honorable families and tribes" — and in Ibn Ishaq's words, he "was the best among them in status." The messenger was no outsider; he was their own kinsman and one of their finest. Maʿārif also notes, on the mention of Iram, that the commentators discuss an "ʿAd the First" and a second branch — the better-known view being that Iram was the name of ʿAd's grandfather, with ʿAd and Thamud both counted as branches of Iram — and records the report (from Bayān al-Qurʼān) that a deputation of ʿAd visiting Makkah at the time of the punishment was spared.

## The exchange: "foolishness" versus prophethood

**Why so brief a warning?** Hud's whole opening message in ayah 65 is: worship Allah, you have no god but Him — "will you then not have taqwa?" (taqwa: the fear of Allah joined with obedience to Him, which makes one guard against His displeasure). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes something easy to miss: the grave punishment sent upon the people of Nuh, long before ʿAd, was still alive in the minds of the people of that time — so there was no need to describe the severity and gravity of the punishment that comes upon disobedient people; "do you not fear Allah?" was considered quite sufficient. (A small textual note for the careful reader: the printed text of Maʿārif here names "Sayyidna Nuh" as the one who had no need to describe the punishment, even though the paragraph is commenting on Hud's words in ayah 65 — apparently a slip in the printed text, which we record as it stands; the point itself plainly concerns the brevity of the warning in this ayah.)

**The chiefs answer with contempt (66).** It is *al-malaʼ* — the chiefs, masters and commanders of the people, as Ibn Kathir glosses the word — who reply, and their answer is a double insult: "We surely see you in *safāhah* (foolishness), and we think you are one of the liars." Ibn Kathir explains what they meant: you are misguided *because* you call us to abandon our idols and worship Allah alone. To them, pure monotheism itself was the madness.

**Hud's reply is a portrait of prophethood (67–68).** He does not return the insult. "There is no foolishness in me — but I am a Messenger from the Lord of all that exists. I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am for you a *nāṣiḥ amīn*" — a sincere, trustworthy adviser. Ibn Kathir pauses here: "These, indeed, are the qualities of the Prophets: conveying, sincerity and honesty." Three words carry the whole prophetic office — he delivers exactly what he was given, he genuinely wishes his people well, and he can be trusted absolutely with the message.

**"Do you wonder…?" (69).** Their underlying objection, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, was the same one Nuh's people had raised: how can a mere human like us stand over us as Allah's messenger? Had it been an angel, perhaps. The Qur'an's answer, given already on Nuh's tongue, is that there is nothing surprising in it — it is precisely a human being who can convince other human beings effectively. Ibn Kathir adds that instead of wondering at the warning, they ought to have *thanked* Allah for the bounty of a warner from among themselves.

Hud then holds up two specific favours. First: "He made you successors (*khulafāʼ*) after the people of Nuh" — remember, says Ibn Kathir, that you are the offspring of Nuh, the very man whose supplication brought destruction on the earth's people when they defied him. The privilege of inheriting the earth came with that history attached. Second: the ample stature already mentioned. Then the summons: "So remember the *ālāʼ* of Allah" — His graces and blessings — "that you may be successful." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts its finger on the tragedy of ʿAd here: Allah had opened the doors of His blessing upon them, "but their crooked thinking made these very blessings a curse." Intoxicated with power and grandeur, they took no notice of the Lord in whose blessings they were bathing, and bowed instead to idols carved out of rocks.

## History repeating — and a mirror for Makkah

Both commentaries insist that this scene is not unique. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the chiefs' stance in ayah 66 "resembles the one taken by the people of Nuh — the only difference is that of some words," and that Hud's reply in 67–68 is nearly the same as Nuh's in ayat 61–63. And Ibn Kathir repeatedly turns the mirror toward the sūrah's first audience: when ʿAd sneered at the call to worship Allah alone, they anticipated the chiefs of Quraysh, who marvelled that he had "made the gods (all) into one" (38:5); when ʿAd demanded the punishment be brought on (70), they anticipated Quraysh's prayer, "O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones on us from the sky" (8:32). The Makkans hearing this sūrah were being shown their own script, already acted out once — with its ending.

## The challenge and the verdict (70–71)

**"So bring us that with which you threaten us."** Ayah 70 is the sound of a people past persuasion: have you come so that we should worship Allah *alone* and abandon what our fathers worshipped? Ibn Ishaq (cited by Ibn Kathir) even preserves the names of their idols: Sudaʼ, Samud and al-Habaʼ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paraphrases their answer: abandoning the faith of our ancestors is something we will never do — and as for your threatened punishment, go ahead and bring it, if you are truthful.

**"Rijs and wrath have already fallen on you" (71).** Hud's reply uses a striking past tense: the punishment has, in effect, *already* landed — you have earned it by what you said. Ibn ʿAbbas explained *rijs* here as scorn and anger. Then comes one of the sharpest phrases in the passage: "Do you dispute with me over **names which you have named — you and your fathers — for which Allah has sent down no authority (sulṭān)?**" Ibn Kathir unpacks it: these "gods" are nothing but labels your ancestors invented — they bring neither harm nor benefit, and no proof from Allah ever licensed their worship. An idol is a name with nothing behind it. "Then wait — I am with you among those who wait": a threat and a warning, says Ibn Kathir, from the Messenger to his people. Yet Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches the tone beneath the warning: even now Hud's "paternal affection and the desire to do good to them" breaks through — he *grieves* that his people have taken lifeless, senseless things as objects of worship and become so devoted to falsehood that they quarrel with a prophet of Allah.

## The end of ʿAd (72)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that the punishment came in stages. First, the rains stopped for three full years; lands became deserts and gardens dead wood — yet they clung to their shirk (associating partners with Allah). Then came the wind. Ibn Kathir gathers the Qur'an's own description: "a furious violent wind… subjected to them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so that you could see men lying overthrown, as if they were hollow trunks of date palms" (69:6–8) — the wind lifted them into the air and dashed them down headfirst.
