Maʿārif adds (from al-Bahr al-Muhit) the remarkable scene of the rescue: Hud and his companions took refuge in an open area enclosed with stakes, and the very storm that was toppling palaces on their columns would change pace and enter that enclosure gently. They sat in peace through the destruction, and afterwards moved to Makkah, where they lived until death. Some commentators, Maʿārif notes, hold on the basis of 23:41 that a terrible sound (*aṣ-Ṣayḥah*) was also part of ʿAd's punishment — and there is no contradiction; both may have occurred.

Ayah 72 states the outcome with perfect balance: "So We saved him and those with him **by mercy from Us**, and We severed the root (*dābir*) of those who denied Our signs." The rescue is attributed to Allah's mercy, not to the believers' merit alone; the destruction is attributed to denial. On "severed the root," Maʿārif records two readings from the commentators: that every one of them then present was destroyed, or that Allah cut off the lineage of ʿAd for the future as well. And the ayah's closing clause — "and they were not believers" — seals the reason. Ibn Kathir notes from Ibn Ishaq that a few *had* followed Hud, concealing their faith; that hidden handful, with their prophet, was precisely who Allah saved.

## From the Sunnah: the emissary of ʿAd

Ibn Kathir cites here a story recorded by Imam Ahmad in the Musnad — with similar wording recorded by at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasaʼi and Ibn Majah. Al-Harith al-Bakri, visiting the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah, blurted out, "I seek refuge with Allah and His Messenger that I become like the emissary of ʿAd" — and the Prophet ﷺ, though he knew the story better, liked to hear it told. When ʿAd suffered famine, they sent an emissary named Qayl to pray for relief. Qayl lingered a month with a host who plied him with drink and singers, then finally prayed at the mountains of Muhrah: "O Allah, give ʿAd water as You used to." Black clouds appeared, and he was told to choose one. He pointed to a black cloud — and heard a voice proclaim: "Take it, as ashes that will leave none in ʿAd." And it was conveyed, the narration says, that the wind sent against them was no more than what would pass through a finger-ring — yet it destroyed them. The story shows how completely ʿAd's fate entered the conscience of the Arabs: "Do not be like the emissary of ʿAd" became a proverb for one sent for relief who brings ruin instead.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the story with three lessons, and they are worth taking exactly as given. For the heedless, it is a summons to keep remembering Allah and to live in obedience to Him — ʿAd's ruin began not with weakness but with blessings received and never traced back to their Giver; "remember the graces of Allah" (69) is the passage's own antidote to arrogance. For those who reject honest advice and refuse to learn, it shows plainly what end to expect. And for preachers and reformers, Hud is "a mirror of the prophetic method" of communication in *tablīgh* (conveying the message) and *iṣlāḥ* (reforming people): insulted as a fool, he answers without rancour, names himself simply a conveyer, a sincere well-wisher, trustworthy; he reasons, reminds of blessings, warns — and even his final warning trembles with a father's grief for his people. Strength of body, tallness of stature, palaces and gardens counted for nothing in the wind; what Allah saved, He saved "by mercy from Us" — and it was the small, hidden company of believers who received it.

passages.title: Salih, Thamud, and the slain she-camel
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the third episode in Surah al-Aʿraf's cycle of destroyed nations: after Nuh and Hud comes Salih, peace be upon them all, sent to the tribe of Thamud. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this chain of prophet-stories — the call of truth, the denial of the people, the terrible consequence — runs as the main subject to the end of the surah. What binds ayat 73–79 into one unit is a single arc: one call to worship Allah alone, a miraculous sign the people themselves demanded, the arrogance of the elite, the killing of the she-camel, and the earthquake that left an entire civilisation lying dead in its carved stone homes.

## Who were Thamud?

Ibn Kathir records from the scholars of tafsir and genealogy that Thamud descended from Thamud bin ʿAthir bin Iram bin Sam bin Nuh — ancient Arabs (al-ʿAribah) who lived before the time of Ibrahim, in the land between the Hijaz and Greater Syria. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that their main city was called Hijr, now known as Madain Salih, and cites Maulana Sayyid Sulaiman Nadvi, who wrote in his book ʿArd al-Qurʼan that their architectural monuments still exist, bearing Iramic and Thamudic inscriptions.

Ayah 74 places them in history: Allah made them **successors (khulafāʼ) after ʿAd** — the very people whose destruction was described in the previous passage. Thamud inherited ʿAd's lands and mansions, and Allah gave them a distinctive skill: "you build for yourselves palaces in plains, and carve out homes in the mountains." Maʿārif unpacks the words: *qusur* is the plural of *qasr*, a palace; the verb comes from *naht*, sculpture or stone-carving. They were wealthy, powerful, brave, and artistically gifted.

And here Maʿārif puts its finger on the tragedy. The flood of Nuh's people was still remembered; the destruction of their own brethren ʿAd was recent history. But "wealth and power have a pull of their own" — no sooner does one affluent structure collapse than another people raises a higher one on the same foundation. Thamud settled in the very places where ʿAd had been destroyed, then sank into the very same idolatry. So ayah 74 ends: "remember the graces of Allah, and do not go about making mischief on the earth." The blessings are named precisely so that gratitude might soften them before it is too late.

## One call, every messenger

Ayah 73 calls Salih "their brother" — he was of their own lineage and land, one of them. His message was word-for-word the message of every prophet: "O my people! Worship Allah! You have no other god but Him." Ibn Kathir stresses that all of Allah's Messengers called to this alone, citing "And We did not send any Messenger before you but We revealed to him: None has the right to be worshipped but I, so worship Me" (21:25) and "We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger proclaiming: Worship Allah and avoid Taghut (false deities)" (16:36). Maʿārif draws the ruling explicitly: all the prophets stand united on tawhid — pure monotheism — as the basis of religion.

## The she-camel they asked for

The "clear sign" of ayah 73 is the she-camel, and its background transforms the whole passage: **this was Thamud's own demand.** Ibn Kathir relates that they pointed to a solid, lone rock in the area of Hijr called al-Katibah and challenged Salih to bring a pregnant camel out of it. Salih first took their covenant — their oaths that if Allah answered, they would believe and follow him. Maʿārif adds that he prayed two rakʿahs (units of prayer) and made duʿāʼ: "For You nothing is difficult." Then the rock rumbled, split apart, and out came a she-camel, pregnant, her unborn calf visibly moving in her belly — exactly as they had specified.

Some believed on the spot, including a chief, Jundu' bin ʿAmr. Ibn Kathir records that the rest of the nobility wanted to believe too, but were talked out of it by a handful of chiefs — among them the keeper of their idols. It is a chilling detail: faith was within reach of a whole people, and a few powerful men holding vested interests in the old religion pulled them back.

She is called **nāqat Allāh — "the she-camel of Allah."** Maʿārif explains why: because she was a proof of Allah's perfect power, brought into being in an extraordinary way. And the command "leave her to eat **in Allah's earth**" carries its own argument: what she ate and drank was not owned by them — the earth and its produce belong to Allah.

Yet the sign became a test. The camel drank the well dry on her day, so Salih, following the divine will, gave the verdict of an alternation: one day the water was hers, the next day theirs — and on her drinking days the people milked her and filled their containers with milk in place of water. Ibn Kathir connects this to "inform them that the water is to be shared between them, each one's right to drink being established by turns" (54:28) and "Here is a she-camel: it has a right to drink, and you have a right to drink, each on a known day" (26:155). She was tremendous and strikingly beautiful; their cattle feared her. Over time, resentment at sharing the water hardened into the intention to kill her.

## Arrogance and the "weakened": ayat 75–76

Before the crime, the Qur'an records a dialogue. "The leaders of those who were **arrogant** said to those who were **counted weak** — to such of them as believed: 'Do you know that Salih is one sent from his Lord?'"

Maʿārif cites Imam Razi (Tafsir Kabir) on a precise point of Arabic grammar. The arrogant are described with an active verb — *istakbarū*, "they were arrogant": their arrogance was their own chosen act, blameworthy, and ultimately the cause of their punishment. But the believers are described with a passive verb — *ustudʿifū*, "they were deemed weak": weakness was not their quality; it was merely a label the disbelievers pinned on them. The blame falls on those who called them weak, not on those so called. In one grammatical contrast the Qur'an dismantles the whole social hierarchy of Thamud.

The believers' reply is a masterpiece of daʿwah — of inviting to Allah. Asked "do you *know* he is sent?", they answered: "We indeed **believe** in that with which he has been sent." Maʿārif quotes the Kashshaf: the believers refused the framing altogether — whether Salih is Allah's messenger is not even worth debating; it is obvious and certain. The only real question is who will believe. The arrogant answered coldly in ayah 76: "Verily, we disbelieve in that which you believe in." Maʿārif comments: even that eloquent answer could not soften them, for "the lust of worldly life is merciless," and the intoxication of wealth and power becomes an invisible curtain before eyes that would otherwise see the obvious.

## The killing: ayah 77

"So they killed the she-camel and insolently defied the commandment of their Lord, and said: 'O Salih! Bring about your threats if you are indeed one of the Messengers.'"

Ibn Kathir relates, from Imam Abu Jaʿfar Ibn Jarir and other scholars of tafsir, how it happened. Behind the plot stood two women. One, ʿUnayzah bint Ghanm, was a wealthy, disbelieving old woman who had the severest enmity among Thamud towards Salih, peace be upon him. The other, Saduf bint al-Muhayya, was a noblewoman — wealthy, beautiful, of noble family — who had been married to a Muslim man of Thamud but left him. These two offered a prize to whoever would kill the camel: Saduf offered herself, and her cousin Musaddiʿ agreed; ʿUnayzah promised Qudar bin Salif any of her daughters he wished. So Musaddiʿ shot the camel's leg with an arrow, and Qudar hamstrung her with his sword and then slaughtered her. Maʿārif observes that Satan's deadliest weapon here was the trial through women, and notes that the Qur'an brands the one who carried out this deed "the most wicked of them" (91:12). Seven others joined them — the "nine men who made mischief in the land and would not reform" of 27:48.

But the Qur'an says **"they** killed the she-camel" — the whole tribe, in the plural. Ibn Kathir explains: the nine were chiefs who lured the entire tribe into agreeing. Qatadah related that he was told that the designated killer canvassed them all — even women in their rooms, even children — and found every one of them consenting. Hence "then they denied him and they killed it, so their Lord destroyed them because of their sin, and made them equal in destruction" (91:14). This is one of the passage's weightiest lessons: a community that approves of a crime shares in it, even if one hand holds the sword. A report conveyed from al-Hasan al-Basri adds pathos: the camel's calf climbed a high rock and cried out, "O my Lord! Where is my mother?"

One note of scholarly honesty, from Maʿārif: important parts of this story are told in the Qur'an itself, some parts appear in hadith narrations, and some others the commentators have taken from Israelite narratives (reports transmitted from earlier communities) — and the truth of the event does not depend on those.

## Three days of respite, then the earthquake: ayah 78

When Salih saw the slain camel he wept and announced: "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days" (11:65) — "a promise not going to be false." Instead of repenting, the nine plotted that same night to murder Salih and his family under cover of darkness (27:49). Ibn Kathir relates that Allah, "to Whom belongs all might and Who protects His Messengers," rained down stones that smashed the heads of the nine before the rest of the tribe — "they plotted a plot, and We planned a plan, while they perceived not" (27:50).

Then the sign Salih had foretold unfolded with terrible precision: on Thursday every face turned yellow; on Friday, red; on Saturday, black. Maʿārif notes that even the first fulfilled sign did not humble them — their fury at Salih only grew, for when Allah's wrath approaches, hearts turn upside down and people mistake their loss for gain. On the fourth morning, Ibn Kathir relates, they perfumed themselves with hanut — the embalming scent used for the dead — and awaited the punishment. When the sun rose, the Sayhah (a shattering cry) came from the sky and a severe tremor from below, and every soul was taken in a single hour.

Ayah 78 names the punishment *al-rajfah*, the earthquake, while 15:83 names the Sayhah; Maʿārif concludes that both converged at once — the earth convulsing beneath them, the cry tearing from above. The word **jāthimīn** — "lying prostrate" — is from *juthūm*: to be rendered motionless on the spot (al-Qamus); the Mufradat pictures a dead bird fallen on its breast. Everyone lay dead exactly where they were, in the very stone homes they had carved as monuments to their permanence. None escaped — except one man, Abu Righal, who happened to be inside the Sacred Precinct of Makkah; the sanctity of the Haram shielded him until he stepped outside it, and a stone fell from the sky and killed him. ʿAbdur-Razzaq narrates that the Prophet ﷺ later showed his Companions Abu Righal's grave and told them a branch of gold was buried with him — which they dug up and found — and al-Zuhri said Abu Righal is the father of the tribe of Thaqif.

## Salih's farewell: ayah 79

"So he turned away from them and said: 'O my people! I have indeed conveyed to you the Message of my Lord, and have given you good advice, but you like not good advisers.'"

Ibn Kathir understands this as spoken **after** their destruction — words of admonishment and criticism addressed to the dead, who were made to hear him as a miracle for Salih. He draws the parallel with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ at Badr: as recorded in the Two Sahihs, three days after the battle he stood at the well where the slain disbelievers lay and called out, "O Abu Jahl bin Hisham! O ʿUtbah bin Rabiʿah!… Did you find what your Lord promised you to be true? For I found what my Lord promised me to be true." When ʿUmar asked why he addressed people who had rotted, he ﷺ replied: "By He in Whose Hand is my soul! You do not hear what I am saying better than they, but they cannot reply."

Maʿārif records both scholarly possibilities: that Salih spoke these words while departing after the punishment — their benefit being the lesson they carry for all who come later — or that he said them before the punishment, though placed later in the textual order. Salih and those who believed in him then left that place. Some narrations say four thousand believers went with him to Hadramaut in Yemen, and that he passed away there; other narrations report that he went to Makkah, and that it was there he passed away.

## When the Prophet ﷺ passed those ruins

The passage has a living epilogue in the Seerah. In the ninth year of Hijrah, on the march to Tabuk, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by the area and ruins of Thamud. Imam Ahmad recorded that Ibn ʿUmar said that when the Prophet ﷺ camped near the homes of Thamud in al-Hijr, the people drew water from the wells Thamud had used, made dough with it and set their pots cooking; the Prophet ﷺ commanded them to spill the contents of the pots and give the dough to the camels, marched them on to the well the she-camel used to drink from, and forbade the Companions from entering the area where the people were tormented, saying: "I fear that what befell them might befall you as well. Therefore, do not enter on them." And Ahmad narrated that ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said while in the Hijr area: "Do not enter on these who were tormented, unless you do so while crying. If you are not crying, then do not enter on them, so that what befell them does not befall you as well." Ibn Kathir notes that the basis of this hadith is in the Two Sahihs.

This is how a believer relates to the ruins of the punished: not tourism, not indifference, but tears and fear of Allah. Maʿārif adds that Allah in His wisdom has left such habitations standing as signposts on the road — the Qur'an repeatedly told the Arabs, whose Syria trade route passed these very places, to read in them the rise and fall of peoples (28:58).

## What the passage leaves with us

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distils several rulings. All prophets agree on tawhid, and violating it brings punishment in this world and in the Hereafter. It has happened in past communities that the wealthy and the traditional holders of social prestige are the ones who refuse the call of the prophets — and are disgraced and destroyed for it. From al-Qurtubi: Allah's worldly blessings are extended to disbelievers too, as they were to ʿAd and Thamud, to whom Allah had given great wealth and power; and palaces and mansions are in themselves blessings of Allah and permissible to build — though, as Maʿārif adds, the prophets and the men of Allah have not favoured them, because they make people heedless.

The deeper thread is the one Maʿārif keeps returning to: Thamud saw the miracle they themselves designed, gave their word, and still chose water rights, status, and the familiar comforts of wealth over the truth standing in front of them. The she-camel was Allah's sign walking among them; killing her was not the killing of an animal but the deliberate, communal rejection of Allah's command — "and they insolently defied the commandment of their Lord" (ayah 77). What remains of them is carved stone, and a warning.

passages.title: Lot condemns his people's outrage; brimstone falls
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the story of Lūṭ (Lot), peace be upon him, and the people of Sodom — the fourth in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf's running series of prophets sent to their nations, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes. What binds the five ayat together is a single arc told with terrible economy: a prophet's protest against an unprecedented outrage (80–81), a people whose only answer is to expel the pure (82), and a rescue and a ruin that fit the crime exactly (83–84).

## Who Lūṭ was, and where he was sent

Ibn Kathir gives the family background: Lūṭ was the son of Hārān the son of Āzar, and the nephew of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon them both. He believed in Ibrāhīm — Maʿārif cites the Qurʼān's own words, "Then Lūṭ believed in him" (29:26) — and migrated with him from their homeland near Babel in Iraq to the land of Shām. Out of Ibrāhīm's whole family, only his wife Sārah and this nephew accepted his call. Allah then made Lūṭ a prophet in his own right and sent him to Sadūm (Sodom) near Bayt al-Maqdis and its surrounding towns — Maʿārif names five cities in all, with Sodom as their capital, the cluster whose nucleus the Qurʼān refers to in several places as Muʼtafikah and Muʼtafikāt.

Maʿārif adds a detail that explains what went wrong. The land was fertile and green, rich in grain and fruit, and the people were soaked in wealth. It then points to the Qurʼān's diagnosis of human nature: "Indeed man transgresses when he sees himself self-sufficient" (96:6–7). Ease without gratitude ate away their sense of honour and modesty until they lost the very ability to tell good from bad — and they fell into an act no people had fallen into before.

## Ayah 80 — "a lewdness none in all the worlds committed before you"

Lūṭ opens not with a gentle preamble but with a stunned question: "Do you commit the fāḥishah such as none preceding you has committed in all the worlds?"

**The word al-fāḥishah.** Fāḥishah means a shameful, indecent act. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a fine point of Arabic here. When the Qurʼān speaks of zinā (adultery and fornication) it says "surely it is fāḥishah" (17:32) — without the definite article. Here the word carries the Arabic definite article alif-lām: al-fāḥishah, "THE shameful act." The hint, Maʿārif says, is that this act is as if it were the sum of all indecencies gathered into one — a graver crime even than zinā.

**An invented sin.** Both commentaries stress the phrase "none preceding you in all the worlds." Ibn Kathir records the early authority ʿAmr bin Dīnār: "Never before the people of Lūṭ did a male have sex with another male." It had not been known among the children of Adam; it had not even crossed their minds. Maʿārif quotes the Umayyad caliph ʿAbd al-Malik (as cited in Ibn Kathir): had the Qurʼān not mentioned this event, he would never have suspected a human being could do such a thing.

**Why "unprecedented" doubles the guilt.** Maʿārif explains that this clause is not mere historical information — it is part of the indictment, on two grounds. First, people usually slide into sins through social conditions or blind imitation of their forebears; that is no excuse in the Sharīʿah, but it at least makes a sinner humanly understandable. A sin with no precedent and no compelling circumstance is a curse of the highest degree — pure invention of evil. Second, whoever originates an evil practice carries not only his own sin but a share of the sin of everyone who follows his invention until the Last Day. The people of Sodom did not merely sin; they opened a door.

## Ayah 81 — "instead of women… you are a people transgressing beyond bounds"

The second ayah makes the charge explicit: "You approach men with lust instead of women." Ibn Kathir's comment is blunt: you abandoned the women Allah created for you and turned to men — behaviour both evil and ignorant, because "you have placed things in their improper places." Maʿārif adds the positive counterpart: Allah appointed marriage to women as the lawful channel for human desire; to bypass what is natural and lawful for what is unnatural is proof of a corrupted self.

Ibn Kathir fills in the scene from the Qurʼān's parallel tellings. Lūṭ said to them, "These are my daughters, if you must act" (15:71) — meaning the women of the nation, offered in lawful marriage — and they answered, "You know well we have no need of your daughters, and you know well what we want" (11:79). They did not deny the charge; they embraced it.

**Musrifūn — the diagnosis.** The ayah ends: bal antum qawmun musrifūn — "rather, you are a people who cross the limits." Isrāf is exceeding bounds. Maʿārif reads this closing phrase as the root diagnosis: their real disease was that they overran the limits Allah set for everything; in this case the limit they vaulted over was the very boundary of humanity itself.

**The gravity in law.** Because of this passage's severity, Maʿārif records that the Companions, the Tābiʿīn and the mujtahid Imams held this crime to be graver than other acts of shame. Imam Abū Ḥanīfah held that its punishment should mirror what Allah sent upon the people of Lūṭ — the offender pushed down from a high mountain and rocks thrown upon him from above. And both commentaries cite the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, recorded by Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever you find doing the act of the people of Lūṭ, kill them — the doer and the one to whom it is done."

## Ayah 82 — the only answer: "Expel them!"

Notice what the ayah says: "his people's ONLY response" was to demand expulsion. Maʿārif points out the force of this wording — they could find no rejoinder to Lūṭ's argument. Unable to answer him, they moved to silence him: drive him and his believers out of the town.

And their stated reason is the passage's bitterest irony: "These are indeed people who keep themselves pure!" Purity itself had become, in their mouths, the accusation. Ibn Kathir records Qatādah's comment: "They shamed them with what is not a shame at all." Mujāhid's explanation — and similar is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās — spells out that the "purity" they mocked was precisely the believers' refusal of their practice. When a society inverts far enough, cleanliness becomes the crime and the clean become the outcasts.

## Ayat 83–84 — the rescue and the rain

They wanted Lūṭ expelled; Allah instead removed him in safety and destroyed them in disgrace — Ibn Kathir frames the ending exactly as this reversal.

**"Him and his family" — who was saved?** Ibn Kathir cites 51:35–36: "We brought out the believers who were in it, but We found there only a single household of Muslims" — only Lūṭ's own house had believed. Maʿārif records a difference among the commentators over the word ahl ("family"): some said it means strictly his household (including, on one view, two women who had become Muslim), others that ahl here is broader, covering the few outside believers who had joined him. Either way, the saved were a counted few, commanded to leave the town late at night and not look back, for the punishment would fall the moment they were out.

**Except his wife.** She alone of his household did not believe, remaining on the religion of her people. Ibn Kathir relates that she used to conspire with them against Lūṭ, informing them by agreed signals whenever guests came to him — which is why Lūṭ was ordered not to tell her of the departure. The commentators relate two reports about her end: that she set out with them but, eager to see the fate of the people she had left, looked back against the divine command and was seized; or that she never left the town at all — Ibn Kathir inclines to this second reading from the wording of the ayah. She was "of the ghābirīn": literally those who stayed behind, and, as Ibn Kathir says is the more obvious sense here, those who were destroyed. The lesson is stark: nearness to a prophet — even sharing his roof — saves no one whose heart sides with the wrongdoers.

**"We rained upon them a rain."** Ayah 84 compresses the punishment into three Arabic words. Ibn Kathir explains this rain by the Qurʼān's fuller account in Sūrah Hūd: "We rained on them stones of baked clay, layered one upon another, marked from your Lord — and they are never far from the wrongdoers" (11:82–83). Maʿārif assembles the scene from the parallel passages: first a terrible Sound seized them at sunrise (15:73); the angel Jibrāʼīl lifted the whole crust of their land and turned "its highest into its lowest" (11:82); and stones rained down ceaselessly, stacking one upon another, each stone — some commentators say — marked with the name of the person it was destined to destroy. (Maʿārif notes the sequence of these events is not certain, since the Qurʼān's order of mention need not be chronological.)

Maʿārif draws out the fittingness of it: of all the punishments, the overturning of their land upside down corresponds precisely to their crime — a people who inverted the natural order were themselves inverted.

## "Then see what was the end of the criminals"

The passage closes by turning to the reader. Ibn Kathir explains the address: "See, O Muhammad ﷺ, the end of those who dared to disobey Allah and reject His Messengers." The command "see" was no abstraction for the first audience. Maʿārif notes that Sūrah Hūd's warning — "they are not far from the wrongdoers" — was addressed to the people of Arabia, who passed by these overturned habitations on their way to Syria; the wonder is that they took no lesson. And the site remains visible to this day, Maʿārif adds: the region of the Dead Sea — the "Sea of Lūṭ" — between Bayt al-Maqdis and the Jordan river, lying far below sea level; on one particular section of it the water is so unusual that no sea life survives there — hence the name, the Dead Sea. This, Maʿārif says, is held to be the site of ancient Sodom. The geography itself is a standing sermon.

## What the passage leaves with a believer

Three threads run through these five ayat, each drawn by the commentators. First, prosperity without gratitude corrodes: Maʿārif traces Sodom's fall to wealth that bred transgression, the pattern of 96:6–7. Second, the originator of an evil carries the sin of all who follow it until the Last Day — a warning that applies to every invented wrong, not only theirs. Third, when truth cannot be answered it is attacked: a people with no rejoinder to Lūṭ's argument could only cry "expel them," and mock purity as self-righteousness. The believer who is shamed for keeping clean stands where Lūṭ's household stood — and the passage ends by showing whose end was disgrace, and who was carried out to safety. May Allah keep us safe from His punishment and His wrath, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes its commentary.

passages.title: Shu'aib demands honest measure; Midian destroyed
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the fifth prophet-story in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf's great sequence of destroyed nations: Shuʿaib عليه السلام sent to Madyan. What holds ayat 85–93 together is a complete arc — the call (85–86), the argument and the ultimatum (87–90), the punishment (91–92), and the prophet's farewell over the ruins (93). And what makes this story distinct from the ones before it is the sin at its centre: alongside shirk, Madyan's signature crime was **cheating in the marketplace** — the Qur'an places dishonest scales in the same indictment as worshipping false gods.

## Who Shuʿaib عليه السلام and Madyan were

The commentators trace the story's setting through a report of Muhammad bin Ishaq, which the two tafsirs render slightly differently. As Ibn Kathir relates it, the people of Madyan were the descendants of Madyan — of the line of Ibrahim عليه السلام — while Shuʿaib عليه السلام himself was the son of Mikil bin Yashjur, his name in the Syrian language being Yathrun (Jethro). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same report of Ibn Ishaq as placing Shuʿaib عليه السلام among the progeny of Madyan, the son of Ibrahim عليه السلام, and notes that he was also related to Lut عليه السلام. Ibn Kathir adds that Madyan was both the name of the tribe and of a city close to Maʿan on the route to the Hijaz; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the city still survives near Maʿan in Eastern Jordan, and that it is the same "water of Madyan" where Musa عليه السلام would later arrive (28:23). These are also the people of al-Aykah, "the Woods" — some commentators held Madyan and Aykah were two separate peoples to whom Shuʿaib عليه السلام was sent in turn, while others, including Ibn Kathir, favoured the view that they are two names for the same people. Shuʿaib عليه السلام himself was famous for his eloquence: he was called the **Speaker of the Prophets** (Ibn Kathir) for his eloquent words and eloquent advice — and this passage lets us hear why.

## The message: two kinds of rights, both violated

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the whole passage with a principle worth holding onto: the essence of what every prophet brought is the fulfilment of rights, and rights are of two kinds — the **rights of Allah** (like prayer and fasting, whose benefit is not visible in worldly terms) and the **rights of His servants** (ḥuqūq al-ʿibād, what we would call human rights). The people of Madyan were trampling both at once: violating Allah's right by refusing to believe, and violating people's rights by shaving weights and measures — and then, on top of that, sitting at the entry points of roads to terrorise and rob travellers, and to frighten off anyone inclined to believe in Shuʿaib عليه السلام. Thus, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's phrase, they had "made disorder the order of the day" on the good earth of Allah.

So in ayah 85 the message of Shuʿaib عليه السلام comes in exactly that order. First, *"O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him"* — the call of every Messenger, as Ibn Kathir notes. Second, *"a clear proof from your Lord has come to you"* — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains as the miracles manifested at the hands of Shuʿaib عليه السلام, adding that the different forms these miracles took are mentioned in Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit. Third, the command that defines this story: *"give full measure and full weight, and do not make people short of their things."*

**The language here rewards attention.** *Kail* means measure, *mīzān* is used in the sense of weighing, and *bakhs* means causing someone loss by giving them less than their due. Notice the movement of the ayah: first the specific crime is named — under-measuring and under-weighing in buying and selling — and then the prohibition is deliberately widened: *"do not make people short of their things."* Al-Bahr al-Muhit draws the conclusion: this now covers **every** kind of short-changing of rights — in property, in honour, or anything else. Attacking someone's honour, withholding the respect a person is legitimately due, failing those you are obliged to obey — all of it falls under the same crime Madyan committed with their scales. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the declaration of the Prophet ﷺ in his famous Khutbah of the Last Hajj — that people's honour is as worthy of being respected and defended as their blood — stands as a broader confirmation of this reading.

The word the Qur'an elsewhere uses for this sin, *taṭfīf* (giving short measure and weight, as in 83:1, *"Woe to al-Mutaffifin"*), stretches the same way. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that ʿUmar al-Fārūq رضي الله عنه saw a man rushing through his rukūʿ and sajdah and told him he was guilty of measuring and weighing short (Mu'atta Imam Malik) — meaning he had not fulfilled the right of the prayer as it was due. A hurried ṣalāh is a cheated scale. The concept is one: whatever is owed — to Allah or to people — pay it in full.

Ayah 85 closes: *"do not make mischief on the earth after it has been set in order"* — echoing ayah 56 earlier in this sūrah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the earth's physical order rests on using things properly, respecting limits, and maintaining moderation, equity and justice, and its spiritual order on relationship with Allah and obedience to His commands; the people of Madyan had abandoned both, until the earth had become, in the commentary's words, a hotbed of physical and spiritual disorder. And then: *"that is better for you, if you are believers."* The commentary takes this at face value for both worlds — quite apart from the Hereafter, the trader known to be scrupulously honest builds credit and goodwill, and his business grows in volume and reliability. Honesty is not only obligatory; it is *profitable*.

## The highwaymen (ayah 86)

*"And do not sit on every road, threatening…"* The early authorities read this two ways. As-Suddi said they were literally bandits, threatening travellers with death unless they surrendered their money; Ibn ʿAbbas رضي الله عنه, Mujahid and others said they blocked and intimidated believers on their way to Shuʿaib عليه السلام. Ibn Kathir prefers the first for the first clause — since the ayah then *separately* mentions *"hindering from the path of Allah those who believe in Him"* — and al-Bahr al-Muhit likewise treats them as two distinct crimes: highway robbery, and obstructing faith. *"Seeking to make it crooked"* means they were always on the lookout for something in the way of Allah they could twist and misrepresent, manufacturing doubts and objections to wean people away from the true religion.

Al-Qurtubi drew a sharp contemporary application: those who sit on thoroughfares and make people pay taxes the Shariʿah does not permit are criminals of the same kind as the people of Shuʿaib عليه السلام — indeed, he said, *more* oppressive and tyrannical.

The ayah ends with persuasion and warning paired, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes: *"remember when you were few and He multiplied you"* — a reminder of the blessing that turned an insignificant people into a numerous nation, or their economic weakness into need-free financial strength — and *"see what was the end of the mischief-makers"*: the peoples of Nuh, ʿAd, Thamud and Lut عليهم السلام, each a different punishment, all one lesson.

## The taunt of respite, and the ultimatum (ayat 87–90)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reconstructs the objection behind ayah 87. The people argued: if Shuʿaib عليه السلام were truly a prophet, his believers would be flourishing and his deniers suffering — yet both groups live equally comfortably, so how can he be true? His answer: *"be patient until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges."* Allah is Forbearing and Merciful; He grants wrongdoers respite, and His decree comes into action only when they become absolutely wicked and high-handed. Do not mistake the delay of judgment for its absence.

Unconvinced, the arrogant chiefs (*al-malaʼ alladhīna 'stakbarū*) said what, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, is always said by oppressive practitioners of arrogance. In ayah 88: *"We shall drive you out, O Shuʿaib, and those who believe with you — or you shall return to our religion."* Ibn Kathir notes they addressed Shuʿaib عليه السلام but intended his followers too.

But their word *"return"* raises a real puzzle: a prophet never followed a false religion for a single day. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's answer is illuminating: before prophethood, Shuʿaib عليه السلام had lived quietly among his people, keeping silent over their falsehoods, so they simply assumed he was one of them. Only when he proclaimed his call did they "discover" his religion differed — and concluded he had left theirs. His reply, *"Even though we hate it?"*, is a way of saying: it can never be.

**Ayah 89 is the theological heart of the passage.** To return to their religion, Shuʿaib عليه السلام says, would be *"fabricating a lie against Allah."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the double lie: calling kufr and shirk a "religion" already implies falsely that Allah commanded it; and for one who has known the revealed truth to go back would declare the true false and the false true — a compounded slander against Allah.

Then comes a moment of exquisite prophetic manners. Having asserted "we can never return," Shuʿaib عليه السلام immediately catches the flavour of claim and self-assertion in his own words — which sits ill with the selfless submission (*ʿabdiyyah*, being a true slave of Allah) of those who are close to Him and have come to know Him. So he adds: *"and it is not for us to return to it unless Allah, our Lord, should will. Our Lord encompasses everything in knowledge; in Allah we place our trust."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the three virtues shining here: *ʿijz* (humility — owning that one has no power of one's own), *tawakkul* (trust in Allah), and *tafwīḍ* (resigning one's affairs to Him) — master virtues of the prophets. Our guidance and our steadfastness are not our achievement but Allah's grace, as the Prophet ﷺ himself expressed: had it not been for the grace of Allah, we would not have been guided, nor given charity, nor prayed.

And when Shuʿaib عليه السلام saw that nothing would move these people, he stopped addressing them and turned to his Lord: *"Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth, and You are the best of all who decide."* Ibn ʿAbbas رضي الله عنه explained that *fatḥ* here means "decide" — so *fātiḥ* takes the sense of judge, and Allah is *"the Most Just Who never wrongs any in His judgment"* (Ibn Kathir). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states plainly what this duʿāʼ amounted to: a prayer for the destruction of the deniers — and it was answered.

The chiefs got in one last word (ayah 90), spoken among themselves or to their followers (al-Bahr al-Muhit, from ʿAtaʼ): *"If you follow Shuʿaib, you will surely be the losers."* Hold onto that word, *losers* — the Qur'an is about to return it to sender.

## One punishment, three names (ayat 91–92)

Ayah 91 says *the Rajfah* — the earthquake — seized them. But Sūrah Hud (11:94) says it was the *Ṣayḥah*, the deafening cry; and Sūrah ash-Shuʿaraʼ (26:189) says it was the punishment of the *Day of the Shadow* (Yawm aẓ-Ẓullah). Ibn Kathir shows the fit is deliberate: in Hud they had mocked his prayer — *"Does your ṣalāh command you…?"* (11:87) — so the cry that silenced them is mentioned there; in ash-Shuʿaraʼ they had jeered, *"cause a piece of the heaven to fall on us"* (26:187) — so the falling torment from a cloud is mentioned there. His conclusion: **all three struck together on the Day of the Shadow** — a gloomy cloud above containing fire, flames and a tremendous light, a cry descending from the sky, and a tremor from beneath, until their souls were taken and *"they lay prostrate in their homes."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, citing al-Bahr al-Muhit, how Ibn ʿAbbas رضي الله عنه reconciled the verses by describing how it unfolded: first an unbearable heat, as if a door of Hell had been thrown open towards them — no shade or water relieved it; they fled into basements and found them hotter; they ran from the city to the nearby forest, where Allah sent a thick cloud with a cool breeze passing beneath it. Out of their senses with heat, they all rushed for refuge under its shade — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the dreadful irony of that gathering: here were the criminals walking on their own two feet to the exact spot where they were to be destroyed, without a warrant of arrest and without a police gun pointed at them. Then the whole cloud became a cloud of fire raining on them, and the earthquake shook the earth, and it was over. (Some commentators alternatively held that the people were split into groups, some struck by the earthquake and others by the punishment of the shade.)

Ayah 92 delivers the epitaph, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this lesson is the real purpose of the whole narrative. *"Those who denied Shuʿaib — as if they had never dwelt there."* One meaning of the word *ghinā* is living somewhere in peace and comfort, and that is the sense here: homes that had been full of ease turned so deserted it was as if peace and comfort had never existed in them. And then the Qur'an picks up the chiefs' own taunt from ayah 90 and reverses it word for word: *"Those who denied Shuʿaib — they were the losers."* The men who threatened to expel the believers from their city were themselves the ones the loss struck. Ibn Kathir notes that it looked as if they had never dwelled in the very land from which they wanted to expel their Messenger and his followers.

## The prophet's farewell (ayah 93)

Shuʿaib عليه السلام turned away — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says he and the believers moved off with the punishment in sight, and the majority of commentators relate that they travelled to Makkah and remained there to the end. His parting words over his people are among the most human in the Qur'an: *"O my people, I delivered to you the messages of my Lord and gave you sincere counsel — so how can I grieve over a disbelieving people?"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the emotional truth beneath them: it was his own total disappointment at their obstinacy that had moved him to pray for their punishment; yet when it actually fell, his heart still ached with a prophet's concern and affection for his people. These words were spoken *for the peace of his own heart* — the consolation of a man who knows he withheld nothing, and must now let go.

## Living it

The passage's demands on a believer are unusually concrete. Give full measure — at the till, in the contract, in the hours you bill. But remember the ayah's own widening: *bakhs* covers every right you can shave — a person's property, their honour, the respect they are due, and the rights of Allah Himself, down to a rukūʿ rushed like a cheated scale. And Madyan's other lesson is about the reading of history: their comfort alongside the believers' comfort was not vindication but respite. Allah is *khayr al-ḥākimīn* — the best of judges — and His verdict, when it comes, needs no second hearing.

passages.title: Allah's pattern: hardship, ease, false security
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is doing

Sūrah al-Aʿrāf has been telling the stories of the early prophets and the nations that rejected them — five such accounts so far — and it will shortly turn to Mūsā (peace be upon him). In ayat 94–99 the Qur'an pauses between the stories and states the law that ran through all of them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Qur'an is not a history book: it does not narrate events in full or in chronological order, but selects the portion that carries the lesson. Here the lesson itself is laid bare. Ayah 94 warns that the fate described in the preceding accounts was not something peculiar to the peoples of Nūḥ, ʿĀd and Thamūd; it is Allah's regular way with every town that receives a prophet and denies him — first hardship, sent so that hearts might humble themselves; then ease, sent to test gratitude; and when both fail, a sudden seizure while the people are unaware. The passage then turns that history into a direct question aimed at every later generation: *did they feel secure against Allah's plan?*

## The first test: hardship sent as a summons (ayah 94)

In ayah 94, Allah says that whenever He sent a prophet to a town, He seized its people with **baʾsāʾ** and **ḍarrāʾ**. The commentators unpack this pair of words slightly differently. Ibn Kathir explains baʾsāʾ as the physical sicknesses and ailments they suffered, and ḍarrāʾ as the poverty and humiliation they experienced. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the Companion ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd took baʾsāʾ to mean hunger or poverty and ḍarrāʾ to mean illness, and that some linguists likewise assigned baʾsāʾ to financial distress and ḍarrāʾ to loss of health. However the two words are distributed, together they cover the two things human beings fear most: the breaking of the body and the breaking of livelihood.

The purpose is given in the ayah itself: *laʿallahum yaḍḍarraʿūn* — "so that they might humble themselves." Ibn Kathir explains this as supplicating, humbling oneself and invoking Allah so that He might lift the affliction. In other words, the suffering was never vengeance for its own sake; it was a summons. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it a blessing of Allah in disguise, meant for the people's own good, because it is simply human to turn to the Creator in distress. It cites the great spiritual leader Maulana Rumi, who versified this very fact: the people are made to misbehave with you in order that you turn to your Lord in tears. Yet, Ibn Kathir observes, these nations did not do what the affliction was designed to produce — they did not invoke Him.

## The second test: ease (ayah 95)

So the test was reversed. In ayah 95 Allah says He "changed the evil for the good" — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that **sayyiʾah** here means distress and **ḥasanah** means prosperity — *until they ʿafaw*, a word both commentaries explain as increase: they grew in numbers, wealth and offspring. Ibn Kathir spells out the exchange: hardship became prosperity, disease became health, poverty became rich provision — *so that they might be thankful*. Prosperity after long adversity should have melted them into gratitude and repentance.

Instead, it produced a philosophy. They said: "Our fathers were touched with evil and with good." Ibn Kathir voices their reasoning: hardship came and prosperity followed, exactly as it did for our forefathers — it is just a cycle; sometimes you suffer, sometimes you enjoy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it sharply: they concluded that suffering and prosperity had nothing to do with their deeds; it was merely the natural course of changing phenomena. This is the oldest way of neutralising a warning — explain it away as weather. Ibn Kathir's verdict is that they failed both tests: neither affliction nor abundance moved them to change, because they never comprehended that Allah was testing them in both.

Then the sentence falls with no further warning: *"So We seized them all of a sudden while they were unaware."* The word **baghtatan** — suddenly — is the hinge of the whole passage. The seizure comes precisely when the cycle-theory has explained the warnings away; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that it came only after their obstinate persistence in evil and ignorance.

## How a believer reads the same two tests

Against this double failure, Ibn Kathir sets the believer, who is grateful in good times and patient in hard times, and he cites the hadith recorded in the Sahih: *"The matter of the believer is amazing, for nothing that Allah decrees for him but it is better for him. If a ḍarrāʾ (harm) strikes him, he is patient, and this is better for him; and if he is given sarrāʾ (prosperity), he thanks Allah for it, and this is better for him."* The believer, Ibn Kathir says, is aware of the test hidden inside both adversity and ease. He also cites another hadith: the believer will continue to be tested by afflictions until he ends up pure from sin, while the parable of the hypocrite is that of a donkey — it does not know why its owners tied it or released it. And on the sudden seizure itself, Ibn Kathir cites a hadith describing sudden death: it is a mercy for the believer, but a sorrowful punishment for the disbeliever.

## The door that never opened: barakah (ayah 96)

Ayah 96 states the counterfactual — what these towns forfeited. Had they believed and had **taqwa** — which Ibn Kathir defines concretely as hearts believing in what the Messenger brought, obeying him, performing the acts of obedience and abstaining from the prohibitions — Allah would have "opened for them blessings (**barakāt**) from the heaven and the earth": in Ibn Kathir's words, the rain that falls from the sky and the vegetation of the earth. Ibn Kathir adds a sobering cross-reference: reading this ayah alongside Sūrah Yūnus (10:98), no city believed in its entirety except the city of the Prophet Yūnus — when his people believed, the torment of disgrace was removed from them and they were permitted to enjoy for a while.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on the word **barakah** itself, which signifies increase or growth, and observes that it works in two distinct ways. Sometimes the thing itself multiplies — as is reported happening with the Holy Prophet ﷺ, when a large number of people drank their fill from one small pot of water, or a whole army was fed to satisfaction from a small quantity of food. And sometimes the quantity stays the same but its usefulness multiplies: a single morsel gives great strength while a large meal gives none; an hour holds what would otherwise take four or five. The "blessings of heaven and earth," then, are not merely more rain and more crops but the carefree, anxiety-free enjoyment of what one has.

From this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws its striking modern observation: the earth's produce today is greater than ever before, and inventions serve us in ways past generations could not imagine — yet man is proportionally more worried, depressed and deprived of peace than ever. No explanation fits except that barakah is missing. The ayah quietly diagnoses the modern condition: abundance without faith and taqwa is abundance without blessing.

**A necessary caution.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that prosperity is therefore not automatically a sign of Allah's favour. Sometimes it is given out of anger, as Sūrah al-Anʿām (6:44) says: when they forgot the reminder, "We opened to them the doors of all good things" — and then they were seized suddenly. Outwardly, favour and wrath can look identical. The men of Allah suggested a sign to tell them apart: when prosperity and health make a person more grateful and more devoted in worship, it indicates favour; when they draw him deeper into sin, they are a sign of wrath — and we seek Allah's shelter from that state.

## The three questions of false security (ayat 97–99)

The passage now closes in on its target with three questions. In ayah 97: did the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment would not come **bayātan** — by night — while they slept? In ayah 98: or that it would not come in the **ḍuḥā** — the forenoon — while they played? The two images bracket a whole day and a whole life: the punishment can arrive when you are unconscious in bed or when you are wide awake and absorbed in amusement — "busy in their affairs and unaware," as Ibn Kathir puts it. There is no hour of safety for the heedless.

Ayah 99 gathers both into the decisive question: *"Did they then feel secure against Allah's plan (makr Allāh)?"* Ibn Kathir explains this as His torment, His vengeance, and His power to destroy them while they are inattentive and heedless. And the ayah answers itself with one of the most piercing lines in the Qur'an: *"None feels secure from Allah's plan except the people who are the losers."* Feeling safe from Allah is not confidence; the ayah itself defines it as the mark of the loser.

Ibn Kathir seals the point with the words of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: "The believer performs the acts of worship, all the while feeling fear, in fright and anxiety. The Fājir (wicked sinner, or disbeliever) commits the acts of disobedience while feeling safe (from Allah's torment)!" The two states of heart are exactly inverted from what one would expect — and that inversion is the whole psychology of this passage.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that these questions were aimed first at the people living in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, who should not have felt themselves secure from a punishment that could come while they slept at night or while they were busy in their worldly pursuits — and through them at every reader: the fate of the early nations should be a lesson, for the wise person takes his lesson from the events of other people, and avoids the road that led them to death and disaster.

## Living it

The passage asks something quite specific of a believer. First, read your own circumstances as this passage reads history: hardship is a summons to turn to Allah in humility and duʿāʾ, and ease is a test of gratitude — the believer of the Sahih hadith wins both, with patience in one and thanks in the other. Second, refuse the "natural cycle" narrative by which the ancient towns talked themselves out of repenting; the moment good times and bad times mean nothing, the heart has failed both tests at once. Third, apply the diagnostic of the men of Allah to your own prosperity: is it making you worship more, or sin more? And finally, hold al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's contrast before you: worship with a fearing heart, and never let obedience — still less disobedience — breed the feeling of being safe from Allah's plan. That security belongs only to the losers.

passages.title: The lesson for inheritors of ruined lands
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:100–102 — The Lesson for the Inheritors of Ruined Lands

These three ayat are the hinge of Sūrah al-Aʿrāf's long historical section. Ibn Kathir notes that they come immediately after the stories of the peoples of the Prophets Nūḥ, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lūṭ and Shuʿayb — may Allah's peace and blessings be on them all — five nations whom Allah warned by explaining the truth through the words of His Messengers, then destroyed the disbelievers among them and saved the believers. Here the narration pauses and the lesson is drawn out. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān states the purpose plainly: after relating the events of the early peoples, these verses invite the people of Arabia and the people of the whole world to take lesson from them — to abstain from the deeds that incurred Allah's wrath, and to follow the practices that led the prophets and their believers to eternal success. The passage is held together by a single, sobering question: you who now live on land whose former owners were wiped out for their sins — has none of this taught you anything?

## History that is meant to guide

Ayah 100 opens: *"Is it not a guidance for those who inherit the earth from its previous inhabitants — that had We willed, We would have punished them for their sins?"* The early master-commentator Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī, whom Ibn Kathir cites, unpacks the address: Allah is speaking to those who succeeded on the earth after the previous nations who dwelt in it were destroyed — and who then followed the very same ways, behaving as those nations did and being unruly with their Lord. The Companion Ibn ʿAbbās explained the ayah in the same sense, and Mujāhid and several others said similarly: did We not make clear to them that, had We willed, We could have struck them for their sins just as We struck those before them?

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws attention to the verb itself. The word *yahdi* is from *hadā*, which signifies "to guide" or "to inform" — and strikingly, it is the *events* that are made the subject of the verb. The ruined nations are not merely information; they are meant to be a means of guidance for every later generation that has inherited the land from its earlier owners. The warning is direct: the inheritors can incur the punishment of Allah for their disbelief exactly as their predecessors met ruin and disaster for their disobedience.

Ayah 101 then holds the whole gallery of ruined towns up before the Prophet ﷺ: *"Those were the towns whose story We relate unto you."* Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes two precise word choices in this sentence. The word *nabaʼ* is not just "news" but *great* news — events of weight. And the little word *min* ("some of their stories") signals that what the sūrah has narrated is only a selection from a much larger number of events, all bearing the same lesson. Ibn Kathir adds the essential context of divine justice by citing: *"And We never punish until We have sent a Messenger (to give warning)"* (17:15) and *"That is some of the news of the towns which We relate unto you; of them, some are standing, and some have been reaped. We wronged them not, but they wronged themselves"* (11:100–101). No town was destroyed unwarned.

Ibn Kathir shows that the Qurʼān returns to this theme of history-as-guidance again and again, citing parallel ayat: *"Is it not a guidance for them: how many generations We have destroyed before them, in whose dwellings they walk?"* (20:128, and similarly 32:26); *"And you dwelt in the dwellings of men who wronged themselves"* (14:44–45); and *"How many a generation before them have We destroyed! Can you find a single one of them or hear even a whisper of them?"* (19:98). The image is deliberate: people literally walking through the houses of the destroyed, and still not hearing. Many other ayat, Ibn Kathir adds, testify to the same pattern — Allah's torment strikes His enemies, while His bounty reaches His faithful believers.

## The seal that runs through both ayat

The seal of the heart binds ayah 100 and ayah 101 together. Ayah 100 ends: *"And We seal up their hearts so that they hear not"* — and ayah 101, after exposing the nations' obstinacy, concludes with the same verb: *"Thus Allah does seal up the hearts of the disbelievers."* The Arabic root here, *ṭabʿ*, is the word used for printing or stamping — pressing a mark onto something so that it takes a fixed impression. Aṭ-Ṭabarī glosses the phrase in ayah 100: We place a cover over their heart, so that they do not hear words of advice or reminding.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains the sequence carefully: these people took no lesson from the past events, and by that refusal they incurred the wrath of Allah, with the result that their hearts were sealed and they became unable to listen to the truth at all. The seal is not arbitrary; it is the end-stage of a person's own accumulated choices. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān cites a Tradition of the Prophet ﷺ describing how this happens: when a person commits a sin for the first time, a black dot is placed on his heart; if he keeps committing sins a second and third time, a second and third dot are placed; and if he goes on increasing in his sins without repenting to Allah, these black spots keep increasing until the whole heart is painted black. This ultimately deprives a person of the natural faculty of distinguishing right from wrong: he comes to receive evil as good and good as evil, the harmful as useful and the useful as harmful. The Qurʼān elsewhere terms this perversion of understanding *raʼn*, signifying the rust of the heart; in this ayah, as in many others, the finished state is named *ṭabʿ*, the seal.

There is a beautiful linguistic point here. One might expect ayah 100 to end "so that they do not *understand*" (*lā yafqahūn*), since a sealed heart damages comprehension, not the ears. Instead it says "so that they do not *hear*" (*lā yasmaʿūn*). Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān offers two explanations. First, understanding is usually the result of listening to the truth — so once the heart is sealed, they are rendered unable even to listen to it. Second, all the human faculties and limbs are controlled by the heart, so when the heart malfunctions, everything connected to it is adversely affected. Just as a person who loves someone or something likes everything in it — good or bad — a corrupted heart bends every faculty to its own bias.

How does the seal set in? Ayah 101 supplies the answer through the middle of the verse: *"And there came indeed to them their Messengers with clear proofs, but they were not such who would believe in what they rejected before."* Ibn Kathir relays the explanation of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, which he judges sound: they would not have believed later in what the Messengers brought, because they had denied the truth when it first came to them — *although they recognized it*. Their first rejection locked them in. Ibn Kathir supports this with the ayah: *"And We shall turn their hearts and their eyes away (from guidance), as they refused to believe therein for the first time"* (6:109–110). This, he says, is why Allah then declares, *"Thus Allah does seal up the hearts of the disbelievers"* — and Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān spells out what that sealing means here: Allah seals the hearts of those who disbelieve and reject the truth, making them unable to accept good as good.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān presses on what "clear proofs" (*bayyināt*) implies. Since the ayah says the messengers — all of them — came with clear signs, we learn that miracles were given to *every* prophet, even though the Qurʼān mentions the miracles of only some; one may not infer that the prophets whose miracles go unmentioned were given none. When the people of Hūd, peace be upon him, said "you did not bring any clear sign" (as appears in Sūrah Hūd), this very ayah shows their statement was simply obstinacy — or perhaps they thought his miracles of less significance. Miracles are a definite means of deciding between right and wrong; these nations rejected them for one reason only: to prove that what they had once said was true.

And here Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān (citing *Masāʼil al-Sulūk*) turns the mirror on us: most Muslims, even some ʿulamāʼ — the religious scholars — are seen to have the same habit of supporting their wrong statements in the face of clear proofs of the truth. The book states plainly that this condition is a usual cause of incurring Allah's wrath. The disease of the destroyed nations was not lack of evidence; it was the refusal to lose an argument.

## The broken covenant

Ayah 102 gives the final verdict on those same nations: *"And most of them We found not true to their covenant, but most of them We found indeed rebellious"* — *fāsiqīn*, deviating away from obedience and compliance, as Ibn Kathir glosses it. But which covenant? The sources record differing explanations from the early authorities:

**The covenant of the fiṭrah.** Ibn Kathir explains it as the pure natural disposition (*fiṭrah*) Allah instilled in every human being while still in their fathers' loins — the taking of their covenant that He is their Lord and King and that there is no deity worthy of worship except Him. They affirmed it and testified against themselves to it; then they defied it, threw it behind their backs, and worshipped others besides Allah with no proof or plea, no support from rationality or divine law. The pure fiṭrah itself defies such actions, and all the honorable Messengers, from beginning to end, forbade them. Ibn Kathir cites two hadiths here: Muslim collected the hadith in which Allah says, "I created My servants ḥunafāʼ (monotheists), but the devils came to them and deviated them from their religion and prohibited them what I allowed them"; and it is recorded in the Two Sahihs: "Every child is born upon the fiṭrah; it is only his parents who turn him into a Jew, a Christian or a Zoroastrian."

**The covenant of "Am I not your Lord?"** Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān relates from the Companion ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās (as cited in Tafsīr Kabīr) that this is the covenant Allah made with the spirits of all creatures before creating them, when He asked, *"Alastu bi-rabbikum?"* — "Am I not your Lord?" — and every human spirit answered "Yes." Most people forgot this covenant after they came to earth and got involved in worshipping false gods instead of worshipping Allah.

**The covenant of īmān.** The Companion ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd held that it is the covenant of faith (*īmān*) itself, as indicated in the ayah, *"Except the one who entered into a covenant with the Raḥmān (Allah)."* On this reading, the verse implies that most people deviated from their covenant of staying obedient to Allah.

Following this last explanation, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān makes the ayah uncomfortably contemporary. Nearly every person, when trapped in real distress — no matter how sinful he is — turns to Allah and promises, in words or in his heart, that if he is relieved he will be faithful and obedient and avoid disobedience. And once out of the mess, he indulges in his mundane desires with no regard for his covenant with Allah. The Qurʼān mentions many such people. Notice, too, the precision of the wording: *most* of them, not *all*. Some are so perverted that even in distress they do not turn to Allah or think of making any promise; and — the other side of the exception — there are those who fulfil their promise and stay obedient to Him. The ayah leaves that door open.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān closes the section by stating its purpose outright: five events of earlier peoples were described so that people today may learn the lesson and avoid following the course that led their forefathers to disaster. Concretely, the passage asks three things of a believer. First, let history do what the ayah's verb says it is for: the sources note that *hadā* can mean both to inform and to guide, and the events are meant not merely to be known but to guide the generations who now hold the land. Second, guard the heart before the seal: sins darken it dot by dot, and it is the one who goes on increasing in sin without repenting to Allah whose heart is finally painted black — so never defend a wrong position just because you once voiced it, for that obstinacy is precisely the trait that marked the destroyed nations and, the sources warn, is a usual cause of incurring Allah's wrath among Muslims and even scholars. Third, keep the covenant when the crisis passes: the promise made to Allah in distress still binds in ease, and the ayah's "most of them" is an invitation to be among those who fulfil their promise and stay obedient to Him.

The sūrah then turns (from ayah 103) to the story of Mūsā, peace be upon him, which is described in some detail in the verses that follow — because his miracles were larger in number and more prominent in their nature, and because his people, the Israelites, were more obstinate and ignorant than other people; those verses also carry injunctions and points of discussion of their own.

passages.title: Moses before Pharaoh with staff and hand
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat bring Mūsā (peace be upon him) into the presence of Pharaoh: announcing his prophethood, demanding the release of the Children of Israel, and — when challenged — producing the two miracles of the staff and the shining hand. What holds the passage together is a single dramatic scene: Ibn Kathir describes it as "a debate that took place between Mūsā and Firʿawn," in which Mūsā refuted Firʿawn with unequivocal proof and clear miracles, in the presence of Firʿawn and his people, the Copts of Egypt — claim, challenge, and proof, all in the open.

## "Then, after them" — a new chapter in the surah

The passage begins with *thumma baʿathnā min baʿdihim* — "Then after them We sent…" (ayah 103). Ibn Kathir explains the "them": the messengers the surah has just recounted — Nūḥ, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lūṭ and Shuʿayb (may Allah's peace and blessings be on them and the rest of Allah's Prophets). Now Mūsā (peace be upon him) is sent "with Our signs" — proofs and clear evidences, as Ibn Kathir puts it — to Firʿawn, who was the ruler of Egypt in Mūsā's time, and to his *malaʾ*, his chiefs, whom Ibn Kathir glosses simply as "the people of Firʿawn."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two useful background notes. First, "Pharaoh" (Firʿawn) was not a personal name but the title of the Egyptian kings, and the Pharaoh of Mūsā's time is said to be Mernephtah. Second, the "signs" Mūsā brought may refer either to the verses of the Torah or to his miracles.

## Doing wrong *to* the signs

Ayah 103 says of Pharaoh's people *fa-ẓalamū bihā* — literally, they did *ẓulm* to the signs. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up this word beautifully: *ẓulm*, usually translated "wrong" or "injustice," really means **using a thing for the opposite of the purpose it was created for**. Instead of receiving Allah's verses with gratitude and faith, they met them with indifference and rejection. That is injustice done to the sign itself.

Ibn Kathir sharpens the point with a parallel ayah: "And they belied them wrongfully and arrogantly, **though they were themselves convinced thereof**" (27:14). Their disbelief was not honest doubt — it was denial out of injustice and stubbornness, rejecting what their own souls knew to be true. Hence the ayah's closing warning: "So see how was the end of the mischief-makers." Ibn Kathir notes that this "end" was public drowning — a punishment whose openness added disgrace for Firʿawn and his people, while adding comfort to the hearts of Allah's party, Mūsā and those who believed in him, who were watching. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the phrase is an invitation to every reader: take lesson from these events and think of your own fate.

## The messenger's declaration (ayat 104–105)

Mūsā's opening words are a complete declaration of prophethood. "O Firʿawn! Verily, I am a Messenger from the Lord of all that exists" — meaning, as Ibn Kathir puts it, the One who sent me is **the Creator, Lord and King of all things**. Before the ruler of Egypt, Mūsā announces an authority above every throne.

Then comes a striking phrase in ayah 105: *ḥaqīqun ʿalā an lā aqūla ʿalā Allāhi illā al-ḥaqq* — "Proper it is for me that I say nothing concerning Allah but the truth." Ibn Kathir explains: it is incumbent on me, a duty, to convey only the truth from Him, "because of what I know of His might and power." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the doctrine underneath: the message Allah gives His prophets is a **sacred trust**, and tampering with it would be a great sin — which is why all the prophets of Allah are free of all sins and cannot do so. Mūsā is telling Pharaoh: my truthfulness is beyond question; I have never uttered a word of lie; and my miracles stand as clear proof behind my claim.

The declaration ends in a demand: "So let the Children of Israel depart along with me." Ibn Kathir spells out what this meant — release them from your slavery and subjugation, and let them worship your Lord and their Lord. And he reminds us who these enslaved people were: the offspring of an honourable Prophet, Isrāʾīl — that is, Yaʿqūb, son of Isḥāq, son of Ibrāhīm, the *Khalīl* (intimate friend) of Allah.

## Pharaoh's challenge (ayah 106)

Pharaoh's reply is pure obstinacy. Ibn Kathir reads it as: "I will not believe in what you have said, nor entertain your request" — *but* if you have a proof, produce it for us to see, so we know if your claim is true. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Pharaoh, out of his obstinacy, "did not listen to anything" and simply demanded: "If you have come with a sign, bring it out, if you are among the truthful."

## The staff (ayah 107)

Mūsā threw down his staff — *fa-idhā hiya thuʿbānun mubīn*, "and behold, it was a manifest serpent." Both words repay attention.

**Thuʿbān.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this Arabic word signifies a **huge serpent** — not a mere snake. Ibn Kathir records from ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah that Ibn ʿAbbās said it refers to "the male snake," and As-Suddī and Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said similarly.

**Mubīn.** The adjective means "clear, prominent, manifest" — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a sharp contrast from it: the miracle happened **openly, before the eyes of Pharaoh's people**, not in some hidden or secluded place "as is usually done by magicians." A miracle has nothing to hide.

The early commentators paint the scene vividly. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās, cited by Ibn Kathir, says the staff became a huge snake that opened its mouth and rushed towards Firʿawn — who leapt from his throne and cried to Mūsā for help to remove it, which Mūsā did. As-Suddī's description is even more dramatic: the serpent placed its lower jaw on the ground while its upper jaw reached the top of the palace wall; Firʿawn was so frightened that he jumped and wet himself — something that had never happened to him before — and cried, "O Mūsā! Take it away and I will believe in you and release the Children of Israel to you." So Mūsā, peace be on him, took it, and it became a staff again. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a report cited on the authority of the Companion Ibn ʿAbbās (via Tafsīr Kabīr) that as the serpent moved towards Pharaoh, he jumped from his throne and sought shelter near Mūsā himself, and many of his courtiers died of extreme fear. The tyrant who would not "entertain the request" of the Lord of the worlds fled, in the moment of terror, to the Lord's own messenger.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also pauses on the miracle itself: the transformation of a staff into a real serpent is not actually impossible — it is only surprising because it is *unusual*. That is precisely what a miracle is: an unusual act beyond the power of any ordinary person, which Allah shows through His prophets so that people understand they are true prophets of Allah.

## The shining hand (ayah 108)

Then the second sign: *wa-nazaʿa yadahu fa-idhā hiya bayḍāʾu lil-nāẓirīn* — "And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white for the beholders."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks each word. **Nazaʿa** means to extract something with force — Mūsā pulled his hand out with a deliberate motion. This ayah does not say from where, but other ayat fill in the picture: "enter your hand under your robe" (27:12) and "put your hand under your arm" (20:22) — so he would draw it out either from under his arm or from under his shirt. **Bayḍāʾ** means white — and since whiteness of skin can also be due to disease, the Qurʼān elsewhere adds "without an evil" (27:12, 28:32) to eliminate any such doubt. Ibn Kathir cites Ibn ʿAbbās on exactly this: "without hurt" means "not because of leprosy" — the hand was shining, not sick, and when Mūsā put it back into his sleeve it returned to its normal colour; Mujāhid and several others said the same. A Tradition reported by the Companion ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās (cited via Qurṭubī in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān) says this whiteness was no ordinary kind: it was a **light that illuminated the whole surrounding**. Even the word **nāẓirīn** ("the onlookers") carries meaning — the light was so surprising that people gathered to see it.

## Two signs, two messages

Why two miracles? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a lovely reading of the pairing. Mūsā (peace be upon him) performed both on this occasion at Pharaoh's demand. The serpent was to serve as a **warning** for the unbelievers — power unleashed, terror before the throne. The radiant hand aimed at **inviting them to the truth** — pure light, drawing the onlookers in. And the light of the hand carried its own symbolism: the message Mūsā brought was itself a light, and to follow it would lead people to eternal success.

## Taking the lesson

Ayah 103 tells us where this story ends — "so see how was the end of the mischief-makers" — before the confrontation even begins, and Ibn Kathir tells us what that end was: public drowning, disgrace for Firʿawn's party and comfort for the believers who watched. The *ẓulm* of ayah 103 is the whole story in one word: to be given clear signs and to use them for the opposite of what they were sent for. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's closing counsel on that ayah is addressed to us: take lesson from these events, and think of your own fate.

passages.title: Pharaoh's chiefs plot and summon the magicians
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:109–114 — Pharaoh's chiefs plot and summon the magicians

These six ayat show what happens in Pharaoh's court in the moments after Musa (peace be upon him) has displayed his great signs — the staff turned serpent and the hand emitting strong white light. Instead of belief, the court produces a counter-narrative and a counter-plan: label the miracle as magic, frighten the people with talk of losing their land, and summon every expert sorcerer in the kingdom to defeat him. The unit holds together as a single scene of conspiracy — from the first accusation in ayah 109 to the sealed bargain between Pharaoh and his magicians in ayah 114 — and it sets the stage for the public contest that follows.

## "A sorcerer — but a knowing one" (ayah 109)

The speakers in ayah 109 are *al-malaʾ* — a word Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains as the influential chiefs. Ibn Kathir, speaking of these same men as the chiefs and noblemen of the people of Firʿawn, notes that it was actually Pharaoh who first said "this is indeed a well-versed sorcerer" once he felt safe and had returned to his throne, and the chiefs then agreed with him. The accusation was the court's official line, echoed downward by the elite.

But notice the wording they chose: not merely *sāḥir* (sorcerer) but *sāḥir ʿalīm* — a *knowing* sorcerer, one of great expertise. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws out what this concession betrays. These men believed Pharaoh to be their god and had never seen anything in their lives beyond the magical charms of professional sorcerers, so "sorcery" was the only category they had. Yet even they sensed that what Musa (peace be upon him) had shown was not comparable to the acts of ordinary magicians — so they had to add *ʿalīm*, admitting in the very act of denial that this was something beyond the normal trade.

## Miracle and magic are not the same thing

Because the whole plot rests on confusing the two, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān pauses here to set out how miracle and sorcery differ:
