- **The bearer.** Sorcerers usually live in impurity — indeed, the more unclean they are, the more successful their sorcery — while the prophets are by nature the cleanest and purest of people.
- **The claim.** A sorcerer is never successful when he makes a claim to prophethood.
- **The mechanism.** Acts of sorcery work through physical causes like other things; the causes are simply hidden from common people, so people imagine something causeless has happened. A miracle, by contrast, is directly a manifestation of Allah's power and has nothing to do with physical causes. This is why the Qur'an ascribes miracles directly to Allah rather than to the prophets themselves — as when it says "but Allah threw the pebbles," though the pebbles were thrown by the Prophet ﷺ at the battle of Badr.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān adds that Allah has provided these obvious distinctions precisely to eliminate any possible confusion for a common individual — and, tellingly, even Pharaoh's people found Musa's miracles somehow different from the normal acts of sorcerers, which is why they called him a sorcerer "of great knowledge" rather than a common one.

## The fear behind the plot (ayah 110)

"He wants to drive you out of your land" — this is the political move. Ibn Kathir describes how the chiefs held counsel, conspiring to extinguish the light Musa (peace be upon him) had brought and to bring down his word, plotting to portray him as a liar and a fake. Their stated fear was that he would lure the people to his side "by his magic," as they claimed, and so prevail over them and drive them from their land.

Ibn Kathir then points out a piercing irony: the very thing they feared is exactly what Allah brought about. He cites Allah's words, "And We let Firʿawn and Haman and their hosts receive from them that which they feared" (28:6). Their scheming did not avert the outcome; it walked them into it.

## The plan: stall him and summon the experts (ayat 111–112)

Introducing these verses, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān frames the deeper failure behind the plot: after seeing staves turn into serpents and a hand emit strong white light, logic and sense demanded that Pharaoh be convinced and believe. But it is the common practice of wrongdoers to seek false interpretations of the truth in order to conceal it — so instead of submitting, Pharaoh and his people belied him and told the people that this man was a great sorcerer who wanted to expel them from their homes and take over the rule of the country.

The chiefs' advice comes in ayah 111: *arjih wa-akhāhu* — concerning which Ibn Kathir records the comment of Ibn ʿAbbas that *arjih* means "delay him (for a time)." Put him and his brother off for now, while the counter-move is prepared. Then: "send to the cities *ḥāshirīn*" — which Ibn Kathir explains as sending throughout the areas and provinces of Pharaoh's kingdom to gather magicians from various lands.

Why did this seem like a winning strategy? Ibn Kathir explains that at that time magic was "the trade of the day," widespread and popular. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān adds that, sorcery being the custom of the day, the sorcerers enjoyed a high status among people. Working from the false assumption that what Musa brought was simply their kind of magic done better, they brought all the magicians in order to defeat the miracles he had shown. Ibn Kathir connects this to Pharaoh's boast recorded elsewhere: "Then verily, we can produce magic the like thereof; so appoint a meeting between us and you… in an open place where both shall have a just and equal chance," to which Musa (peace be upon him) answered, "Your appointed meeting is the day of the festival, and let the people assemble when the sun has risen" (20:58–60).

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān sees divine wisdom in this very setup. It is Allah's usual practice to send each prophet with miracles appropriate to the demand of his time. Musa (peace be upon him) was sent with the miracles of the staff and the white-lit hand so that people might clearly observe the misery of the sorcerers after they entered into contest with him. In the time of ʿIsa (peace be upon him), when Greek philosophy and medical sciences were at their zenith, the miracles were restoring the sight of the born-blind and curing lepers instantly with a touch. And in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, when the Arabs were boastful of their oratory and linguistic capabilities, the greatest miracle was the Qur'an itself — whose diction and style so bewildered the Arabs that they instantly acknowledged a superhuman element in it.

## The sorcerers name their price (ayat 113–114)

The plan succeeds, and the sorcerers arrive from all over the country. Their very first words to Pharaoh are a demand: "There must surely be a reward (*ajr*) for us if we are the victors" (ayah 113). Pharaoh answers, "Yes — and you will certainly be among the *muqarrabīn*," those nearest to him (ayah 114). Ibn Kathir describes how Pharaoh promised them tremendous provisions and made them hope for what they wished, including a place among his private audience and best associates.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān records, citing Qurtubi, that historical reports differ wildly on their number — from nine hundred up to three hundred thousand — and that the staves and strings used in the contest are reported to have been as much as was loaded on three hundred camels. Whatever the true figure, the picture is of an empire's full magical resources mobilised against one man with a staff.

Then Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws the moral contrast at the heart of this exchange. The first thing the sorcerers did was secure assurance of their reward — because worldly people are always after worldly gains and do nothing unless they are sure of them. The prophets and their disciples stand at the opposite pole, always declaring: "I do not ask you for a reward, as my reward is with the Lord of all the worlds" (26:109). The prophets preach and convey Allah's message only for the good and guidance of people, seeking no financial gain and looking for their reward from Allah alone. Asking "what do I get?" before serving falsehood, versus serving truth for Allah's sake alone — that is the dividing line this dialogue quietly exposes.

## Setting the stage — and a hint of what is coming

After this discourse with Pharaoh, the sorcerers got the place and date fixed for the great encounter: an open land, after sunrise, on their festival day — as mentioned in the verse where Musa (peace be upon him) said, "Your appointed day is the day of *zīnah*, so that the people may be gathered after sunrise" (20:59). The truth would not be tested in a corner but in the open, before the gathered people, in daylight.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān also relays a report (from Mazhari and Qurtubi) that Musa (peace be upon him) had a short conversation with the chief of the sorcerers, asking whether they would accept faith if he defeated them. The chief replied that defeat was out of the question, given magical powers no one could overcome — but that if Musa did defeat them, they would declare their faith openly in Pharaoh's presence. On the report's own terms it is a striking foreshadowing: the very champions hired to crush the truth had already promised to embrace it openly if it prevailed.

## Taking it to heart

Two threads run through the passage for the believer. First, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān's observation about these verses: wrongdoers, faced with clear truth, commonly seek false interpretations of it in order to conceal it — here re-labelling the miracle ("a knowing sorcerer") and changing the subject to fear ("he wants your land"). Recognising that pattern is half the defence against it. Second, the test of sincerity embedded in ayah 113: those who serve falsehood negotiate their reward first, while those who carry Allah's message seek their reward from Him alone. And over the whole scene stands the quiet sovereignty of Allah: the plotters' own plan — delay, gather, contest in public — became the very stage on which their fears were realised, "and We let Firʿawn and Haman and their hosts receive from them that which they feared" (28:6).

passages.title: The contest: truth prevails, magicians prostrate
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are the climax of the public contest between Musa (peace be upon him) and the sorcerers arrayed against him. What binds the passage together is a single dramatic arc — a challenge (115), a display of dazzling falsehood (116), one decisive act of truth (117), and then a total reversal (118–122) in which the defeated sorcerers themselves fall in prostration as believers. Ibn Kathir calls it "that tremendous moment, in which Allah differentiated between Truth and Falsehood."

## The exchange before the throw (ayat 115–116)

The contest opens with the magicians' question in ayah 115: "O Musa! Either you throw (first), or shall we have the (first) throw?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the word itself: *ilqāʼ* means to drop something down — hence the repeated imagery of "throwing" or "casting" that runs through the whole scene. It also reads the psychology of the question: the magicians were showing off their confidence in their art. The way they phrased it suggests they actually wanted to go first, but by offering Musa the choice they hoped to project an air of power over their opponent.

Musa (peace be upon him), who had nothing to fear, simply invited them: "Throw you (first)." Ibn Kathir — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes — saw courtesy in this: Musa behaved with them politely by inviting them to have their turn first, and the effect of that behaviour was that they accepted the faith after their defeat.

But why let falsehood go first at all? Ibn Kathir relates the wisdom that was given for this (adding "Allah knows best"): so that the people would witness the magicians' sorcery first. Once the magic had captured every eye and the crowd stood in suspense, the clear and unequivocal truth would arrive exactly when everyone was waiting for it — making the truth even more impressive to their hearts. And that is precisely what happened.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a sharper question here, answered from Bayān al-Qurʼān: sorcery is impermissible, and using it against a Prophet is outright disbelief — so how could Musa say "you throw," seemingly granting permission for magic? The answer: the magicians were certain to perform their magic in any case; the only thing being decided was who should begin. By letting them start, Musa also gained a strategic advantage — the people could watch the sorcerers display their art in full, turning their staves into apparent snakes, so that when his own staff became a serpent and ate up all the snakes, the open defeat of magic would be exhibited before the people.

## What their magic really was (ayah 116)

Notice what ayah 116 says the magicians actually did. In the rendering of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "So, when they threw, they bewitched **the eyes** of the people, and made them frightened, and came out with great sorcery." Ibn Kathir explains: they deceived the eyes and made people think the trick was real, when it was only an illusion. Ibn ʿAbbas described what they threw — "thick ropes and long sticks, and they appeared to be crawling, an illusion that they created with their magic."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a careful lesson from the wording. This verse shows that this particular display did not change the ropes and staffs physically; it was a bewitching of the eyes, a kind of mesmerism that hypnotised the minds of the onlookers into seeing the staffs and strings as snakes leaping on the ground. But it then adds a note of scholarly restraint: this does not prove that *all* magic is confined to illusion. The words "magic" and "sorcery" are usually applied to all acts that seem to happen in unusual ways — sleight of hand, telepathic influence, mesmerism — and whether magic can genuinely transform one thing into another is a possibility for which we have no valid proof either way. The verse settles what happened that day; it does not settle the metaphysics of every kind of sorcery.

Even so, the spectacle was overwhelming — "great sorcery," in the words of the ayah — and it struck terror into the watching people.

## One throw from heaven (ayat 117–119)

Then the turning point, in ayah 117 — in the rendering of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "And We revealed to Musa 'Throw your staff.' Then, of a sudden it began to swallow all that they had concocted." Ibn Kathir highlights that at that tremendous moment Allah sent revelation to His servant and Messenger Musa, peace be upon him, ordering him to throw the stick he held in his right hand. Ibn Kathir also connects this scene to Surah Ta-Ha, where Musa "conceived fear in himself" and Allah reassured him: "Fear not! Surely, you will have the upper hand… That which they have made is only a magician's trick, and the magician will never be successful, to whatever amount of skill he may attain" (20:67–69). Even a Prophet felt the human weight of that moment — and Allah steadied him.

The reports Ibn Kathir gathers paint the scene vividly. Ibn ʿAbbas said Musa's stick swallowed all the ropes and sticks the magicians threw. Muhammad bin Ishaq adds that it followed the ropes and sticks one after another until nothing the sorcerers had thrown remained — and then, when Musa held it in his hand, it became a stick again, just as it was before. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records from the historical accounts that thousands of staffs and ropes seemed to be turned into snakes leaping all over the ground, and the great snake of Musa (peace be upon him) ate them all within no time while the crowd stood bewildered and stunned.

Ayat 118–119 state the verdict in four tight clauses — in the rendering of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "So, the truth prevailed (*fa-waqaʿa al-ḥaqq*) and what they were doing became a nullity. So there they were overcome and turned humiliated." Falsehood was not merely outshone; it was annulled — swallowed so completely that nothing of it was left on the ground.

## Thrown down in prostration (ayat 120–122)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders ayah 120: "And the sorcerers were constrained to fall in prostration" — not simply that they decided to bow, but that something overwhelmed them. It explains this in two complementary ways: they were so overawed by the miracle of Musa (peace be upon him) that they fell in prostration — and it may also imply that it was Allah Himself who blessed them with this favour and put them in prostration. The men who came to throw down falsehood ended in the noblest posture a human being can take.

Their words in ayat 121–122 are precisely weighted: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun." Why the second phrase? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains: they added "the Lord of Musa and Harun" after "the Lord of the worlds" to make it clear that the Lord worshipped by Musa and Harun is, in fact, the Lord of the Universe — and not Pharaoh, as he pretended to be. In one sentence, their declaration of faith stripped away his pretence.

There is also powerful testimony in why *they in particular* believed. Ibn Kathir notes that the magicians realized instantly that what Musa's staff did "was from heaven and was by no means magic." In the report of Muhammad bin Ishaq, they said it themselves: "Had Musa been a magician, he would not have prevailed over us." The very art they had come to display became their reason for certainty that this was no art at all. Ibn Kathir also cites the comment of al-Qasim bin Abi Bazzah that when they fell in prostration they did not raise their heads before seeing Paradise, the Fire, and the recompense of their inhabitants — a report conveying how completely, in a single prostration, they passed to certainty about the Hereafter.

## What the passage leaves with us

Read as a whole, the movement of these ayat teaches what the sources draw from it. Falsehood may be given the first turn and a terrifying spectacle — the ayah itself calls it "great sorcery" — yet one act of truth, done at Allah's command, annuls it entirely: "the truth prevailed and what they were doing became a nullity" (118). Musa's courtesy toward his opponents, which Ibn Kathir highlights, was not weakness; it opened the door through which his fiercest adversaries walked into faith. And the sorcerers who began the day casting spells against a Prophet ending it constrained to fall in prostration is the passage's final word: when truth is made manifest, the honest response is to submit to the Lord of the worlds — the Lord of Musa and Harun.

passages.title: Pharaoh's threats and the magicians' steadfast faith
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the aftermath of the great contest. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recounts, the preceding verses gave a detailed account of the encounter between the prophet Musa (peace be upon him) and the sorcerers, and after their defeat the sorcerers declared their faith in Allah. Now the tyrant answers — not with argument, but with spin and terror. What binds the passage together is a single confrontation of two kinds of power: Pharaoh's power over bodies (permission, amputation, crucifixion) against the power that īmān — faith — has just planted in hearts that were, only hours earlier, worshipping him. Ayat 123–124 are Pharaoh's voice; ayat 125–126 are the believers' answer, ending in a prayer for patience and for a Muslim death.

## Ayah 123 — the tyrant's spin

Pharaoh's first words are telling: "How dare you believe in him **before I give you permission**." He speaks as though faith itself were a state licence — as though hearts could not turn to their Maker without clearance from the throne. But Ibn Kathir draws attention to what Pharaoh does next, because it is the real key to the ayah: he immediately converts a religious defeat into a political conspiracy. *"Surely, this is a plot which you have plotted in the city to drive out its people."* In other words: you and Musa arranged this in advance; your aim is to seize power in Egypt and expel its ruling class.

Ibn Kathir dismantles the accusation from the story itself. It was **Pharaoh** who sent emissaries across the cities of his kingdom to collect the scattered magicians of Egypt; it was Pharaoh who chose them, summoned them, and promised them great rewards. The magicians arrived eager to defeat Musa (peace be upon him) precisely so they could draw closer to Pharaoh. Musa neither knew any of them nor had ever met them. Pharaoh knew all this perfectly well — "Fir'awn and all those who had any sense of reason knew for sure that what Fir'awn said was utterly false" — yet he said it anyway, to deceive the ignorant masses. Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's description of him elsewhere: *"Thus he fooled his people, and they obeyed him"* (43:54), and remarks that a people who could believe a man saying *"I am your lord, most high"* (79:24) were among the most ignorant and misguided of Allah's creatures. In Surah Ta-Ha Pharaoh pushes the same lie further: *"He (Musa) is your chief who has taught you magic"* (20:71).

Ibn Kathir also cites a report in the Tafsir of As-Suddi, from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and several other Companions, that gives the accusation its thin pretext: before the contest, Musa had met the leader of the magicians and asked, "If I defeat you, will you believe in me and bear witness that what I brought is the truth?" The magician answered, "Tomorrow I will produce a type of magic that cannot be defeated by another magic. By Allah! If you defeat me, I will believe in you and testify to your truth." Pharaoh had been watching that exchange — and this, the report says, is why he said what he said.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains **why** Pharaoh needed the lie so urgently. Some historical reports say that after the magicians declared their faith, six hundred thousand more people believed — whereas before the contest only two individuals had believed in Allah. An embarrassing situation for Pharaoh, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it; so "like a clever politician he managed to conceal his state of mind before the people" and reframed the whole event. The phrase "before I permitted you" did double work: it threatened the magicians, and it planted in the crowd the idea that the converts had merely been hasty — had fallen into a trap — implying that Pharaoh himself would of course have believed *if* Musa had really proven truthful. And "to drive out its people" turned a miracle into a coup attempt. It is the oldest move of threatened power: when you cannot answer the truth, criminalise it.

## Ayah 124 — the threat spelled out

Notice the sequence Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out: first the vague, looming menace at the end of ayah 123 — *"but you shall come to know"* — then the specification in ayah 124. **"I will certainly cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides, then I will crucify you all."**

"From opposite sides" (*min khilāf*) means the right hand with the left foot, or the reverse — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the intent: to leave the victim "completely disabled and invalid." Ibn Kathir adds from the parallel passage that Pharaoh vowed to crucify them *"fī* the trunks of date palms" (20:71), noting that *fī* — ordinarily "in" — there means "on": crucified on the trunks of the palms. And he transmits a striking historical note from Ibn 'Abbas: **Pharaoh was the first person ever to crucify and to cut off hands and feet on opposite sides.** The tyrant of this story is not merely using cruelty; he is inventing it.

## Ayah 125 — the answer of freed hearts

Against amputation and crucifixion, the magicians' entire reply is one sentence: *"Surely to our Lord we will all return."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on what this brevity reveals. These men knew Pharaoh's power over them intimately — they had served it. So notice what they do **not** say: they do not claim their new faith will shield them from him, and they do not deny that he can kill them. Their serenity comes from somewhere else entirely. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two readings of their words, and both fit. First: this temporary worldly life has simply lost its value in their eyes — they are certain of meeting the Lord of the worlds after leaving it, where an everlasting life of peace awaits. Second, with a quiet edge aimed at Pharaoh himself: yes, you can end our lives, but *you too* are returning to that same Lord, and there you will be taken to account for your despotism. In Surah Ta-Ha their answer is fuller: *"So decide whatever you desire to decree, for you can only decide for the life of this world"* (20:72) — your writ, Pharaoh, runs no further than this dunya.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the deeper lesson: īmān is itself a power. "When it finds its way into one's heart, one finds himself as powerful as to face the whole world and all the forces gathered together against him." Only a few hours earlier these same men were worshippers of Pharaoh; now they face his worst threats with perfect composure.

Ibn Kathir voices their inner reasoning: we are now certain we are going back to Allah — and Allah's punishment is more severe than yours, His torment for the disbelief and magic you are calling us back to is greater than anything you can inflict. So we will bear your punishment today, in order to be safe from His punishment forever. It is not bravado; it is arithmetic done by hearts that finally see both scales.

## Ayah 126 — naming the crime, and the prayer

The magicians then expose the emptiness of the charges: *"Your rage towards us is only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they reached us."* No conspiracy, no coup — strip away the spin and their only "crime" is faith. Then they turn away from Pharaoh altogether, upward:

**"Our Lord! Pour out on us patience, and cause us to die as Muslims."**

Ibn Kathir glosses the two halves: pour patience upon us *"with Your religion and being firm in it"*, and let us die *"as followers of Your Prophet Musa, peace be upon him."* They do not pray for rescue. They pray for steadfastness until the end, and for the right ending — because they have understood that the only thing truly at stake is the state in which one meets Allah. In the fuller speech recorded in Surah Ta-Ha they say: *"Verily, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our faults, and the magic to which you did compel us. And Allah is better and more lasting… whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell… but whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds — for such are the high ranks"* (20:72–75). Note their honesty even here: they seek forgiveness for the magic itself, the craft Pharaoh had pressed them into.

Ibn Kathir seals the passage with the famous comment of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ubayd bin 'Umayr, Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj: **"They started the day as sorcerers and ended it as martyrs."** One sunrise to one sunset — from serving the tyrant's court to dying for the Lord of the worlds.

## A miracle within the miracle

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes an observation worth sitting with: the instant, total transformation of the sorcerers was itself no lesser miracle than the other miracles of the prophet Musa (peace be upon him). Men who had spent whole lives in disbelief and ignorance became, in a moment, among the most knowing and true of believers — ready to give their lives for faith they had held for only a few hours. And their prayer proves the change was not mere emotion: asking for *ṣabr* (patient perseverance) and a Muslim death was, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, both a manifestation of real knowledge and wisdom *and* the most practical response to their situation — "because perseverance and patience are the only keys to success over one's enemy." It even relates (citing Tafsir al-Manar) how a commission formed to investigate the causes and effects of the World War observed that Muslims who believed in Allah and the Hereafter were the bravest in battle and the most patient in hardship — so much so that German military experts urged cultivating honesty and a sense of accountability in the Hereafter among their own soldiers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's closing regret is pointed: Muslims chase every other means of strength while neglecting the real source — faith, perseverance and patience.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with three plain things. First, recognise the pattern: when truth cannot be refuted, power will try to rebrand it as a plot — Pharaoh's accusation in ayah 123 was known to be false even by him, and it worked only on those who let themselves be fooled. Second, the magicians' calm in ayah 125 did not come from expecting safety; it came from certainty about where everyone — victim and tyrant alike — is heading. Third, their prayer in ayah 126 is a gift to every believer under pressure of any kind: do not ask merely for the trial to lift; ask as they asked — *"Our Lord! Pour out on us patience, and cause us to die as Muslims."*

passages.title: Persecution intensifies; Moses counsels patient hope
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat form a single dramatic scene from the middle of the Mūsā narrative: Pharaoh's court presses him to act, the persecution intensifies into a decree of killing — and Mūsā (peace be upon him) answers that terror not with a counter-threat but with a two-part spiritual strategy and a promise about who really owns the earth. What binds the passage together is a contest over power: ayah 127 shows power as Pharaoh understands it (decrees, killing, "we have irresistible power over them"), and ayat 128–129 dismantle that understanding piece by piece, ending with the Qur'an's own definition of power — a trust from Allah, given to test how its holders behave.

## Ayah 127 — a frightened tyrant, pushed by his court

The scene opens with *al-malaʼ* — the chiefs of Pharaoh's people — protesting to him: "Will you leave Mūsā and his people to spread mischief in the land, and abandon you and your gods?"

Ibn Kathir pauses on the sheer inversion in this sentence. These people were worried that Mūsā would cause *mischief* — when, as he puts it, "Fir'awn and his people are the mischief-makers, but they did not realize it." What the court calls "mischief" is simply, in Ibn Kathir's words, calling the people "to worship their Lord instead of you." Tyranny always speaks this language: the caller to truth is branded the disturber of order.

**"You and your gods."** This small phrase carries two revelations. First, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, it exposes Pharaoh's fraud from inside his own palace: he claimed to be the god of his people, yet his own chiefs speak of "your gods" — Pharaoh himself used to worship other deities. Second, Ibn Kathir transmits the explanation of Ibn ʿAbbās (as narrated by as-Suddī): those gods "were cows. Whenever they saw a beautiful cow, Fir'awn would command them to worship it." Ibn Kathir adds a striking connection across the whole story: this Egyptian cow-cult is why as-Sāmirī would later make the statue of a calf that seemed to moo for the Children of Israel.

**Pharaoh's answer — and what it gives away.** Pharaoh responds: "We will kill their sons, and let their women live, and we have indeed irresistible power over them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to what is *missing* from this threat. As even his own people strangely noted, all of Pharaoh's fury and rage was limited to the sorcerers only; he did not dare say a word against Mūsā and Hārūn (peace be upon them), his real opponents. Maʿārif observes that Pharaoh was so frightened by the miracle of Mūsā (peace be upon him) that even here, announcing the killing of the Israelite men, he could not utter a single word of threat against the two prophets. The commentator sees in this the truth of Maulānā Rūmī's couplet, which he quotes: "Whoever adopts 'Taqwa' and fears Allah is feared by all human beings and spirits" — *taqwā* being conscious fear of Allah that keeps a person away from disobeying Him. The tyrant who terrified a nation was himself afraid.

There is a second layer of futility. This was the *second* promulgation of the killing decree — the first, before Mūsā's birth, was designed to prevent Mūsā from ever living. Ibn Kathir notes the bitter irony: "the opposite of what Fir'awn sought and intended occurred." Not only did Mūsā survive that first decree, but the huge crowd of Israelites present at this very occasion was living proof that the policy had failed once already (as Maʿārif observes). And the end of the story seals it: Allah gave victory to the Children of Israel, humiliated and disgraced Pharaoh, and caused him to drown along with his soldiers — "the same end struck Fir'awn that he intended to subjugate and humiliate the Children of Israel with." Maʿārif states the principle behind it: when Allah intends to bring disgrace to a people, everything they contrive leads to nothing but disaster.

## Ayah 128 — the two-part remedy

Maʿārif sets the scene: after being defeated by Mūsā (peace be upon him), Pharaoh enforced the law of killing the male children of the Israelites, and they were greatly alarmed — they remembered the punishment they had experienced before Mūsā came. Mūsā was mindful of this, and out of his kindness he offered his terrified people not false comfort, and not a battle plan, but two instructions: **"Seek help in Allah, and be patient."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this "the sovereign remedy which never fails against any difficulty," and unpacks its two ingredients.

**First: seeking help from Allah.** This is the essence of the remedy, "for the obvious reason that if the Creator of the universe comes to one's help, who is there to stop Him?" The commentary quotes Rūmī again: earth, air, water and fire are all servants of Allah — dead to you and me, but to Allah full of life. A hadith cited in Maʿārif teaches that when Allah wills to do something, everything turns in favour of that purpose. But the commentator adds a crucial caution: *simply uttering formula words is not enough*. Seeking help must come "with all the sincerity of one's heart" — it is a state of dependence, not a phrase.

**Second: ṣabr — patience.** Maʿārif gives the word's literal sense: *ṣabr* means to keep oneself under one's own control against unfavourable happenings. It is not passivity; it is self-mastery under pressure. Nothing significant, the commentary notes, is ever achieved without hardship, and the one who readily prepares himself to face hardship is generally successful. The Prophet ﷺ said, "No greater blessing has been given to anyone other than patience" (Abu Dawud).

Mūsā then grounds both instructions in a fact about reality: **"Verily, the earth is Allah's. He gives it as a heritage to whom He wills of His servants; and the blessed end is for the muttaqīn"** — the people of taqwā, those who guard themselves against disobeying Allah. Pharaoh had just claimed "we have irresistible power over them"; Mūsā answers that the land Pharaoh thinks he owns belongs to Allah, who hands it to whomever He wills. Maʿārif reads this as a conditional promise: if the Israelites observe taqwā by acting upon those two instructions — help-seeking and patience — they will ultimately inherit and rule the whole land. Ibn Kathir reads it the same way: Mūsā "promised them that the good end will be theirs and that they will prevail."

## Ayah 129 — the complaint, and the answer that reframes everything

The people's reply is achingly human: **"We suffered troubles before you came to us, and since you have come to us."** Ibn Kathir paraphrases their meaning: humiliation and disgrace were inflicted on us both before and after your arrival, O Mūsā — some of it you witnessed yourself. Maʿārif adds a poignant reading of what perhaps lay beneath the words: they had been looking for a prophet to *deliver* them from Pharaoh's oppression — and yet even after he came, their fate seemed unchanged. It is the complaint of people who could not understand how patience alone could free them from Pharaoh's punishment and bring them success against him.

Mūsā's answer looks forward: **"It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors on the earth, so that He may see how you act."** Ibn Kathir notes the pastoral purpose in this reply — Mūsā is preparing them to *appreciate Allah* when the affliction is finally removed and replaced by bounty. Relief is coming; the question is what kind of people they will be when it arrives.

**"So that He may see how you act" — sovereignty is a test.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on this closing phrase as the wisdom of the whole passage. Dominion is not itself the goal; it is a means, "a sacred trust bestowed by Allah for making good prevail over evil" and for establishing peace and justice. Though the direct addressees are the Israelites, the verse is a warning to everyone ever entrusted with rule: sovereignty belongs to Allah alone, who makes man His deputy on earth, gives power and strips it away as He wills — as the Qur'an says elsewhere, "You give power to whom You please, and You strip off power from whom You please" (3:26). The Israelites are being warned in advance: if you are given this trust, do not forget the ill fate of those who held it before you.

Maʿārif relates a story recorded by Abū Ḥayyān in his tafsir *Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ* that captures this perfectly. ʿAmr ibn ʿUbaid once visited Manṣūr — before he became the second Abbasid caliph — and recited this verse to him: "It is likely that Allah will destroy your enemy and make you successor in the earth," a kind of prediction of his rise. Manṣūr did become caliph, and when ʿAmr next came to him, the caliph reminded him of the prediction. ʿAmr replied at once: the first half has come true — but the verse has a second half still hanging over you: *"then He will see how you act."* Gaining power, he was saying, is nothing to be proud of; it is the moment Allah's scrutiny of you truly begins.

## What the passage asks of us

Read as a whole, the three ayat trace a complete arc: worldly power at its most menacing (127), the believer's response to it (128), and the true nature of the power the believers will eventually receive (129). The practical teaching sits in Mūsā's two instructions — seek Allah's help with real sincerity, not recited formulas, and hold yourself steady (*ṣabr*) while circumstances are still against you. And the passage closes the loop with a warning worth carrying into any position of authority, however small: relief and success, when they come, are not a reward to enjoy but a trust to be examined on. Pharaoh's "irresistible power" ended with Allah drowning him and his soldiers; the power promised to the patient comes with the words *"so that He may see how you act."*

passages.title: Plagues, broken promises, drowning, inherited land
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat tell the final act of the long confrontation between Musa (peace be upon him) and Firʿawn in Egypt. Allah sends warning after warning upon Firʿawn's people — first famine, then a succession of devastating plagues — and each time the same cycle repeats: desperation, a solemn promise to believe and free the Children of Israel, relief, and then betrayal. When the last promise is broken, the sea closes over them, and the people they had deemed weak inherit the land. What holds the passage together is that it is one sustained anatomy of a hardened heart, told through repetition — and it ends with one of the Qur'an's great reversals: the "weak" made inheritors.

## The famine that came first (ayat 130–131)

Ayah 130 says Allah seized the people of Firʿawn *bis-sinīn* — years of drought, which Ibn Kathir glosses as famine due to little produce — "and loss of fruits." Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān notes that according to historical reports this famine lasted seven years, and cites Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatadah that the two phrases describe two spheres of the punishment: drought struck the people of the rural areas, while those living in the cities and towns suffered the loss of fruits. Ibn Kathir records Mujahid's view that the loss of fruits was the less severe of the two, and — through Abu Ishaq's narration — quotes Rajaʾ bin Haywah's vivid picture of how far it went: "The date tree used to produce only one date!"

The purpose is stated in the ayah itself: *laʿallahum yadhdhakkarūn* — "that they might take heed." Hardship, in Allah's dealing with nations, is first of all a mercy in disguise: a shaking meant to wake the sleeper before the end comes.

But ayah 131 shows what a corrupted heart does with that mercy. When good times came, they said "This is for us" — Ibn Kathir explains: *because we deserve it*. When evil struck, "they saw an evil omen in Musa and those with him" — this hardship, they claimed, was his fault, brought on by him and his people. Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān opens up the key word here: *ṭāʾir*, translated "omen," literally signifies a **bird**. The Arabs held the superstition that a bird coming down on one's right or left foretold good or bad fate, and the Qur'an uses their own vocabulary to demolish the idea. "Their omen is only with Allah": Ibn ʿAbbās — as reported by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah — explained that their afflictions are with Allah and *from* Him. Nothing in creation independently brings good or bad fortune; everything happens under the will of Allah, and — as Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān puts it — it is sheer ignorance to base one's life on such baseless assumptions. The same commentary adds a sobering diagnosis: when a people are stamped with the wrath of Allah, they lose the very faculty of distinguishing right from wrong. That is why seven years of famine produced not repentance but scapegoating.

## "Whatever sign you bring" (ayah 132)

Ayah 132 records their formal declaration of closed-mindedness: "Whatever sign you bring us to bewitch us with, we will never believe in you." Ibn Kathir says this proclamation flowed from their rebellion, tyranny, defiance of the truth and insistence on falsehood: whatever miracle, proof or evidence Musa brought, they had decided in advance neither to accept it nor to believe in him. A heart that has pre-committed to disbelief will always find a label for the truth.

## Five plagues, one repeating cycle (ayat 133–135)

Ayah 133 then names five punishments sent as a succession of manifest signs — in Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān's phrase, "signs distinct from each other": the *ṭūfān*, the locusts, the *qummal*, the frogs, and the blood. Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān sets these in a wider frame: Musa (peace be upon him) stayed in Egypt for twenty years according to historical reports, preaching consistently, and was given nine miracles — the Qur'an says elsewhere, "Surely, We gave him nine miracles." Two were performed before Firʿawn and his people, the third was the famine of ayah 130, and these verses recount the rest.

The commentators unpack each term:

- **Aṭ-ṭūfān.** Ibn ʿAbbās said it was a heavy rain that ruined produce and fruits; he is also reported to have explained it as mass death, and Mujahid said it was water that carried plague everywhere. The great commentators cited in Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān understood it as a flood that filled and surrounded their lands and houses, leaving nowhere to farm or live — while, remarkably, the lands and houses of the Israelites nearby were untouched.
- **The locusts.** Ibn Kathir pauses here, in classic tafsir style, to note that the locust is the well-known insect which is permissible to eat. It is recorded in the Two Sahihs that Abu Yaʿfur said he asked ʿAbdullah bin Abi Awfa about locusts, and he replied: "We participated in seven battles with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and we used to eat locusts." And Ash-Shafiʿi, Ahmad bin Hanbal and Ibn Majah recorded from ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam, that his father narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "We were allowed two dead animals and two kinds of blood: fish and locust, and kidney and spleen." As for the plague itself, Mujahid said the locusts ate even the nails on their doors and left the wood — and in the account of Muhammad bin Ishaq they consumed the doors until they fell from the houses.
- **Al-qummal.** The early authorities differed over this word: Ibn ʿAbbās said it is the grain bug, or on another view small wingless locusts — similar is reported from Mujahid, ʿIkrimah and Qatadah — while al-Hasan and Saʿid bin Jubayr said they were small black insects. Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān notes that the Arabic word covers both the louse and a grain-eating pest, and suggests both may have been sent: pests devouring their stored grain while lice ate away even their hair and eyelashes.
- **The frogs and the blood** are explained through the narratives below.

Ibn Kathir preserves a detailed account recorded by Abu Jaʿfar bin Jarir from Saʿid bin Jubayr — with a similar account attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, as-Suddi, Qatadah and several others of the Salaf — which lets us watch the cycle turn. When Firʿawn refused to release the Children of Israel, Allah sent the rain until they feared it as a torment; they begged Musa to pray, promising faith and release; he prayed, the rain stopped — and they broke their word. That very year the earth produced as never before, and they said, "This is what we hoped for." So the locusts came and fed on the grass until they knew no vegetation would be spared; again the promise, again the relief, again the betrayal. They gathered their grain into their houses and said, "We saved our crops" — and the qummal got into the stores, so that a man would take ten bags of grain to the mill and reap only three small bags. Then the frogs: once, in Firʿawn's presence, Musa heard the sound of a frog and asked him, "What will you and your people suffer from this?" Firʿawn scoffed, "What can frogs do?" — and by nightfall a person would be sitting in a crowd of frogs that reached up to his chin, unable to open his mouth to speak without a frog jumping in. Finally the blood: the rivers, the wells and every container they owned filled with blood. They complained to Firʿawn, who told them, "Musa has bewitched you" — and they answered: how could that be, when every time we look for water in our containers we find it has turned to blood? Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān records the historical report that when Egyptians and Israelites sat together at a meal, the morsel taken by the Egyptian turned to blood while the Israelite's did not change — the same strange precision the reports note of the flood and the locusts, which spared the Israelites' houses and fields close by.

Ibn ʿAbbās — as cited through Ibn al-Mundhir in Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān — said each punishment lasted seven days, beginning on a Saturday, followed by three weeks of relief before the next. This rhythm matters: ayah 135 says Allah removed the punishment "for a fixed term, which they had to reach." The reliefs were periods of respite given to them to reflect and realize their error — a genuine opportunity, and a countdown. Imam al-Baghawi, citing Ibn ʿAbbās, adds that it was after they broke their first promise that Musa (peace be upon him) prayed that they be afflicted with painful punishment that would serve as a lesson to his people and to their descendants.

Their plea in ayah 134 — "O Musa! Invoke your Lord for us because of His promise to you. If you remove the punishment from us, we indeed shall believe in you, and we shall let the Children of Israel go with you" — became the refrain of the whole ordeal. The word for the punishment, *rijz*, drew different treatments from the commentators: in the narrations Ibn Kathir gathers, this plea is what they said, in one form or another, under each of the five plagues, while Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān records that the *rijz* was a sixth distinct punishment — a plague or pestilence, in which more than seventy thousand of the Egyptians are reported to have died, and after relief from which they broke their promise yet again. On either reading, the ayah's verdict is the same: the moment the pressure lifted, "behold, they broke their word."

## The sea, and the inheritance (ayat 136–137)

Ayah 136 states the end with terse finality: "So We took retribution from them and drowned them in the sea (*al-yamm*), because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them." Ibn Kathir describes it: the sea that Musa parted by Allah's power, through which he and the Children of Israel passed, closed in on Firʿawn and his soldiers when they went into it in pursuit, and all of them drowned. Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān adds that they left behind all their lands, houses and possessions to chase Musa (peace be upon him) and his people to their own deaths. And the ayah is explicit about the cause — not denial alone, but denial joined with heedlessness of sign after sign.

Ayah 137 then delivers the reversal. "And We made the people **who were deemed weak** inherit the easts and wests of the land which We had blessed." Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān draws out a precise point of wording: the ayah does not say "the people who *were* weak" but "who were *taken to be* weak" (*yustaḍʿafūn*) — because a people who have Allah as their support are never truly weak, however they may appear; all dignity and honour belong to Allah. And the word "inherit" (*awrathnā*) suggests, as Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān puts it, that like a son who deserves to be the real inheritor of his father's land and possessions, the Israelites were the real inheritors of the land and wealth of Firʿawn's people. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatadah said the blessed land refers to the Sham area (Greater Syria); Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān records that according to the experts in exegesis it is the land of Egypt and Syria which came under Israelite domination, and notes that "easts" and "wests" are plural perhaps to denote the different points of sunrise and sunset in summer and winter — the whole horizon of the land, in every season. On the blessedness of Egypt it adds that the Caliph ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab called the Nile the prince of all rivers, and the Companion ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar said Egypt holds nine of the ten parts of blessing, the tenth being divided throughout the rest of the earth (al-Bahr al-Muhit).

"And the fair word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel **because of their patience**." Mujahid and Ibn Jarir explained this "fair word" through Surah al-Qasas: "And it was Our will that We favour those considered weak in the earth and make them leaders, and make them the inheritors" (28:5–6). Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān adds that it may equally refer to Musa's own promise to his people back in ayah 129 — and that the two are really one, since Musa's promise derived from Allah's.

The condition of the promise — *bimā ṣabarū*, "because they endured" — is where this passage reaches forward into every believer's life. Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān records the counsel of al-Hasan al-Basri: when a wronged person who cannot defend himself takes revenge by his own wrongdoing, Allah leaves him alone to manage his own affairs, to succeed or fail on his own; but when he seeks help from Allah against the affliction and remains patient, Allah Himself opens the door of success upon him. And the same commentary points out that the identical promise was made to this Ummah in Surah an-Nur: "Allah has promised those of you who believe and do good deeds that He will make them inherit the land, as He made those before them inherit it" (24:55) — a promise the Muslim Ummah witnessed fulfilled just as the Israelites did.

The passage closes: "And We destroyed what Firʿawn and his people had made, and what they used to erect." Ibn Kathir explains this as their agriculture and their buildings — Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujahid said *yaʿrishūn* means "they built" — while Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān adds that "what they used to build" may also refer to their ill designs against Musa (peace be upon him). Everything the tyrant produced, planted and plotted was levelled.

## Living it

Three lessons sit in this passage for every reader. First, the trap of ayah 131: crediting ourselves for every good and blaming others — the righteous especially — for every hardship, when in truth all of it is with Allah and from Him. Second, the promises of ayah 135: vows made under pressure and abandoned the moment relief comes are the signature of Firʿawn's people, who persisted in their arrogance and took no lesson from warning after warning. Third, the condition named in ayah 137 — "because of their patience." Maʿārif ul-Qurʾān notes that when Musa (peace be upon him) promised his people rule over the land, he had emphatically said that perseverance, patience and seeking help from Allah was the only key to success — and it finds in the verse an understated indication that any people or individual who follow the same example, at any time and in any place, shall receive the same reward. However long oppression lasts, the "weak" who hold to patience and seek Allah's help are the ones the promise is for.

passages.title: After the sea: Israel demands an idol
passages.tafsir:
This passage records one of the most startling moments in the story of Banū Isrāʾīl: just after Allah has brought them safely across the sea — after they had, as Ibn Kathir puts it, crossed the sea and witnessed Allah's signs and great power — they pass a community devoted to idols, and ask Musa (peace be upon him) to make them a god of their own. What binds ayat 138–141 into one unit is a single conversation: the demand (ayah 138), then Musa's answer unfolding in three waves — the idolaters are doomed and their worship is worthless (ayah 139), how could I seek for you another god when Allah has given you superiority over the nations (ayah 140), and remember when Allah rescued you from the people of Pharaoh (ayah 141).

## The scene: across the sea, straight into temptation

Ayah 138 opens with Allah Himself narrating the crossing: "We brought the Children of Israel across the sea." Ibn Kathir stresses the timing — these were words that "the ignorant ones among the Children of Israel" uttered to Musa *after* they had crossed the sea and witnessed Allah's signs and great power. The request did not come from people who had never seen a miracle; it came from people who had just seen one.

On the far shore they came upon "a people devoted to some of their idols (in worship)" — the Arabic *yaʿkufūna ʿalā aṣnāmin lahum*. Some scholars of tafsir, Ibn Kathir notes, said these people were from Canaan, or from the tribe of Lakhm. Ibn Jarir adds a detail that turns this scene into a seed of later tragedy: they were worshipping idols they had made in the shape of **cows**, and this, he comments, influenced the Children of Israel later when they worshipped the calf.

And so came the request: "O Musa! Make for us a god as they have gods."

## Musa's reply: ignorance, ruin, and futility

Musa's first word names the root of the request: "Verily, you are an ignorant people" (ayah 138). Ibn Kathir explains what exactly they were ignorant of: **Allah's greatness and majesty, and His purity from any partners or anything resembling Him**. This is the heart of the passage's theology. Their error was not merely a bad choice of ritual; it was a failure to grasp who Allah is — that nothing shares in His divinity and nothing resembles Him.

In ayah 139 Musa then dismantles the very thing they had asked to copy, in two strokes:

- **"Verily, these people will be destroyed for that which they are engaged in"** (*mutabbar mā hum fīhi*). Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: they will perish.
- **"And all that they are doing is in vain"** (*bāṭil mā kānū yaʿmalūn*). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders Musa's point sharply: the labour of worship of those people was to go waste — and it records that Musa (peace be upon him) was greatly annoyed by their ignorance.

So the answer covers both the destination and the road: the people are doomed, and the worship itself is worthless.

## Ayat 140–141: the argument from favour and from rescue

In ayah 140 Musa turns from the idolaters to his own people: "Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, while He has given you superiority over the nations?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the sense of this favour: the people who believed in Musa were, in their age, superior to all the people of that age. How could the prophet through whom Allah had given them excellence over the people of all the worlds go looking for a substitute deity? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the absurdity plainly: shall they be so ungrateful to their Lord as to take abject stones as gods and make them partners with Allah?

Ayah 141 then turns to memory: "And (remember) when We rescued you from Fir'awn's people, who were afflicting you with the worst torment, killing your sons and letting your women live. And in that was a great trial from your Lord." Ibn Kathir summarises the reminder: Musa recalled for them Allah's blessings — saving them from Fir'awn, his tyranny, and the humiliation and disgrace they suffered; and the glory and revenge they were given against their enemy, whom they watched suffering in disgrace, destroyed by drowning and meeting utter demise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the picture of that "worst torment": their sons killed, their daughters spared only to serve as maid-servants. Allah relieved them of that disgraceful chastisement through His prophet — and yet it was to that same prophet that the request for an idol was made. The only fitting response, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, is that they must repent to Allah for their transgression.

## Why did it happen? The danger of sudden ease

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a piercing observation about the setting of this request. After the miraculous victory over Pharaoh and his people, and now having a life of ease and comfort, the Israelites started to show the signs of ignorance **that people of wealth show when given a life of luxury and opulence**. It calls this "the first impertinent request" they made to Musa (peace be upon him). The lapse the passage records, in other words, is located by the commentators not in their years of persecution but in their new season of comfort.

## "You said just as what the people of Musa said": the Sunnah's commentary

Commenting on this ayah, Ibn Kathir cites a report recorded by Imam Abu Jaʿfar bin Jarir from the Companion Abu Waqid al-Laythi. The Companions had gone out from Makkah with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for the battle of Hunayn. Abu Waqid relates that some of the disbelievers had a lote tree in whose vicinity they used to remain, and upon which they would hang their weapons; that tree was called **Dhat Al-Anwat**. When the Muslims passed by a huge, green lote tree, some of them said: "O Messenger of Allah! Appoint for us a Dhat Al-Anwat as they have." He ﷺ replied: "By He in Whose Hand is my soul! You said just as what the people of Musa said to him: 'Make for us a god as they have gods.' He said: 'Verily, you are an ignorant people. Verily, these people will be destroyed for that which they are engaged in, and all that they are doing is in vain.'"

The Prophet ﷺ swore an oath and placed that request in exactly the same category as the request made to Musa, reciting the very ayat before us. The lesson lies in the shared wording of the two requests — "as they have" — the desire to copy the visible religious attachments of others. The report shows that this pull can surface even among believers travelling with a prophet, and that it calls for the same correction Musa gave.

## Living it

Three demands emerge from the passage as the sources present it. First, guard the meaning of *tawḥīd* (the oneness of Allah) at the level of real knowledge of Him, not just formal belief — the ignorance Musa named was, in Ibn Kathir's words, ignorance of Allah's greatness and majesty and His purity from any partners or anything resembling Him. Second, be watchful in seasons of ease: the sources place this lapse precisely in the Israelites' new life of comfort, and ayah 141's own command is the remedy — "remember when We rescued you." Third, when the lapse happens — and Dhat Al-Anwat shows the pull can touch even the Companions — the door Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to is repentance to Allah.

passages.title: Forty nights, the Tablets, and Allah's speech
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the summit of Musa's story — literally. After the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, and the Children of Israel delivered, Musa (peace be upon him) climbs the mount of Sinai for a forty-night appointment with his Lord, hears Allah's speech directly, asks for something no living soul can bear — to see Allah — and receives the Tablets. The unit closes (ayat 146–147) with a warning that explains everything that follows in the story: it is arrogance that shuts a heart out from Allah's signs, and denial that empties deeds of all worth.

## Forty nights, not thirty (ayah 142)

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān sets the scene: with Pharaoh gone and life at peace, the Israelites asked Musa for a system of law to live by, and Musa prayed to Allah for a code of guidance. The answer was an appointment — Allah promised to send His word to Musa if he would go to the mount of Sinai and spend thirty nights there in devotion. The word **wāʿadnā** ("We appointed") comes from *waʿdah* — a worded expression of offering something good to someone: a promise.

The commentators report that Musa fasted the whole thirty days and nights continuously. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes the striking contrast with his journey to meet Khidr, where he could not wait even half a day before saying, "Give us our food, because this journey has made us tired." Ruh al-Bayan explains the difference by the nature of the two journeys: the Khidr journey was of a created being for another created being, while the Sinai journey was for the Creator, made by a devoted servant who had separated himself from creation in quest of his Lord — and that spiritual pull weakened the body's demands of hunger and thirst so much that thirty days of continuous fasting became possible.

**Why thirty and then ten?** Ibn Kathir relates from the scholars of Tafsir that Musa fasted the thirty nights, and when they ended he cleaned his teeth with a twig; Allah then commanded him to complete the term with ten more days, making the total forty. The commentators explain the added ten as restoring the fasting odour of his mouth, which Allah loves — though Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān is careful to note this report comes without a chain of narrators, and that it cannot mean using the miswak while fasting is disliked for us: it may have been a commandment specific to Musa or to the followers of the Torah, and al-Baihaqi reports on the authority of Sayyidah Aʼishah that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The best act of the one who is fasting is brushing one's teeth (with miswak)" — a hadith whose status al-Jamiʿ al-Saghir gives as Hasan (a kind of authentic tradition).

Deeper wisdoms are offered too. Ruh al-Bayan sees in the two-stage appointment Allah's way of enjoining things **gradually**, to make practice easier; al-Qurtubi sees a lesson for people in authority — give your subordinates more time when they cannot finish in the period first set. Qurtubi draws the principle wider: Allah created the universe in six days though He had all the power to create it instantly, and the Torah too was given over a fixed period rather than in a moment — teaching us to approach our aims by stages, for haste and hurry are not approved by Allah. And it was precisely by ignoring this principle that the Israelites lost their faith: when Musa did not return in the thirty days he had announced, they hastily concluded he was lost, fell prey to the sorcerer Samiri, and began worshipping the golden calf. Had they been a people of patience who practised gradualism, they would not have committed that fatal error.

**Nights, not days.** The verse counts *nights* because the lunar calendar was the standard in the laws of the Prophets — the lunar month begins with the sighting of the moon, which is possible only at night, so dates change at sunset. Al-Qurtubi reports on the authority of Ibn al-ʿArabi: "The solar calendar is for the benefits in worldly matters while the lunar calendar is for religious observances." According to the commentary of the Companion ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿAbbas, the thirty nights were the nights of Dhul-Qaʿdah and the added ten were the first ten nights of Dhul-Hijjah — meaning the Torah was given to Musa on the day of Eid al-Adha (Qurtubi). Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān also relates, from a report of the Prophet ﷺ cited in Ruh al-Bayan, that anyone who worships Allah for forty days with sincerity of heart, his heart is made a source of wisdom — the number forty carries a special effect in the spiritual rectification of the heart.

**Harun's deputyship.** Before leaving, Musa told his brother: "Take my place among my people, keep things right, and do not follow the way of the mischief-makers." Ibn Kathir stresses this was only a reminder — Harun was himself an honourable and noble Prophet with an exalted standing before Allah. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān draws the practical rule: anyone holding a responsible office should appoint a deputy in his absence and leave him clear instructions, as the Prophet ﷺ used to do whenever he left Madinah, appointing ʿAli or ʿAbdullah ibn Umm Maktum on different occasions (Qurtubi). And since a Prophet like Harun could never *commit* mischief, "do not follow the way of the mischief-makers" meant: do nothing that would help or encourage them — which is exactly what Harun did when the calf appeared, preventing his people and admonishing Samiri against his mischief.

## "Show me Yourself, that I may look upon You" (ayah 143)

Musa came at the appointed time, and his Lord spoke to him. Standing in that intimacy — hearing Allah's own speech — Musa asked for the one thing beyond it: *rabbi arinī anẓur ilayk*, "O my Lord! Show me (Yourself), that I may look upon You."

The answer, **lan tarānī** ("You cannot see Me"), is one of the most carefully weighed phrases in the Qur'an, and both commentaries dwell on it:

- **It does not mean seeing Allah is impossible.** Ibn Kathir insists that *lan* here by no means indicates that seeing Allah will never occur, as the misguided sect of the Muʿtazilah claimed; hadiths of the *mutawatir* grade (mass-transmitted beyond doubt) narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ affirm that the believers will see Allah in the Hereafter — "Some faces that Day shall be radiant. Looking at their Lord" (75:22–23).
- **But it will not happen in this life.** Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān (citing Mazhari) notes the precision of the wording: the phrase is "you shall never see me," not "I cannot be seen" — the barrier is not in Allah but in Musa's present physical disposition, which could not endure it. Sighting Allah is thus a logical possibility even in this world, yet this verse precludes its occurrence here — the unanimous view of the majority of scholars. Sahih Muslim records: "None among you can see his Lord unless he dies."

Then came a **physical demonstration** of why. "But look upon the mountain; if it stands still in its place then you shall see Me" — a demonstration, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān says, that in his present state the addressee could not endure the impact of such an experience. Ibn Kathir cites from earlier Scriptures that Allah said to Musa: "O Musa! No living soul sees Me, but will perish, and no solid but will be demolished."

**The Tajalli.** *Fa-lammā tajallā rabbuhu lil-jabal* — "So when his Lord appeared to the mountain, He made it collapse to dust, and Musa fell down unconscious." The word *tajallā* signifies exposure or disclosure; Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes that the Spiritual masters (Sufis) understood it as seeing something indirectly through some other means, like a thing reflected in a mirror — which is why the verse can affirm the *tajalli* while negating the seeing. How small was this disclosure? In his Musnad, Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas bin Malik that the Prophet ﷺ said about this ayah, "Like this" — then he held out the tip of his little finger. At-Tirmidhi recorded this in the chapter of Tafsir for this ayah and said, "This Hadith is Hasan Sahih Gharib"; Al-Hakim recorded it in his Mustadrak through the route of Hamad bin Salamah and said, "This Hadith is Sahih according to the criteria of Muslim." And As-Suddi reported that ʿIkrimah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas about this ayah: only the extent of the little finger appeared from Him, He made the mountain collapse as dust, and Musa fell down unconscious — reports Ibn Jarir also recorded. Only that much — and a mountain could not stand it.

When Musa recovered his senses, he said: "Glory be to You, I turn to You in repentance and I am the first of the believers." Mujahid explains the repentance: from asking to look upon You. And "first of the believers" means, according to Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid — the view Ibn Jarir preferred — first among the Children of Israel; another narration from Ibn ʿAbbas reads it as: none shall see You in this life.

**The swoon remembered on the Last Day.** Al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri that a Jew came to the Prophet ﷺ after his face was smacked by a man of the Ansar — the Ansari had heard him swearing, "No, by He Who has chosen Musa over mankind!", asked "Over Muhammad too?", and struck him in anger. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not prefer me above the Prophets. Verily, on the Day of Resurrection, people will be struck unconscious, and I (feel that I) am the first to wake up. Thereupon I will find that Musa is holding onto a pillar of the Throne ('Arsh of Allah). I will not know if he woke up before me or he received his due (because of his) unconsciousness on (Mount) At-Tur." Al-Bukhari recorded this hadith in many locations of his Sahih, as did Muslim and Abu Dawud; the narration of Abu Hurayrah was collected by Imam Ahmad and the Two Shaykhs (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). The Prophet's ﷺ humility here is itself instruction — and in the hadith's own wording lies a remarkable honour for that moment on the mountain: perhaps Musa's swoon at Tur was counted as his due.

## Chosen by message and by speech (ayah 144)

Allah consoles and elevates Musa: "O Musa, I have chosen you above men by My Messages, and by My speaking (to you). So hold that which I have given you and be of the grateful." Ibn Kathir explains: Allah informed Musa that He had chosen him above the people of his time by His Message and by speaking to him, and the closing words are gentle counsel — hold to what you have been given of My Speech and conversation, be grateful for it, *and do not ask for what is beyond your capacity to bear*. The denial of the vision is folded into a gift.

Ibn Kathir adds the necessary perspective: there is no doubt that Muhammad ﷺ is the chief of all the Children of Adam, the earlier and later ones among them, chosen as the Final and Last Prophet and Messenger whose Law shall remain dominant and valid until the commencement of the Last Hour, and whose followers outnumber those of all Prophets and Messengers; after him, the next in rank of honour and virtue is Ibrahim, upon him be peace, then Musa, son of ʿImran, who spoke to the Most Beneficent directly.

**What was this speech like?** Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān confirms that Allah spoke to Musa directly twice — first when he was entrusted with Prophethood, and now, with additional characteristics, at the giving of the Torah. But as to the *nature* of that speech: it cannot be ascertained by anyone but Allah. Bayan al-Qur'an states that the best practice here is the one followed by the Companions, their disciples, and the elders who followed them: they left such matters to Allah and never tried to resolve them by ungrounded supposition.

## The Tablets (ayah 145)

"We wrote for him on the Tablets the exhortation for all things and the explanation for all things." Ibn Kathir relates that in the Tablets Allah wrote advice and the details of the commandments for lawful and prohibited matters. Were the Tablets the Tawrah itself, or given before it? Ibn Kathir cites both views and concludes, "Allah knows best" — a difference the footnote in Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān also records.

Two commands accompany the gift. **"Hold unto these with firmness"** — Ibn Kathir: be firm on the obedience; revelation is not merely received but gripped. And **"enjoin your people to take the better therein"** — Sufyan bin ʿUyaynah said, "Abu Saʿd narrated to us from ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas that Musa, peace be upon him, was commanded to adhere to the toughest of what was ordained on his people": the leader holds himself to the highest standard while his people take what is best.

**"I shall show you the home of the rebellious."** Ibn Kathir reads this as a promise that Musa's people will witness the recompense of those who defy Allah's order and deviate from His obedience — the destruction, demise and utter loss they will suffer. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān reads it as a promise of inheritance: the Israelites would soon take over the abode of the sinners — Egypt, or Syria, or both, depending on whether they had already returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh (as ayah 137's mention of their inheriting the land may indicate).

## Who is barred from the signs — and why (ayat 146–147)

Then a sudden widening of the lens. "I shall turn away from My Ayat those who behave arrogantly on the earth, without a right." Ibn Kathir renders Allah's meaning: *I shall deprive the hearts of those who are too proud to obey Me of understanding the signs and proofs that testify to My Might, Law and Commandments* — and just as they acted arrogantly without justification, Allah has disgraced them with ignorance. He cites the parallel ayat: "And We shall turn their hearts and their eyes away (from guidance), as they refused to believe therein for the first time" (6:110), and "So when they turned away (from the path of Allah), Allah turned their hearts away (from the right path)" (61:5). Arrogance is punished in kind: the one who looks down cannot look up.

Sufyan bin ʿUyaynah put it starkly: "I shall snatch away comprehension of the Qur'an from them and turn them away from My Ayat." Ibn Jarir took this to indicate the ayah addresses this Ummah; Ibn Kathir gently corrects — this is not necessarily so, for Ibn ʿUyaynah actually meant that it occurs in *every* Ummah, with no difference between one Ummah and another. The law that barred proud hearts from the Torah bars them from the Qur'an.

The ayah then describes the barred heart with terrible precision: it can see *every* sign and not believe (Ibn Kathir compares 10:96–97); shown the way of righteousness it will not adopt it, shown the way of error it adopts that way — "that is because they have rejected Our Ayat and were heedless of them." Rejection first, then heedlessness: the blindness is earned.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān opens up two further points. First, the phrase **"without right"** implies that assuming arrogance in response to the arrogant is a justified act — arrogance in appearance, not in reality — as the known dictum in Masail as-Suluk puts it: "Showing arrogance to the arrogant is an act of humbleness." Second, the "signs" here may refer both to the revealed verses of the Torah, the Evangel and the Qur'an, and to the signs inherent in all the things of the heavens and the earth; the false sense of superiority shuts a person out of *all* of them. Ruh al-Bayan calls arrogance a wicked habitude that raises a wall between man and the knowledge from Allah: divine knowledge comes only through the mercy of Allah, and His mercy visits those who are humble. Sheikh Rumi's line captures it: "Water flows down towards the slope, and solution goes where difficulty appears."

Ayah 147 seals the passage: those who deny Allah's signs *and the meeting in the Hereafter* — vain are their deeds. Ibn Kathir specifies: whoever remains on this path until death finds all his deeds in vain; "Are they requited with anything except what they used to do?" — recompense according to deeds, good for good and evil for evil; as you sow, so you reap.

**Living it.** The passage teaches by contrast. Musa fasts forty days and nights for Allah's word; his people cannot wait ten extra days without inventing a god. Musa, granted the greatest intimacy short of vision, is told: hold what you have been given and be grateful. And the closing ayat name the single disposition that decides which of the two you become: humility receives the signs; arrogance is turned away from them — and takes every deed down with it.

passages.title: The golden calf and Moses' furious return
passages.tafsir:
# The Golden Calf and Moses' Furious Return (7:148–154)

This passage tells the darkest episode in Israel's desert history: while Musa (peace be upon him) was away receiving the Torah, his people melted down their gold and worshipped a calf. What binds these seven ayat into one unit is a complete moral arc — the sin (148), the remorse (149), the prophet's furious confrontation (150), his prayer (151), Allah's twin verdicts of wrath and mercy (152–153), and the calm in which the Tablets are taken up again (154). It is a story about how shirk — directing worship to something other than Allah — happens to believing people, and about how far the door of repentance opens even after it does.

## How the calf was made (ayah 148)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. Musa had gone to Mount Sinai for an appointed term — thirty days, after which he was to pass ten more nights on the mount — and when he did not return after the thirty, his people, "a hasty and impatient people," began to make a fuss. Among them was As-Samiri, a prominent man who harboured superstitious beliefs. He told the people that the Egyptian jewellery in their possession was not permissible for them (booty taken from the enemy was not lawful for the Israelites), so they gathered their ornaments and handed them over. He melted them down and forged a golden calf.

Both commentaries record the strange detail that Samiri had collected dust from under the hoofs of the horse of the angel Jibril, dust to which Allah had given the effect of some kind of life; he mixed it into the molten metal, and the calf emitted a sound like the mooing of a cow. Ibn Kathir notes that the scholars of tafsir differed over what this sound really was: one opinion holds the calf actually became alive and mooed; the other, that it remained made of gold and only the air entering it made it appear to moo. He leaves the matter with "Allah knows best" — and so should we.

Samiri then made his claim. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that he told the people Musa had gone to Mount Sinai to speak with Allah, while — so he claimed — the deity had come to them in the form of this calf: "this is your god and the god of Musa, but Musa forgot it!" Because he already enjoyed a place of respect among them, this unusual demonstration increased their trust in him, and it was reported that when the statue mooed they started dancing around it and fell into misguidance because they adored it. Ibn Kathir links this ayah to Surah Ta-Ha, where Allah says: "Verily, We have tried your people in your absence, and As-Samiri has led them astray" (20:85).

Notice how the Qur'an dismantles the sin in a single question at the end of ayah 148: *Did they not see that it could neither speak to them nor guide them to the way?* Ibn Kathir pairs this with 20:89 — the calf could not return them a word for answer, and had neither power to harm them nor to do them good. This is the Qur'an's standing argument against every false object of worship: they abandoned the Creator of the heavens and the earth, the Lord and King of all things, for a statue that neither spoke to them nor brought them any benefit. Their very sense of reason, Ibn Kathir says, was blinded because of ignorance and misguidance.

## The first turning: remorse (ayah 149)

Before Musa even returns, the tide begins to turn. The Arabic opens with the phrase *wa-lammā suqiṭa fī aydīhim* — which Ibn Kathir explains as: when they regretted and felt sorrow for their action, and saw that they had gone astray. Their response is the raw language of people who suddenly understand their position: "If our Lord have not mercy upon us and forgive us, we shall certainly be of the losers." Ibn Kathir calls this their recognition of their sin and their way of seeking salvation from Allah, the Most Mighty and Majestic. Real repentance begins exactly here — not with excuses, but with the admission that nothing except Allah's mercy stands between the sinner and ruin.

## Musa's return: the anger of a prophet (ayah 150)

Musa returns *ghaḍbān asifā* — angry and grieved. Abu Ad-Darda' said that *asif*, or regret, is the severest type of anger. His first words are to the people: "What an evil thing is that which you have done during my absence. Did you hasten in the matter of your Lord?" — that is, in the words of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, you must have waited until the Book of Allah came to you. Some commentators, it adds, understood it as: did you hastily decide that Musa was dead? Ibn Kathir paraphrases it as: you wanted me to rush back to you, even though being there was Allah's decision.

Then comes the moment that has drawn the most scholarly attention: *he threw down the Tablets* and seized his brother by the head, dragging him towards himself.

**Why did he throw the Tablets when he already knew?** Allah had told Musa on the mountain what had happened — yet only on seeing it did the Tablets fall. Ibn Kathir says this ayah demonstrates the meaning of the hadith, "Information is not the same as observation," and he cites what Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May Allah grant His mercy to Musa! Surely, he who observes [something] is nothing like he who is informed about it.
