His Lord, the Exalted and Most Honored, told him that his people were tested after him, but he did not throw the Tablets. When he saw them with his eyes, then he threw the Tablets." Hearing of a calamity and standing in front of it are two different experiences — even for a prophet.

**Did he really "throw" them?** Here the commentators genuinely differ, and both views deserve their place. Ibn Kathir reports that according to the majority of scholars, early and late, Musa threw down the Tablets out of anger at his people — and later, commenting on ayah 154, he describes it as an act of *jealousy for Allah and anger for His sake*: righteous indignation, not disrespect. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Bayan al-Qur'an) reads the word *ilqāʼ* — which can mean dropping or throwing — differently: since throwing down the Tablets of the Torah would be a great sin and the prophets are innocent and free of all sins, the meaning is that Musa put the Tablets down so quickly, in order to free his hands, that it seemed like dropping; the Qur'an described it with this word as a gesture of warning. Either way, the scene conveys the same truth: the honour of Allah mattered to Musa more in that moment than anything else in his hands.

**Harun's defence.** Musa had left his brother Harun (peace be upon him) as his deputy, and he feared Harun might not have tried hard enough to forbid the people from their evil action. Harun's answer is one of the most humanly tender moments in the Qur'an: "O son of my mother! Indeed the people judged me weak and were about to kill me, so make not the enemies rejoice over me, nor put me among the people who are wrongdoers." Ibn Kathir draws out two fine points. First, Harun addressed Musa as "son of my mother" — though Harun was also the son of Musa's father — precisely so that Musa would feel more mercy and leniency towards him. Second, his plea not to be put among the wrongdoers means: do not place me on the same level as they are, as if I was one of them. And he was not: Ibn Kathir cites Surah Ta-Ha, where Harun had already warned the people beforehand — "O my people! You are being tried in this, and verily, your Lord is (Allah) the Most Gracious, so follow me and obey my order" (20:90) — and where the fuller exchange between the brothers appears (20:92–94). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the people were so obstinate they were about to kill him. Harun had done his duty; the people simply refused to listen.

## The prayer (ayah 151)

Once satisfied of his brother's innocence, Musa's anger turns instantly to supplication: "O my Lord! Forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the Most Merciful of those who show mercy."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on a question the attentive reader will ask: Harun's inclusion is understandable — forgiveness for any shortcoming with regard to his duties — but why does Musa ask forgiveness *for himself*? Two answers are offered: perhaps for his putting away the Tablets of the Torah in a hurry, which the Qur'an had described as having been "dropped" to make a gesture of warning; or perhaps to teach all of us that when we seek forgiveness for others, we should include ourselves — so that interceding for another never breeds complacency about our own state. A man fresh from speaking with Allah still says "forgive *me*" first.

## Two verdicts: wrath for the obstinate, mercy for the repentant (ayat 152–153)

Ayah 152 pronounces the sentence on those who took the calf: wrath from their Lord, and humiliation in the life of this world. Ibn Kathir explains what the "wrath" concretely was: Allah did not accept their repentance until some of them who had not worshipped the calf killed others who had — the command recorded in Surah Al-Baqarah: "So turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves (the guilty), that will be better for you before your Creator. Then He accepted your repentance" (2:54). The "humiliation," he says, is the disgrace and humiliation that the Jews then suffered in the life of this world.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a broader principle from this — *a part of the punishment of some sins is also given in this life* — and illustrates it with Samiri's fate. Musa commanded him to live apart from the people, touching no one and touched by none, so he spent the rest of his life in seclusion, walking about with animals. Al-Qurtubi reports on the authority of the Companion Qatadah that whenever Samiri touched anyone, or was touched by anyone, both of them suffered from fever. The man who invented a religion for the crowd ended utterly alone.

**"Thus do We recompense those who invent lies."** Both commentaries insist this closing sentence is not sealed in the past. Ibn Kathir applies it to all those who invent an innovation in the religion: the disgrace resulting from inventing an innovation and defying Allah's Message, he says, will be placed in the heart and from there on to the shoulders. Al-Hasan Al-Basri put it vividly: "The disgrace of innovation will weigh on their shoulders even if they were to gallop on their mules or trot on their work horses." Abu Qilabah swore, "By Allah! This Ayah is for all those who invent a lie, until the Day of Resurrection," and Sufyan bin 'Uyaynah said, "Every person who invents a Bid'ah (innovation in the religion) will taste disgrace." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records — as reported by al-Qurtubi — that Imam Malik likewise inferred from this verse that those who invent new practices in the Shari'ah deserve the same punishment of Allah's wrath in the Hereafter and disgrace in this life. The calf was, after all, the archetypal innovation: a form of worship no prophet taught, dressed up as devotion.

**Then the door swings open (ayah 153).** Immediately after the severest warning comes one of the Qur'an's widest statements of hope: those who commit evil deeds, then repent afterwards and believe — "verily, your Lord after (all) that is indeed Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." Ibn Kathir states the principle without hedging: Allah accepts repentance from His servants for *any* sin — even shirk, kufr (disbelief), hypocrisy and disobedience. If the calf-worshippers could be forgiven, no sincere penitent is beyond reach.

Ibn Abi Hatim reports a striking illustration of how the early Muslims used this ayah: 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud was asked about a man who committed fornication with a woman and then married her. He simply recited this ayah — and recited it ten times, neither allowing nor disallowing the marriage, letting the verse's promise of forgiveness after repentance speak for itself.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān completes the Israelites' story: they fulfilled the formidable condition laid upon them, killing each other as was stipulated in Allah's command; those killed in this combat were awarded martyrdom, and those who survived were forgiven. Musa then called them to him and informed them that Allah had accepted their repentance. The practical lesson it draws is direct: whoever falls into sin should turn to Allah *instantly* — He forgives in His mercy with no regard to the gravity of the act, so long as the repentance and corrected belief are real.

## When the anger subsided (ayah 154)

The passage closes gently: "And when the anger of Musa calmed, he took up the Tablets; and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord." Ibn Kathir reminds us why they had fallen in the first place — thrown "out of jealousy for Allah and anger for His sake" — so that picking them up again marks the restoration of order: the trial dealt with, the prophet returns to the Book.

The word *nuskhah*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, signifies a writing copied from a book or other writings — hence "in their inscription." Several scholars of tafsir, Ibn Kathir relates, said the Tablets shattered when thrown on the ground and Musa collected the pieces afterwards, finding guidance and mercy in the inscription though the specific details of the Law were lost; they also claimed the shattered pieces remained in the treasury safes of some Israelite kings until the Islamic State came into existence. Ibn Kathir's verdict on all this is the model of scholarly restraint: "Only Allah knows if these statements are true." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records reports that the Tablets had broken when Musa put them away quickly, and that Allah then gave him the Torah written on other material. What the ayah itself guarantees is what matters: whatever the Tablets' physical fate, what they carried was guidance and mercy — and, pointedly, *for those who fear their Lord*. Revelation profits the one who approaches it with awe; the calf-worshippers had the prophet, the miracles and the Book among them, and none of it availed them until fear of their Lord returned to their hearts.

## What the passage leaves with us

Read as a whole, these ayat trace the full circle a believer needs to know: how quickly a community can slide into false worship when a persuasive voice exploits impatience; that a god who can neither speak nor guide refutes itself; that remorse which throws itself on Allah's mercy is the beginning of rescue; that anger for Allah's sake has its place but must give way to prayer and fairness (Musa heard his brother out); that inventing worship brings disgrace in this world before the next; and that after everything — even the worship of a golden calf — the last word belongs to *Ghafūr Raḥīm*: Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

passages.title: Mercy promised through the unlettered Prophet
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the turning point of the Sinai story — and in a sense of the whole Qurʼanic account of the Children of Israel. It opens with seventy chosen men lying lifeless at the foot of the mountain while Musa (peace be upon him) pleads for mercy, and it closes with that mercy being formally "written" — not for the people Musa led, but for a community yet to come: those who follow "the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet" ﷺ. Ayah 155 is the crisis; ayah 156 carries the request and the beginning of Allah's answer; ayah 157 names the people in whom that answer settles; ayah 158 throws the door open to all mankind. Read together, they show how a prayer uttered at Sinai came to rest upon the ummah of Muhammad ﷺ.

## The seventy at the mountain (ayah 155)

Allah commanded Musa to choose seventy of the best men of his people for the appointed meeting. The early authorities differ over what went wrong there, and Ibn Kathir gathers the reports. Ibn ʿAbbas (through ʿAli bin Abi Talhah) said they were taken to supplicate, but prayed with breathtaking arrogance — "O Allah, give us what You have never given anyone before us and will never give anyone after us!" — and Allah disliked it. As-Suddi said they went to apologise for the calf-worship, but on arriving demanded, "We shall never believe in you until we see Allah plainly." Muhammad bin Ishaq tells the fullest version: Musa ordered them to fast, purify themselves and clean their clothes, then led them to Mount Tur. The mountain was wrapped in columns of cloud; when Allah spoke to Musa, a brilliant light no human could bear surrounded him, and the seventy, falling prostrate within the cloud, heard Allah speaking to Musa, commanding and forbidding him. Yet the moment it ended they said, "We will not believe in you unless we see Allah directly" — and the thunder shook them and they died. A fourth explanation, from Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and Ibn Jarir at-Tabari, is that they were seized because they had neither shunned nor forbidden their people who worshipped the calf — silence in the face of evil counted against even the community's best men.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a linguistic reconciliation: Surah al-Baqarah calls what struck them a *ṣāʿiqah* (thunderbolt), while this verse uses *rajfah* (earthquake). Both can be true — punished by thunder from above and quaking earth from beneath. And it records the outcome the verse itself leaves unstated: as a result of Musa's prayer, all seventy were raised to life.

## Anatomy of a prophet's prayer

Musa's plea repays slow reading. "If You had willed, You could have destroyed them and me before" — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the reasoning: had Allah wanted them dead, easier occasions had passed (they could have drowned with Pharaoh, or perished at the calf); so this must be warning, not annihilation. "Would You destroy us for the deeds of the foolish among us?" — the whole must not perish for the folly of some.

"It is only Your *fitnah*" — Your affliction, test and trial, as Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Abu al-ʿAliyah, ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas and many of the Salaf explained; Ibn Kathir calls this the only plausible meaning. Musa is confessing sovereignty: the decision is Yours; You misguide whom You will and guide whom You will; none can avert what You give or give what You withhold.

Then he asks: "Forgive us and have mercy on us, for You are the best of those who forgive." Ibn Kathir notes a subtle pairing — forgiveness covers the mistake and lifts the punishment, while mercy joined to forgiveness carries the hope that Allah will not let one fall into that act again. And "best of those who forgive" — because none but Allah can forgive sin.

In ayah 156 the prayer turns: "Ordain (*uktub* — write) for us good in this world and in the Hereafter; indeed we have *hudna* to You." *Hudna*, explained by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and others, means "we repent, go back and return to You." Ibn Kathir marks the turn in the prayer itself: the first part of Musa's supplication was to fend off what should be avoided, while this part is a request for what is sought.

## "My mercy embraces all things"

Ibn Kathir observes that Allah's reply in ayah 156 answers Musa's own words. To "It is only Your trial" Allah responds: "My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will; but My mercy embraces all things." Punishment is selective; mercy is vast beyond measure. Ibn Kathir links it to the supplication of the angels who carry the Throne: "Our Lord, You comprehend all things in mercy and knowledge" (40:7).

Two hadiths in Ibn Kathir open up its vastness. A bedouin prayed aloud, "O Allah! Grant Your mercy to me and to Muhammad, and do not give a share in it to anyone else." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "You have restricted a vast mercy! Allah, the Exalted, the Most Honored, has created a hundred mercies and sent down one of them, by which the creation — men, jinn and animals — show mercy to each other. He left with Him ninety-nine mercies" (Ahmad and Abu Dawud collected this hadith). In Salman's narration: with that one mercy the creations show mercy to each other and even the beasts show kindness to their offspring; ninety-nine mercies are kept with Him for the Day of Resurrection (Muslim recorded it).

Yet the verse immediately narrows: "I shall *write* it for those who have taqwa, give zakah, and believe in Our ayat." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves a sharp discussion here. Satan reportedly claimed this mercy — "I am one of 'everything'" — and the Jews and Christians claimed it too. The author's teacher Shaykh Anwar Kashmiri answered: the verse says Allah's mercy *can* encompass everything, not that it *shall*; another verse makes it explicit — "Your Lord has all-encompassing mercy; but His punishment cannot be warded off from the evil-doers" (6:147). In this world Allah's mercy reaches even those who rebel and deny; in the Hereafter it is written only for those who meet the conditions. And zakah here, Ibn Kathir notes, may mean purification of the soul or of wealth — possibly both, since the ayah came down in Makkah before zakah was fixed in shares.

## Was Musa's prayer answered? The pivot to this ummah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a striking observation: elsewhere the Qurʼan states plainly that Musa's prayers were granted — "O Musa, you are given what you asked for" (20:36) — but here no such approval is voiced. Some commentators concluded that this prayer was accepted not for the Israelites but for the Muslim ummah (the author of Ruh al-Maʿani thought that a remote possibility). The resolution Maʿārif prefers: the prayer had two parts. The plea for mercy and forgiveness for the punished was granted instantly — the seventy lived. The request that perfect good be *written* in both worlds was answered with conditions — taqwa, zakah, belief in Allah's ayat — and ayah 157 then names the people in whom those conditions are perfectly realised: "those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet." This clause excluded Satan's claim, and its requirement of faith in the final Prophet ﷺ excluded those Jews and Christians who refused him. Ibn Kathir says it directly: those for whom the mercy is written "are the Ummah of Muhammad" ﷺ.

## The unlettered Prophet, written in their books (ayah 157)

The verse calls him *ar-rasūl an-nabiyy al-ummī*. *Ummī* means one who cannot read or write — normally a defect, not a virtue. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns the word over: when a lettered man displays wisdom, we credit his education; but when a man who lived forty years in Makkah with no opportunity to learn suddenly speaks a book whose smallest part none in the world could match, his very illiteracy makes it "as bright a miracle as daylight" — proof that the Qurʼan is from Allah, not from him. What disqualifies others crowns him.

"Whom they find *written* with them in the Tawrah and the Injil" — Maʿārif notes the verse does not say they find his *description* written; they find *him*, so vivid is the portrait. And this claim was made publicly to communities holding those scriptures; had it been false, the Jews and Christians of that age would have seized on it — they never did.

Ibn Jarir recorded (through Al-Muthanna) what that portrait looked like. ʿAtaʼ bin Yasar met ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr and asked him to describe the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as he appears in the Tawrah. He answered: "Yes, by Allah! He is described in the Tawrah just as he is described in the Qurʼan — 'O Prophet! Verily, We have sent you as a witness, and a bearer of glad tidings, and a warner' (33:45) — as a safe refuge for the unlettered ones. 'You are My servant and Messenger. I have called you al-Mutawakkil (the one who trusts in Allah), not hard or harsh.' Neither uttering foul speech in the markets nor returning an evil deed with one in kind; rather, he forgives and forgoes. Allah will not end his life until He straightens through him the crooked religion, so that they might proclaim: there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah — and He will open through him sealed hearts, deaf ears and blind eyes." ʿAtaʼ then asked Kaʿb the same question, and his answer did not differ from ʿAbdullah's even concerning one letter. Al-Bukhari recorded it from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr.

And a scene from the Prophet's ﷺ own life: passing a Jewish man reading from an open copy of the Tawrah while mourning his dying son, he ﷺ asked, "I ask you by He Who has sent down the Tawrah — do you not find the description of me and my advent in your Book?" The father gestured no; the son said, "Rather, yes, by He Who has sent down the Tawrah! We find the description of you and your advent in our Book. I bear witness that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah." The Prophet ﷺ then personally took care of the boy's funeral and led the funeral prayer over him (recorded by Imam Ahmad; the hadith is sound, supported by a similar hadith in the Sahih narrated from Anas).

## Burdens lifted, shackles broken

The ayah then lists what he ﷺ does: he commands *al-maʿrūf* and forbids *al-munkar*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the words: *maʿrūf* is literally "the recognised" — what Islam knows and acknowledges; *munkar* is "the unrecognised" — the stranger. From this it draws a principle: what the first generation recognised as good is good; what the Companions and their students did not recognise is *bidʿah*, innovation, however attractive it looks.

"He makes lawful for them the good things (*ṭayyibāt*) and forbids them the evil things (*khabāʼith*)" — as ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: he made lawful the Bahirah, Saʼibah, Wasilah and Ham — prohibitions people had invented for themselves, which were only hard on themselves — and forbade the evil things: the flesh of the pig, riba, and foods treated as lawful though Allah had forbidden them.

"He releases them from their *iṣr* and the *aghlāl* that were upon them." *Iṣr* is a burden so heavy it stops movement; *aghlāl* (plural of *ghull*) is the shackle binding a criminal's hands to his neck. Maʿārif lists what these had meant for the Israelites: cloth touched by impurity had to be cut away, not washed; war spoils were forbidden — reportedly consumed by a heavenly fire; limbs involved in sin were to be cut off; a murderer had to be killed with no option of ransom. The Prophet ﷺ came, in his own words, "with the easy way of Hanifiyyah" — pure monotheism made light. He told Muʿadh and Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, the two commanders he sent to Yemen: bring glad tidings and do not drive people away; make things easy and do not make them difficult. His ummah is forgiven what occurs within itself so long as it is not uttered or acted upon, and its unintentional errors, forgetfulness and what it is forced to do. This is why Allah guided this community to proclaim the closing prayer of al-Baqarah — "lay not on us a burden like that which You laid on those before us" — and, as recorded in Sahih Muslim, Allah said after every one of those supplications: "I shall accept."

The ayah ends with four conditions of success: those who *believe* in him, *honor* him, *help* him, and *follow the light* sent down with him. The word for honoring, *ʿazzarūhu*, derives (Maʿārif explains) from *taʿzir* — lexically, to stop someone from something with love and affection, and to guard him; Ibn ʿAbbas read it as reverence, and al-Mubarrad as reverence of the highest degree. Notice the frame: the verse opens with "those who follow the Messenger" and closes with "follow the light" — the Sunnah and the Qurʼan. Maʿārif draws the conclusion plainly: eternal salvation depends on obeying both, and obedience to the Prophet ﷺ is only realised by following his Sunnah — not the grudging obedience owed to a high official out of necessity, but obedience born of love and respect. The Companions embodied it: Abu Bakr, after the verse forbidding raised voices, spoke to him ﷺ as one whispers a secret; they knocked on his door with their fingernails to avoid a loud sound; ʿUrwah ibn Masʿud, sent to spy on the Muslims, reported back to Makkah that he had seen the courts of the kings of Rome and Persia, but never reverence like this — "I think you shall never succeed against them." The Qurʼan is called "light" because light needs no external proof of its own existence: it is bright in itself, and it brightens what was dark — so the Qurʼan enlightened a mankind lost in darkness.

## "O mankind, I am the Messenger of Allah to you all" (ayah 158)

Now the passage widens to its full span. The Prophet ﷺ is commanded to declare his message to *all* mankind — "red and black, and the Arabs and non-Arabs alike," as Ibn Kathir puts it — unlike earlier prophets sent to one people for one time. From this verse Ibn Kathir infers that he ﷺ is the seal of the prophets: a message addressed to all people of all ages to come leaves no room for another prophet. Imam Ahmad recorded that Ibn ʿAbbas said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been given five things which were not given to any Prophet before me, and I do not say it out of pride: I was sent to all mankind, black and white alike; Allah made me victorious by fright (His frightening my enemies) for a distance of one month's journey; the spoils of war are lawful for me, yet were not lawful for anyone before me; the earth has been made for me a place for praying and a thing to perform purification with; and I have been given the Shafaʿah (right of intercession), and I saved it for my ummah on the Day of Resurrection — it will reach those who associate none with Allah in worship" (the hadith's chain is suitable, though the Two Sahihs did not record it). And Imam Ahmad reported on the authority of Abu Musa al-Ashʿari that whoever hears of him — be he Muslim, Christian or Jew — must believe in him.

Al-Bukhari recorded a scene that shows what this declaration cost. Abu Bakr and ʿUmar quarrelled; ʿUmar shut his door in Abu Bakr's face; both later came to the Prophet ﷺ. When anger toward Abu Bakr persisted, the Messenger ﷺ said: "Will you leave my Companion alone! I said, 'O people! I am the Messenger of Allah to you all,' and you said, 'You lie' — but Abu Bakr declared, 'You said the truth.'"

The verse grounds the claim in Allah Himself: he is sent by the One "to Whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; there is no deity worthy of worship but He; He gives life and causes death." And it describes the Prophet ﷺ as one "who believes in Allah and His Words" — his actions conform to his words, says Ibn Kathir; the *kalimāt* being the words of Allah revealed to His prophets: the Tawrah, the Injil and the Qurʼan (Maʿārif). Then the decisive command: "believe in Allah and His Messenger… *and follow him*, so that you may be guided." Belief is named first, following second — because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists, sheer verbal belief without practice does not save. The passage that began with Musa begging that mercy be written ends by telling every human being where that written mercy is collected: in believing, loving, and walking behind the unlettered Prophet ﷺ.

passages.title: Twelve tribes, manna, and the twisted command
passages.tafsir:
Before Allah recounts His favours upon the Children of Israel and the failure that followed, He first — with striking fairness — sets apart those among them who remained upon the truth (ayah 159). Then come the favours themselves (ayah 160), the gracious command that would have brought forgiveness (ayah 161), and the deliberate twisting of that command, which drew down punishment instead (ayah 162). Praise where praise is due, then blessing, then the light obedience asked in return, then the substitution that forfeited it — that arc is the passage.

## Ayah 159: the truthful among Musa's people

"And of the people of Musa there is a community who lead (the men) with truth and establish justice therewith." Ibn Kathir explains that of the Children of Israel there are some who follow the truth and judge by it, and he reads this ayah alongside its sister-verses across the Qur'an: the party of the People of the Scripture who "stand for the right, they recite the verses of Allah during the hours of the night, prostrating themselves in prayer" (3:113); those among them who believe in Allah, in what was revealed to the Muslims and what was revealed to them, "humbling themselves before Allah" and never selling His verses for a small price (3:199); those given the Scripture before the Qur'an who believe in it and "will be given their reward twice over, because they are patient" (28:52–54); and those given knowledge who, when the Qur'an is recited to them, "fall down on their faces weeping and it increases their humility" (17:107–109). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same observation: the Qur'an has referred to this group in a number of verses in commendable terms.

**Who exactly are they?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks the question directly and gives a two-part answer: those who faithfully followed the commandments of the Torah and the Injil at the time those books were revealed, and those who readily accepted Islam after the appearance of the Prophet ﷺ, in keeping with the predictions their own scriptures contained.

**The hidden community.** Under this verse, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates a remarkable narrative found in the commentaries of Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir. A group of Israelites who despised the corrupt practices of their people prayed to Allah for a separate land, away from the other tribes, where they could live by the original faith preached by Musa (peace be upon him). Allah carried them to a land somewhere in the Far East, where they practiced their faith faithfully. Then a second favour: on the Night of Ascension (the Miʿrāj), the archangel Jibra'il took the Prophet ﷺ to these people on the way to the heavens. They accepted Islam at his hands, and he taught them some surahs of the Qur'an. Their conversation with him paints a portrait of a society built on sincerity: asked about weights and measures, they said they had none — they heaped their harvest together and each took according to need; asked whether anyone among them lied, they said no one did, for a liar would be consumed by a heavenly fire; their houses were all identical, so that no one could show off his affluence over another; and their graves stood in front of their houses, to keep death before their eyes at all times.

The commentators handle this story with scholarly honesty, and so must we. Al-Qurtubi narrated the event but remarked that the narrative was not authentic; Ibn Kathir termed it an unusual event but did not reject it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the sound conclusion that does not depend on the story at all: whether it refers to these people or to those who embraced Islam when the Prophet ﷺ appeared, the verse establishes that there has always been a group among the Israelites who followed the truth.

## Ayah 160: twelve tribes, twelve springs, and food from the sky

The passage then turns to the favours. Allah divided them into twelve tribes, each a distinct community. When they asked Musa (peace be upon him) for water, Allah revealed to him: "Strike the stone with your stick" — and twelve springs gushed from it, "each group knew its own place for water." Notice the correspondence: twelve tribes, twelve springs. The provision was measured to their order; every tribe had its own appointed drinking place. Above them, clouds gave shade; upon them came down the manna and the quail, with the invitation, "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you." Water, shade, and food — all supplied by miracle.

The ayah closes with a line that reframes everything that follows: "They harmed Us not but they used to harm themselves." Whatever ingratitude came next took nothing away from Allah. The damage of sin lands entirely on the sinner — a principle this passage states before it narrates the sin.

## Ayat 161–162: a light command, a twisted word

Ayah 161 records the command as it was given: "Dwell in this town" — which Ibn Kathir's rendering identifies as Jerusalem — "and eat therefrom wherever you wish, and say, '(O Allah) forgive our sins'; and enter the gate prostrating (bowing with humility)." And the promise attached to it: "We shall forgive you your wrongdoings. We shall increase (the reward) for the good-doers." Weigh what was asked against what was offered. The demands were light — eat freely, speak one word of seeking forgiveness, pass through the gate in a posture of humility. The return was enormous — sins forgiven, and for those who do good, increase on top of forgiveness.

Ayah 162 records what happened: "But those among them who did wrong, changed the word that had been told to them." Note the Qur'an's precision — *those among them who did wrong*, not all of them; the same fairness that opened the passage in ayah 159 governs its end. And note the nature of the offence: they were given a word to say and substituted something else for it. It was not that obedience was beyond them; they swapped it out. "So We sent on them a torment from the heaven in return for their wrongdoings" — the punishment, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises, was the direct result of their deviation from the commands of Allah: favours enumerated, transgression chosen, heavenly punishment following.

## A Makkan retelling of a familiar story

Ibn Kathir points out that these ayat closely parallel the account in Surat al-Baqarah — but with a difference worth knowing: al-Baqarah was revealed in Madinah, while these ayat were revealed in Makkah, and there are differences of wording between the two tellings, which he discusses in his commentary there. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise refers the reader to its detailed treatment under al-Baqarah 57–59. The same history, told twice by revelation in two cities — each telling with its own emphases.

## Living it

The passage's lessons lie on its surface. First, fairness: even in a passage of censure, Allah opens by praising the truthful minority, and in ayah 162 blames only "those among them who did wrong" — a standard for how believers speak about any people. Second, perspective on sin: "They harmed Us not but they used to harm themselves" — disobedience diminishes Allah in nothing; it only wounds the one who commits it. Third, obedience in the form it was given: forgiveness had been placed within reach in a single word and a humble posture, and it was lost not through hardship but through substitution. Take Allah's commands as they come, without editing them to taste.

passages.title: The Sabbath-breakers of the seaside town
passages.tafsir:
This passage tells the story of a Jewish fishing town on the sea whose people were tested through the very livelihood they depended on — and who tried to cheat Allah's law with a clever legal trick. What binds the four ayat together is a single, complete drama: the test (ayah 163), the town's split into three camps when the sin took hold (ayah 164), the rescue of those who spoke up and the seizure of the wrongdoers (ayah 165), and the final, terrible sentence on those who persisted (ayah 166).

## A question that is really a warning

Ayah 163 opens with a command to the Prophet ﷺ: "Ask them about the town which was by the sea." Ibn Kathir explains who "them" is: the Jews who were with the Prophet ﷺ in his own time. He is to ask them about the story of their fellow Jews who defied Allah's command, so that His punishment overtook them all of a sudden for their evil actions, transgression, and defiance by way of deceit. Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah explains Allah's earlier statement in Surah al-Baqarah (2:65), "And indeed you knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath." And alongside the question, Ibn Kathir records a second instruction: the Prophet ﷺ is to warn the Jews against hiding the description of him that they find in their books, so that they do not suffer what their forefathers suffered. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān states the purpose of the passage plainly: the Prophet ﷺ has been asked to warn the Israelites present in his time by reminding them of these events — the question itself carries the warning. (The detailed account, it notes, is given in its commentary on Surah al-Baqarah, under verses 58–60.)

Which town was it? Ibn Kathir says the village mentioned here is **Aylah**, on the shore of the Qulzum (Red) Sea. He records that Muhammad bin Ishaq related, from Dawud bin al-Husayn, from 'Ikrimah, that Ibn 'Abbas described it as "a village called Aylah between Madyan and At-Tur" — At-Tur being in Sinai. 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah and as-Suddi said similarly.

## A test designed to expose the heart

The heart of ayah 163 is the shape of the trial itself. On the Sabbath — the day these people were commanded to keep sanctified, and on which they were forbidden to fish — their fish came to them *shurraʿan*: openly, visible on top of the water, as ad-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas. And on every other day, when fishing was permitted, the fish stayed hidden. Ibn Jarir, quoted by Ibn Kathir, explains: "This is how We tested them, by making the fish swim close to the surface of the water, on the day which they were prohibited to fish," while the fish would be hidden from them on the day they were allowed to fish.

Notice what kind of test this is. It is not random hardship; it is temptation calibrated to press exactly on the point of obedience. And the ayah tells us why: "Thus We made a trial for them, **for they used to rebel against Allah's command**" — *bimā kānū yafsuqūn*. Ibn Jarir, in the same passage Ibn Kathir quotes, explains this rebellion as "defying His obedience and rebelling against it." The trial did not create their disobedience; it exposed a rebellion that was already in them.

## The legal trick

Ibn Kathir then names the specific sin, and it is subtler than simply casting a net on Saturday. These were a people, he says, "who used a trick to violate Allah's prohibitions, taking an action that seemed legal on the surface" — but which in reality was designed to transgress the prohibition. The outward form of the law was kept while its purpose was gutted.

This is where the passage reaches directly into the life of every believer. Ibn Kathir cites a hadith reported by the imam and scholar Abu 'Abdullah Ibn Battah, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not repeat what the Jews committed, and violate Allah's prohibitions using deceitful tricks." Ibn Kathir remarks that this hadith has a reasonable chain. The lesson is that Allah's rulings bind the intention and the reality, not merely the paperwork. A person who engineers a loophole — technically compliant, deliberately disobedient — stands in the tradition of the Sabbath-breakers, not the believers.

## Three groups, one town

Ayah 164 reveals that the town did not sin as one body. Ibn Kathir explains that its people split into three groups:

- **The transgressors**, who caught fish on the Sabbath.
- **The preachers**, who forbade them and kept away from them.
- **The passive group**, who neither joined the sin nor spoke against it.

The exchange recorded in ayah 164 is between the last two. The passive group asked the preachers: "Why do you preach to a people whom Allah is about to destroy or to punish with a severe torment?" — in Ibn Kathir's paraphrase: why do you forbid these people from evil, when you know that they are destroyed and have earned Allah's punishment? There is, they said, no benefit in forbidding them.

The preachers' answer is one of the great statements in the Qur'an on why a believer speaks against wrong even when it seems futile. They gave two reasons. First, *maʿdhiratan ilā rabbikum* — "in order to be free from guilt before your Lord": we were commanded to enjoin righteousness and forbid evil, and we will be able to stand before Allah having discharged that duty. Second, *wa-laʿallahum yattaqūn* — "and perhaps they may fear Allah": Ibn Kathir unfolds this beautifully — perhaps, on account of our advice, they will stop this evil and repent; and if they repent to Allah, Allah will certainly accept their repentance and grant them His mercy. The preachers never closed the door of hope on the sinners, even while the questioners had already written them off. Success, for the one who commands good, is measured by faithfulness to the duty and hope in Allah — not by whether the audience listens.

## Who was saved?

Ayah 165 delivers the verdict on two of the three groups. When the sinners "forgot the reminder that had been given to them" — Ibn Kathir: when the evildoers refused the advice — Allah "rescued those who forbade evil" and "seized those who did wrong" with a torment described as *baʾīs*. Ibn Kathir records the early authorities on this word: Mujahid said it means "severe," Qatadah said "painful" — meanings, he notes, that are synonymous, and Allah knows best.

But the ayah is conspicuously silent about the third group — the ones who neither sinned nor forbade. Ibn Kathir draws a principle from that silence: "the compensation is comparable to the deed." They did nothing that would warrant praise, and committed no wrong for which they would be admonished — so revelation simply passes over them. It is a quiet, unsettling verdict of its own: neutrality in the face of open sin earns no mention in the ledger of the saved.

Were they at least spared the punishment? The early scholars themselves wrestled with this. 'Ikrimah relates that Ibn 'Abbas said about this ayah: "I do not know whether or not the people were saved who said, 'Why do you preach to a people whom Allah is about to destroy?'" 'Ikrimah continued discussing it with him until he convinced him that they *were* saved — and Ibn 'Abbas then gave him a garment as a gift. Ibn Kathir supports this conclusion from the wording itself: since Allah says "We seized *those who did wrong*," the punishment was limited to the wrongdoers, indicating that those who remained were saved. So the silent group escaped the torment — but only the group that spoke up earned the honour of Allah saying, "We rescued them."

## "Be you monkeys, despised"

Ayah 166 records the end. The sinners did not merely slip once; the ayah says *fa-lammā ʿataw* — "when they stubbornly persisted in violation" of what they had been forbidden. Warning had been given, preachers had pleaded, and they exceeded the limits anyway. Then came the command that no creature can resist: "We said to them: Be you monkeys, despised." As Ibn Kathir's heading states plainly, those who breached the Sabbath were turned into monkeys, while those who had prohibited their actions were saved. The final word, *khāsiʾīn*, Ibn Kathir glosses as "humiliated, disgraced and rejected."

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with three clear charges. First, never play games with Allah's limits: an action that seems legal on the surface but is designed to transgress a prohibition is still a violation, and the Prophet ﷺ forbade repeating what the Jews committed — violating Allah's prohibitions through deceitful tricks. Second, when wrong is done openly, be among those who forbid it — not for guaranteed results, but *maʿdhiratan ilā rabbikum*, to be clear before your Lord, and with genuine hope that the sinner may yet turn back, for Allah accepts those who repent. Third, take the silence about the third group seriously: when the punishment fell, only "those who forbade evil" were named among the rescued. In a town under trial, there is no honoured place on the sidelines.

passages.title: Israel's later history and the Scripture covenant
passages.tafsir:
This passage is Allah's verdict on the later history of the Children of Israel, and on what became of the Scripture they were entrusted to carry. It moves in a single arc: a solemn decree of humiliation for their persistent defiance (ayah 167), their scattering across the earth and their testing with ease and hardship (168), the rise of a generation that inherited the Book yet sold it for worldly gain while presuming on Allah's forgiveness (169), the shining exception of those who hold fast to the Book and establish the prayer (170) — and finally, a return to the founding scene that makes the whole indictment just: the mountain raised over their heads as they took the covenant (171). Two remembrances bracket the passage — "and when your Lord declared…" and "and when We raised the mountain…" — so that the history in between is read in the light of a covenant knowingly taken and knowingly broken.

## A decree until the Day of Resurrection (ayah 167)

The passage opens with the word **ta'adhdhana**. Ibn Kathir records that Mujahid explained it as "declared", and others as "ordained", and that the form of the sentence carries the force of a vow: Allah has bound Himself that He will keep sending against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who will afflict them with a humiliating punishment.

Ibn Kathir then traces this decree through history: it was reported that Musa himself required them to pay a production tax; they later fell under the humiliating rule of the Greek Kushdanin, the Chaldeans, and then the Christians, who subjugated and disgraced them and required them to pay the jizyah (tribute tax); and when Islam came and Muhammad ﷺ was sent, they came under his power and paid the jizyah as well. Al-'Awfi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the "humiliating torment" of this ayah includes both disgrace and the paying of jizyah. Ibn Kathir adds that in the future the Jews will support the Dajjal (the False Messiah), and that the Muslims, along with 'Isa son of Maryam, will kill the Jews — this, he says, will occur just before the end of this world. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same historical line — persecution from the time of the Prophet Sulayman, imprisonment under Nebuchadnezzar, defeat and an ignominious fate at the hands of the Prophet ﷺ and his Caliph 'Umar al-Faruq — and argues that even the modern state in Palestine does not break the pattern, since in its author's reading it survives only by the aid of the great powers, and the Prophet ﷺ informed us in authentic Traditions that 'Isa (peace be upon him) shall descend before the end of the world, the Jews having been gathered together in one place in the last age.

Then comes a pairing that Ibn Kathir asks us not to miss. The ayah ends: "Verily, your Lord is quick in retribution — and certainly He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." Quick in retribution with those who disobey Him and defy His Law; Forgiving and Merciful toward those who repent and return to Him. Ibn Kathir observes that Allah often mentions encouragement and warning together in this way *so that no despair is felt* — so that the heart always travels between hope and fear. Even a decree of punishment closes with an open door.

## Scattered and tested (ayah 168)

"**And We cut them up** in the earth as separate communities." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on the words: *qattaʿnā* signifies breaking something into pieces, and *umam* is the plural of *ummah*, a group, a party. The Jewish people were fragmented across the earth and could not integrate into one solid nation — and the commentary draws a striking principle from this: to be gathered as one people, with your own recognised entity as a nation, is a **blessing** from Allah, while disintegration into scattered fragments is a **punishment** from Him. It contrasts this with the Muslims, who from Madinah in the Prophet's ﷺ time onward have always had independent rule somewhere on the earth.

Yet the ayah is scrupulously fair: "some of them are righteous, and some are otherwise." Ibn Kathir compares this to the confession of the jinn in sūrah 72:11 — "among us are the righteous, and among us are other than that." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the righteous as those who followed the commandments of the Torah faithfully and did not try to distort them — or, on another reading, those who believed in the Prophet ﷺ and followed the Qur'anic guidance once it was revealed — while the "otherwise" includes the infidels and those who obstinately disobeyed their prophets and even killed them.

Then the method of divine dealing: "**We tested them with good and evil, that they might return.**" Ibn Kathir glosses this as times of ease and difficulty, well-being and affliction. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes how deep their perversion ran under both kinds of test — in prosperity they said "Allah is poor and we are rich" (3:181), and in destitution, "Allah's hand is shackled" (5:64) — and draws the universal lesson: prosperity and suffering are both sent as a test, both are temporary and must end, so neither arrogance in one's prosperity nor dejection in one's impoverishment befits a person of understanding.

## The generation that inherited the Book (ayah 169)

Here the passage reaches its centre, and the Arabic carries much of the weight. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up three words:

- **Khalf** — Arabic distinguishes the worthy successor from the unworthy one, and the form used here generally denotes a successor marked by wickedness, standing opposed to the good practices of his elders. A degenerate posterity. Ibn Kathir links it to 19:59: "there has succeeded them a posterity who neglect the Salah (the prayers)."
- **ʿAraḍ** — the "stuff" of this world they grabbed. The word means something bought with money, or simply something possessed, and in Arabic it is the opposite of *jawhar* (substance): an *ʿaraḍ* is a thing that requires something else to show its existence, like a colour, which needs another thing to show itself. The very choice of word, the commentary notes, indicates that anything owned in this world is temporary.
- **Adnā** — "this *lower* life": from *dunuw*, nearness (hence *dunyā*, the near life), or from *danāʼah*, which signifies disgrace. Either way: the close-at-hand, or the disgraced.

So: a generation *inherited the Book* — Ibn Kathir stresses through Qatadah that they were entrusted with it after their Prophets and Messengers, and the ayah itself says "they studied what is in it" — yet they seized the goods of this low life. Mujahid says they would consume whatever they could, lawful or unlawful, *and still wish for forgiveness*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies their trade concretely: they manipulated and distorted the text of the Torah for money offered to them.

As-Suddi preserves a scene that makes the ayah's last clause vivid: whenever the Children of Israel appointed a judge, he took bribes. The best among them held counsel and took covenants from one another not to do so — yet when one of them took a bribe and was asked, "What is the matter with you, taking a bribe to grant judgment?", he answered, "**I will be forgiven.**" The rest of his people admonished him — but when he died or was replaced, his successor took bribes too. That is the meaning of "and if similar gain came their way, they would seize it again": even the ones who admonish, if given the chance to loot this world, would take it.

The ayah then confronts them: "Was not the **covenant of the Book** taken from them, that they should say nothing about Allah but the truth?" Ibn Kathir connects this to 3:187, where those given the Scripture pledged to make it known and clear to mankind and not hide it, then threw it behind their backs and purchased with it some miserable gain. And Ibn 'Abbas — as Ibn Jurayj relates — identifies exactly what untruth they were speaking about Allah: **their claim that He would forgive the sins they kept committing without repenting from them.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point home: Allah's forgiveness is indeed always there — but for the one who is mindful of his error, shows remorse, turns to his Lord in repentance, and makes a firm promise not to repeat the mistake. To persist in the sin while claiming one's own pardon is "sheer self deception." Hence the ayah's closing rebuke: "the home of the Hereafter is better for those who have Taqwa — those who fear Allah, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it. Will you not understand?" — which Ibn Kathir reads as Allah asking whether such people, who preferred this life over what is with Him, have any sense left to restrain them from their foolish ways.

## Those who hold fast (ayah 170)

Against that dark portrait, one bright line: "As for those who **hold fast** to the Book and perform the Salah — certainly We shall never waste the reward of those who do righteous deeds."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the verb: the ayah does not say those who *take* the Book or those who *read* it, but *yumassikūn* — those who hold it fast. Merely keeping the Book of Allah and showing respect to it without following its commandments does not fulfil the very object of its revelation; holding fast requires following all its injunctions and commands. The commentary notes that "the Book" most probably means the Torah — the verse praises those among Israel's religious leaders who truthfully followed its commands and firmly adhered to its guidance — though it may also refer to all the heavenly Books of Allah: the Torah, the Injil, and the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir adds that genuinely adhering to Allah's Book directs a person to follow His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ.

And why, of all the Torah's teachings, is the **Salah** — the prayer — singled out? Because, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, the Salah is the most significant and purposeful act among the precepts Allah has enjoined: the most basic and quintessential way of expressing one's faith in, and obedience to, Allah, and regularity in it makes a person capable of being regular in other worships more willingly and with more ease. The Prophet ﷺ termed the Salah the pillar of Islam: the whole edifice of Islam rests on it, and whoever erects it properly has built the whole structure of his faith on a stronghold — while anyone not regular in the Salah is of no worth to Allah, even if he is seen reciting His name at all times and performs extraordinary acts.

## The mountain overhead (ayah 171)

The passage ends by returning to the beginning of the story — the moment the covenant was taken. "And when We raised the mountain above them as if it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: 'Hold firmly to what We have given you, and remember that which is therein, so that you may fear Allah.'"

The verb here is **nataqnā** — signifying drawing or lifting up — where the parallel account in al-Baqarah uses *rafaʿnā*, "We raised." 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas therefore took *nataqnā* to signify raising high; Ibn Kathir records that Ali bin Abi Talhah reported Ibn 'Abbas commenting, "We raised the mountain," citing as testimony 4:154: "And for their covenant, We raised over them the mountain." And Sufyan Ath-Thawri narrated that Al-A'mash said that Sa'id bin Jubayr said that Ibn 'Abbas said, "The angels raised the Mount over their heads." *Ẓullah* means a sunshade or canopy — the mountain hung over them like an awning.

Ibn Kathir relates the fuller account: Al-Qasim bin Abi Ayyub narrated that Sa'id bin Jubayr said that Ibn 'Abbas said that Musa later proceeded with them to the Sacred Land, took along the Tablets after his anger had subsided, and commanded them to adhere to the orders Allah had ordained to be delivered to them — but these orders became heavy on them and they did not want to implement them, until Allah raised the mountain over them, "as if it had been a canopy" — when the angels raised the mountain over their heads. An-Nasa'i collected this report. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the version in which the Archangel Jibra'il was commanded to raise the Mount of Sinai over their town — an area reported to be three square miles — whereupon they fell down prostrating out of fear and promised obedience to the Law of Musa, the Torah. And yet, the commentary notes soberly, the future events witnessed their deviation from that Law every now and again. Placed at the end of the passage, this scene throws its light back over everything before it: the history of ayat 167–169 befell a people who had seen the mountain overhead and still broke their word.

**Does this contradict "there is no compulsion in religion" (2:256)?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question directly and answers it simply: no disbeliever has ever been forced to *enter* faith, nor is anyone allowed to use force for that purpose. But these people had already believed in Allah and His Prophet and entered the covenant of faith of their own free will; what they refused was the Law of the Torah they had committed to. One who freely takes on the covenant and then deviates from its commandments just to avoid his commitments may rightly be forced to fulfil them — that is enforcement of a commitment, not compulsion in faith.

## What the passage asks of us

The Qur'an tells Israel's story to Israel's successors. The passage marks out the two paths open to those who inherit a Book from Allah. One path studies the Scripture yet trades it for the near, cheap gain, saying "we shall be forgiven" while never turning back: the sources call this sheer self deception, for forgiveness belongs to the one who repents in remorse and resolves not to return, not to the one who presumes. The other path *holds fast* to the Book — implementing its commands and refraining from its prohibitions, not merely honouring it — and anchors that hold in the prayer. And to that second path the passage gives one of the Qur'an's gentlest assurances: "certainly We shall never waste the reward of those who do righteous deeds."

passages.title: The primordial covenant of Adam's descendants
passages.tafsir:
# The Primordial Covenant (7:172–174)

This passage recounts a covenant made before any of us took the form of our earthly existence: Allah brought forth the progeny of Adam, asked them directly, "Am I not your Lord?" — and every soul answered, "Yes, we testify." The three ayat form one tightly argued unit: ayah 172 describes the covenant itself, the end of 172 and ayah 173 cancel in advance the two excuses people might offer on the Day of Resurrection, and ayah 174 explains why Allah spells all this out — "so that they may return."

## The covenant of Alast

The scholars call this event **the covenant of Alast** — named from the first word of Allah's question, *a-lastu*, "Am I not (your Lord)?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, which also calls it the covenant of Eternity, describes it as the great heavenly covenant which the Creator made with all His created beings before they took the form of their existence.

The word the ayah uses for Adam's descendants, **dhurriyyah**, is itself telling. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Imam Raghib al-Isfahani: it comes from the Arabic root *dh-r-ʾ*, "to create," so it signifies *all those created* — the covenant embraced every human being, since all are the progeny of Adam.

One apparent puzzle in the wording: the hadiths (below) describe the offspring coming out of **Adam's** back, while the ayah says "from the Children of Adam, **from their loins**" — the loins of Adam's descendants, plural. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān resolves this simply: Adam's direct children came from his back, and every later generation came from the backs of his descendants in turn. There is no conflict between the two descriptions.

## What the Sunnah tells us about that day

Ibn Kathir gathers the hadiths that fill in the scene. At-Tirmidhi recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: when Allah created Adam, He wiped his back, and every person He would create from him until the Day of Resurrection fell out from his back, with a glimmering light placed between the eyes of each one. Allah showed them to Adam, who asked who they were, and was told, "These are your offspring." Adam noticed one man whose light he admired — Dawud, from the latter generations — and on learning he was given sixty years, Adam gifted him forty of his own. When the angel of death later came, Adam protested that forty years of his life remained; he was reminded that he had given them to his son Dawud. The hadith ends: Adam denied and his offspring denied, Adam forgot and his offspring forgot, Adam erred and his offspring erred. At-Tirmidhi graded this hadith "Hasan Sahih" — a technical grading by which he indicated he considered the report well-authenticated — and noted it was reported through various chains from Abu Hurayrah. Al-Hakim also recorded it in his collection known as the Mustadrak, judging it Sahih (authentic) according to the criteria of Muslim.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas bin Malik — and it is in the Two Sahihs — that the Prophet ﷺ said a man of the Fire will be asked on the Day of Resurrection, "If you owned all that is on the earth, would you pay it as ransom?" He will say yes. Allah will say that He had asked of him something less than that — when he was still in Adam's loins, that he associate none with Him — but he insisted on associating others with Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a narration reported by Imam Malik, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi and Imam Ahmad on the authority of Muslim bin Yasar: people asked the Caliph ʿUmar al-Faruq about this very ayah, and he related the Prophet's ﷺ answer — Allah first created Adam, then placed His hand upon his back and drew forth the righteous descendants, saying, "I have created them for Paradise, and they shall act righteously so as to deserve Paradise," and then the wicked, saying, "I have created them for the Hell, and they shall act wickedly so as to lead them to Hell." Further narrations add texture. Imam Ahmad reports on the authority of the Companion Abu al-Darda' that those who appeared the first time were of fair colour while those appearing the second time were black; and Tirmidhi reports on the authority of Abu Hurayrah that all the children of Adam who were to come into the world had a kind of brilliance on their foreheads. To the natural question of how all humanity to the Last Day could gather in one place, a Tradition narrated by the Companion Abu al-Darda' gives the answer: they did not appear at their usual size, but in the size of a small ant.

**When and where?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the answer of the Companion ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas, reported through authentic sources by Imam Ahmad and Nasa'i: the covenant was taken when Adam was sent down from the heavens to the earth, and the place was the valley of Nauman, known as the plain of ʿArafat, near Makkah.

## Real bodies, real understanding

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a careful inference from the wording of the question. Allah asked, "Am I not your **Rabb**?" — your Lord in the sense of Nourisher and Sustainer. Nourishment is a function of the body, which is made to progress from state to state; a bare spirit needs no such nourishing. So the children of Adam did not appear as spirits alone but with a certain physique made of some fine elements — which the narrations of colour and of brilliance on the foreheads also imply, since colour and brilliance require some material form, and spirits have no colour. And to the question of how beings not yet born could possess the knowledge and reason to answer at all: the Allah who could bring all humanity forth in the size of ants could just as easily imbue them with knowledge and reason enough to recognize their Lord, the Nourisher. We affirm all of this as it has come — Allah wiped Adam's back, placed His hand upon it as the narrations say — without asking how and without likening anything of it to creation.

Ibn Kathir adds a complementary observation about the nature of the testimony itself. Testimony in the Qur'an is sometimes verbal — "They will say: We bear witness against ourselves" (6:130) — and sometimes given by one's very state and conduct, as when the polytheists "testify against their own selves of disbelief" (9:17) simply by how they live, or as in "and to that he bears witness by his deeds" (100:7). So Allah made the children of Adam testify **both by word and by circumstance**: the spoken "Yes" of that day, and the witness of the very nature He created them upon.

## The covenant and the fitrah

That last point opens the door to how the covenant lives on in every person. Ibn Kathir connects the ayah directly to the **fitrah** — the original nature Allah created mankind upon: "Allah's Fitrah with which He has created mankind; no change let there be in the creation of Allah" (30:30). It is recorded in the Two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every child is born upon the Fitrah; it is only his parents who turn him into a Jew, a Christian or a Zoroastrian — just as animals are born with full bodies; do you see any born with a cut-off nose?" And Muslim recorded from ʿIyad bin Himar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ related that Allah said: "I created My servants Hunafa' (monotheists), but the devils came to them and deviated them from their religion, prohibiting for them what I had allowed."

The picture that emerges: the covenant of Alast is not a forgotten formality but a **seed of faith sown in every human heart**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers the natural objection — what value has a pledge no one remembers? — by pointing out that many acts leave their imprint without being remembered or understood. A newborn Muslim has the adhan — the call to the ritual prayer, itself a declaration of Allah's oneness — recited in his right ear; he neither understands it then nor recalls it later, yet the practice exists precisely to revive this pledge and sow the seed of faith in his heart by repeating the message of the covenant in his ears. (A few individuals have even claimed to remember the covenant itself — the great spiritual leader Dhul Nun al-Misri said, "I remember the occurrence of this covenant as clearly as I am hearing it this very moment" — but such cases are rare, and the real answer lies in the effect, not the memory.) The fruit of the seed is visible across humanity: an inbuilt impulse of love and respect for the Creator, which — when misdirected by ignorance — spills out even into the worship of false gods and idols. However distorted the form, the impulse to worship is itself an expression of that love and respect planted in human nature.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also sets this covenant within a wider divine pattern. Allah, whose knowledge needed no evidence, nevertheless chose out of grace and perfect justice that no one be punished without documented proof of his own deeds — recording angels ("he utters not a word but there is by him a vigilant watcher," 50:18), the Balance on the Day of Judgment, and witnesses until the sinner himself confesses (67:11). And out of kindness He did not leave people to bare law: He sent prophets, books, angels, and signs "on the earth… and in your own selves" (51:20–21). Covenant-taking runs through all of it — the pledge taken from all the prophets to believe in and support the final Messenger ﷺ (3:81), and the Prophet's ﷺ own practice of taking bayʿah (the pledge of allegiance) from his Companions, as at Bayʿah al-Ridwan under the tree (48:18) and Bayʿah al-ʿAqabah with the Ansar of Madinah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the pledge later practised with spiritual teachers follows this same pattern — while correcting the misconception that merely placing one's hand in a Sheikh's hand secures salvation; a pledge is only ever a commitment to practice, and treating it as anything else is a deviation from the pledge itself.

## The two excuses cancelled in advance

Why does the ayah say all this was done *"lest you should say…"*? Because the covenant demolishes, before they are ever uttered, the two defences people would raise on the Day of Resurrection.

**The first excuse — ignorance** (end of ayah 172): "We were unaware of this." Ibn Kathir specifies what "this" is: Tawhid — that Allah alone is Lord and King, and that none is worthy of worship except Him. The plea fails because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the pledge lit the candle of faith in their hearts; with even a little reflection they could recognize their Lord. No one arrives at Judgment as a blank slate.

**The second excuse — blaming the ancestors** (ayah 173): "It was only our fathers who associated partners with Allah; we were merely descendants after them — will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?" This plea fails too, and the ayah's own logic is exacting: they will not in fact be punished for their forefathers' deeds, but for their own fault and apathetic attitude. The covenant had sown the seed of Truth in *their* hearts, and it was not difficult for them to see that stones they themselves had shaped into idols, or fire, or trees, could not possibly be their Creator or hold power to help them in their need.

## "They shall act…" — the covenant and human choice

The ʿUmar narration above raised, already among the Companions, the question every reader feels: if Allah has already decided the fate of mankind, why are people asked to do good deeds? The Prophet's ﷺ answer, as the narration relates: whoever is created for Paradise *starts doing the good deeds that make him worthy of Paradise* and dies in that state, and whoever is created for the Fire involves himself in wicked acts until he dies doing them. The destination and the deeds are never separated. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical conclusion: since no one knows which category he belongs to, he must invest all his effort and energy in the deeds that are the characteristics of the people of Paradise, and be hopeful that he is among them. The covenant is not a reason for fatalism; it is a summons to act like someone made for Paradise.

## Ayah 174: the door marked "return"

The passage closes: "And this is how We elaborate the verses, so that they may **return**." As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, Allah has made His signs clear through these detailed verses precisely to make it easy for people to *turn back to their pledge* and acknowledge Him as their Lord — faith, on this reading, is a turning back to a "Yes" the soul has already spoken. Anyone who applies his reason can find the Truth and save himself from everlasting punishment.

For the believer, the passage asks something concrete: to refuse the comfort of blaming forefathers for what the seed of Truth in your own heart could always recognize; to pour your effort into the deeds that mark the people of Paradise, hopeful of being among them; and to guard that inborn seed of faith — for as the hadith of ʿIyad bin Himar warns, the devils' whole project is to deviate the servants of Allah from the religion they were created upon.

passages.title: The scholar who slipped: the panting dog
passages.tafsir:
# The Scholar Who Slipped: The Panting Dog (7:175–178)

This passage tells the story of a man whom Allah gifted with His signs — knowledge, wisdom, and answered prayers — and who then shed it all for the sake of this world. Allah commands the Prophet ﷺ in ayah 175 to relate this account, seals it with one of the most unsettling parables in the Qur'an — the dog that pants no matter what you do to it (ayah 176) — pronounces the verdict on all who belie His signs (ayah 177), and closes with the principle beneath the whole story: whomever Allah guides is truly guided, and whomever He sends astray has lost — a truth the commentary is careful to hold together with the free will Allah has given us to choose (ayah 178). What binds the four ayat together is a single terrifying possibility: that a person can *have* the signs of Allah and still lose everything.

## Who was this man?

The Qur'an itself gives no name or personal identification — a point Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes; what we know of him comes from the many Traditions reported by the exegetes, the Companions and their disciples. Ibn Kathir opens with the report of Abdur-Razzaq, who recorded that ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud said the ayah is about **Balʿam ibn Baʿura, a man from the Children of Israel**, and similar identifications come from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and ʿIkrimah — so, Ibn Kathir concludes, it is well known according to Ibn Masʿud and several others among the Salaf (the early generations of scholars) that the ayah was revealed about a man of the Children of Israel in ancient times. Not every report gives the same name: Qatadah relates that Ibn ʿAbbas said, "He is Sayfi, son of Ar-Rahib," and Kaʿb places him in al-Balqa, a province of Jordan, living in Bayt al-Maqdis among the tyrants.

What the reports agree on is his rank. He was no ordinary man: he **knew Allah's Greatest Name** (*al-Ism al-Aʿzam*) — the name by which, as Ibn Kathir puts it, if Allah is asked, He grants, and if He is called upon, He answers. Malik ibn Dinar says he was one of the scholars of the Children of Israel whose supplication was accepted; people would seek his lead in duʿa in times of difficulty. This is what makes the story so sharp. The Qur'an is not describing an ignorant sinner but a saintly scholar at the summit — and showing how far the fall can go.

## The story

The commentaries preserve several distinct reports of what happened, and it is worth hearing them separately.

**The report of Ibn ʿAbbas.** Ibn Kathir relates, through ʿAli bin Abi Talhah, that Ibn ʿAbbas said: when Musa and those with him went to the city of the tyrants (Jerusalem), the cousins of Balʿam and his people came to him and said, "Musa is a strong man, and he has many soldiers. If he gains the upper hand over us, we will be destroyed. Therefore, supplicate to Allah that He prevents Musa and those with him from prevailing over us." His first answer shows he saw the stakes with total clarity: "If I supplicate to Allah that He turns back Musa and those with him, **I will lose in this life and the Hereafter**." He knew. That is the point. But they kept luring him until he supplicated against Musa and his people — and Allah took away what He had bestowed on him of knowledge. Hence, says Ibn ʿAbbas, Allah's statement: *"but he threw them away; so Shaytan followed him up."*

**The narration of Ibn Ishaq.** Ibn Kathir also cites a fuller narration from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Salim, from Abu an-Nadr: when Musa entered the land of Canaan in the area of Ash-Sham (Greater Syria), the people of Balʿam came to him saying, "This is Musa, son of ʿImran, with the Children of Israel. He wants to drive us out from our land... We are your people and have no other dwelling area. You are a person whose supplication is acceptable, so go out and supplicate to Allah against them." He answered: "Woe to you! Here is Allah's Prophet, with whom the angels and believers are! How can I supplicate against them when I know from Allah what I know?" They pressed — "we have no other dwelling area" — and kept luring and begging him until he was tempted by the trial and set out on his donkey toward Mount Husban, behind the Israelite camp. Even the road resisted him: the donkey sat down and refused to go on; he beat it until it stood, and it balked again, and he beat it again. And when at last he tried to supplicate against Musa and his people, Allah turned his tongue — he found himself mentioning the Children of Israel with good and his own people with evil, and they protested, "O Balʿam! What are you doing? You are supplicating for them and against us!" He said, "It is against my will. This is a matter that Allah has decided." Then, as his tongue was made to loll out of his mouth, he pronounced his own epitaph: **"Now I have lost this life and the Hereafter."**

**The account in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the Tradition reported by Ibn Marduwaih on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, which it calls the most authentic and trusted by the majority of scholars. This event belongs to the period after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, when Allah commanded Musa (peace be upon him) and his people to fight a people called the *Jabbarin* ("the tyrants"). The Jabbarin, who had seen Pharaoh's fate, were terrified when they saw Musa's army approaching, and they came to Balʿam — known to possess the knowledge of the *Ism al-Aʿzam*, whose prayers were generally granted — asking him to pray that Allah turn the Israelites back without war. He refused: Musa, being the prophet of Allah, had the support of Allah's angels; he knew the rank Musa held with Allah, and by praying against him he would ruin himself in this world and the next. Pressed further, he promised to first seek Allah's consent — and in a dream Allah prohibited him from making such a prayer, which he duly reported to them. Then the Jabbarin presented him a gift of considerable value, which he accepted; after that their insistence only increased, and some reports say his wife advised him to accept the gift and pray for them. Blinded, as the commentary puts it, by the love of wealth and wife, he began praying against the Prophet Musa and his people — and by the will of Allah, the words he wanted to utter against Musa came out against the Jabbarin themselves. They cried out in protest; he answered that he could not utter a word against Musa and had no control over his own utterances. The Jabbarin met disaster from a heavenly punishment, and Balʿam's punishment was that his tongue protruded from his mouth until it dangled on his chest.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān carries the story one step darker. Having ruined both his worlds and been deprived of all the spiritual powers he had, Balʿam gave the Jabbarin a purely satanic counsel: send your beautiful girls among the Israelites and let immorality do what your armies cannot, for "an adulterous people can never win over their enemy." The scheme worked on one prominent Israelite — Musa (peace be upon him) made every effort to stop him, but he fell — and a plague followed as punishment, with a death toll of seventy thousand in a single day. The guilty man was killed along with the girl and hung by the Israelites at a public place; then the people turned to Allah in repentance, and the punishment was lifted. The scholar who once led people in prayer ended as a strategist for corrupting them.

## The language of the fall

The ayat compress this whole tragedy into a few devastating words, and each is worth feeling.

**Insalakha — "he wriggled out."** In ayah 175, Allah says of His signs *fa-nsalakha minhā*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this verb describes an animal coming out of its skin — a snake sliding out of its old slough and leaving it behind with no further concern. Revelation had been that intimate to him: not a garment he wore but a skin he lived in. And he shed it. The word tells us the abandonment was total.

**Fa-atbaʿahu ash-shayṭān — "so Shaytan followed him up."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a precise implication from the sequence: as long as he held the knowledge of Allah's signs, Satan could not possess him. Only once he was deprived of that great gift did Shaytan overtake him and lead him into the ranks of *al-ghāwīn*, the misled. Knowledge of Allah's signs is armor; the danger begins the moment it is set aside.

**Akhlada ilā al-arḍ — "he clung to the earth."** In ayah 176, Allah says He could have elevated him by those very signs, "but he clung to the earth and followed his desire." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *akhlada* means to incline toward and cleave to something, and that "the earth" here sweeps in everything the earth yields — wealth, furniture, clothes, food, all worldly possessions gathered into one word. The commentary distills the verse: knowledge of the verses of Allah is the real source of prominence and advancement, but for those who disregard it and prefer worldly desires and possessions, that very knowledge becomes a source of disgrace and disaster. Ibn Kathir reads the contrast the same way: Allah would have raised him above the filth of this earthly life through the ayat He taught him, but he sank instead into its adornments and lusts, "deceived by it, just as life deceived others like him." The image is vertical: revelation pulls a person upward; desire is gravity.

Notice also what ayah 176 establishes about Allah's will: *"Had We willed, We would surely have elevated him."* The elevation was in Allah's hand — yet the ayah immediately assigns the cause of ruin to the man himself: *he* clung, *he* followed his desire. The passage holds both truths together, and ayah 178 will return to them.

## The parable of the dog

Then comes the image the passage is remembered by: *"His parable is the parable of a dog: if you drive him away, he pants; or if you leave him alone, he still pants"* (ayah 176). Ibn Kathir records that the commentators differed over exactly what the comparison targets:

- **Some tied it to the story itself** — his tongue lolled from his mouth like a dog's, as in the narration of Ibn Ishaq; his outward state was made to mirror his inward one.
- **Others read it as a parable of incorrigibility.** A dog pants whether you chase it or leave it in peace; likewise this man — and everyone like him — is unmoved whether you admonish him or not. The call to faith lands on him as if it had never been made. Ibn Kathir links this to Allah's words about the disbelievers, *"It is the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them, they will not believe"* (2:6), and about the hypocrites, that even seventy pleas for their forgiveness would not avail (9:80).
