- **Al-Hasan al-Basri** is reported with a third shade: the heart of the disbeliever, the hypocrite and the wicked is weak and devoid of guidance, and so it keeps faltering — panting, as it were, in every state.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a striking observation about why the dog, of all animals, carries this parable. Breathing is a process Allah has made automatic and effortless for every living creature — the dog excepted. Other animals labor at breathing only when attacked or under strain; the dog alone must labor at it constantly, tongue out, panting whether threatened or at rest. Balʿam is likened to it exactly: his tongue protruded, and he panted like a dog that pants when attacked and pants when left alone. And Ibn Kathir presses the comparison to its moral core: the people who deny Allah's ayat "are equated with dogs that have no interest but to collect food and satisfy lusts." Whoever steps outside knowledge and guidance to chase his lusts and vain desires is just like a dog — what an evil example. In this context Ibn Kathir cites the hadith recorded in the Sahih, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The evil example is not suitable for us: he who goes back on his gift is just like the dog that eats its vomit."*

## Why tell this story — and to whom?

Ayah 176 ends with a command: *"So relate the stories, perhaps they may reflect."* Both commentaries stress that this was aimed first at a live audience. Ibn Kathir explains that the Children of Israel in the Prophet's ﷺ time had knowledge of the story of Balʿam and what happened to him when Allah allowed him to stray and expelled him from His mercy — how Allah favored him by teaching him His Greatest Name, and how he used it in disobedience to Allah, invoking Him against the people of faith of his own day, the followers of Musa. And they were standing in his exact position. Allah had given them knowledge and made them superior to the bedouins around them; He had given them the description of Muhammad ﷺ in their Books so clearly that they could recognize him as they recognize their own children. To defy that knowledge or hide it was to re-enact Balʿam's behavior — and, Ibn Kathir warns, it earns disgrace in this life and humiliation in the Hereafter. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same connection through Ibn ʿAbbas: the Israelites had long been awaiting a prophet and used to describe his attributes to others, yet when he came to them with transparent signs of truth, they "wriggled out" of the commandments of the Torah exactly as Balʿam ibn Baʿura had done — for purely worldly considerations. These are the very people ayah 177 brands: *"Evil is the parable of the people who rejected Our signs — and they used to wrong themselves."* Ibn Kathir is careful with that last clause: Allah wronged no one. They wronged themselves — rejecting guidance, contenting themselves with a life that soon ends, all for desire.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also situates the passage in its surroundings: the preceding ayat spoke of the covenant Allah made with the children of Adam, and these verses go on to mention people who did not fulfill their pledge with Allah — such as the Israelites who awaited the Prophet ﷺ and then, when he appeared, rejected him for worldly considerations.

## Ayah 178: the closing principle

*"Whomever Allah guides, he is the truly guided; and whomever He sends astray — those are the losers."* After a story about a man who had every means of guidance and lost it, this ayah names the reality underneath: guidance and misguidance are both from Allah. Ibn Kathir states it plainly — whomever Allah leads aright, none can mislead; whomever He leads astray has acquired sure loss; whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur. He cites here a hadith narrated from ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud: *"All praise is due to Allah, Whom we praise and seek help, guidance and forgiveness from… He whom Allah guides, will never be misled; and he whom He misguides, will never have one who will guide him…"* — the complete hadith, Ibn Kathir notes, was collected by Imam Ahmad and the collectors of the Sunan and others.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān immediately holds this together with human responsibility: Allah is the Creator of guidance and misguidance, and He has provided clear instructions to distinguish the one from the other, along with a kind of free will to choose between the two paths — so those who willfully choose the right path and do good are rewarded, and those who willfully choose evil are punished. Neither truth cancels the other; Balʿam's story has already shown both operating at once.

The commentary then draws out two subtleties of the wording:

- **Singular versus plural.** The guided one is mentioned in the singular, the misguided in the plural (*ulāʾika hum al-khāsirūn*, "those are the losers"). The path of guidance is one — the single faith preached by every prophet from Adam to the last of the Prophets ﷺ — while the ways of misguidance are thousands in number.
- **No reward is named for the guided.** The losers' loss is stated; for the guided, the ayah says only that he *is guided* — because guidance is itself the greatest blessing of all, encompassing every reward and bounty of this world and the Hereafter, needing no further mention. The elders said that the remembrance and worship of Allah are themselves the reward of the worship. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties this to the Qur'anic phrase *"a recompense from your Lord, a gift"* — even what looks like earned reward (*jazāʾ*) is at root a gift (*ʿaṭāʾ*), since the very deed that earned it was itself given by Allah.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with lessons drawn directly from the story, and they are worth taking as given:

- **Never be proud of knowledge or piety.** Things can change without notice, exactly as they did for Balʿam. Be grateful for what Allah has given, and keep asking Him for firmness in faith.
- **Avoid situations that threaten your faith** — above all where money, wife and children are involved, "because the love of these things is the most powerful agent of misguidance." Balʿam knew the truth; the gift and the household pressure are what broke him.
- **Beware the company of the misguided, and be careful in accepting their gifts and invitations.** Balʿam met his evil fate through accepting the gift of the Jabbarin.
- **Guard society against immorality.** The story's grim epilogue — the scheme of the women and the plague — shows that acts like adultery bring ruin not only on individuals but on a whole people.
- **Know that deviation is itself a punishment.** Stepping outside Allah's commandments opens the door to satanic influences that work unnoticed. Whoever carries knowledge must treat it as a valuable treasure, seek Allah's help in protecting it, and keep correcting himself against error.

The passage began with a command to *relate* this story "so that they may reflect." Its reflection is uncomfortable by design: the signs of Allah, once given, are not a possession but a trust — they can raise a person toward heaven, or, shed like an old skin, leave him panting on the earth with everything lost.

passages.title: Heedless hearts, the Beautiful Names, guiding community
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move like a physician's consultation: ayah 179 gives the diagnosis — souls whose hearts, eyes and ears no longer work for the purpose they were created for; ayah 180 writes the prescription — call upon Allah by His Most Beautiful Names; and ayah 181 shows what health looks like — a community that guides by truth and judges by it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this connection explicit: the people of Hell in ayah 179 wasted their faculties, ayah 180 "has provided with remedy of their disease", and ayah 181 "speaks of those who followed the right path". Read together, the passage is a complete account of heedlessness, its cure, and its opposite.

## "Created for Hell" — what ayah 179 does and does not say

The opening words are deliberately jolting: *"Indeed, We have destined many jinn and humans for Hell."* Ibn Kathir explains that this belongs to the subject of **al-Qadar** — the divine decree. Allah "made a share in the Fire" for many of the jinn and mankind, and, in Ibn Kathir's words, "We prepared them for it by their performance of the deeds of its people. When Allah intended to create the creation, He knew what their work will be before they existed. He wrote all this in a Book, kept with Him, fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and earth." Ibn Kathir cites the hadith recorded by **Muslim** from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Verily, Allah decided the destination and due measurement of the creation fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and earth, and His Throne was over the water." Ibn Kathir then adds that there are many hadiths on this subject and that the matter of al-Qadar is "of utmost importance" — "yet this is not where we should discuss it." We follow his restraint: he affirms the decree and Allah's prior knowledge in the very words above, and stops there; so do we.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān guards the other flank: our *ultimate end* is a divine secret, known to no one — but there are "definite signs which help us to make a surmise". The people of Hell can be recognised, not by peering into the unseen, but by an observable trait: they do not put their faculties of seeing, hearing and understanding to their proper use. The verse therefore functions as a warning we can act on, not a riddle about fate we cannot.

## Hearts that do not understand — the wasted faculties

The verse's description is precise: *hearts wherewith they understand not, eyes wherewith they see not, ears wherewith they hear not.* An obvious question follows, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises it directly: these people are not literally blind or deaf — they see, hear and think perfectly well. How can the Qurʼān negate what plainly exists?

Ibn Kathir's answer is that they fail to benefit from these senses "that Allah made for them as a means of gaining guidance". They are deaf, dumb and blind *in relation to the guidance* — and he stitches this reading together from the Qurʼān itself: "their hearing, seeing, and their hearts availed them nothing since they used to deny the Ayat" (46:26); "it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts which are in the breasts that grow blind" (22:46); and the chilling "whosoever turns away blindly from the remembrance of the Most Gracious (Allah), We appoint for him Shaytan to be an intimate companion to him... they hinder them from the path, but they think that they are guided aright!" (43:36–37). Heedlessness, in this last verse, is not merely being lost — it is being lost while feeling certain of the way.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers the same question with a memorable ladder of creation. Everything is given perception in proportion to its purpose: the stones and the earth have so little sensitivity it can hardly be detected; plants enough for growth and nourishment; animals enough to feed, protect themselves from danger and reproduce. The human being stands at the top, "trusted with the highest and the most perfect degree of life", because his purpose exceeds all of theirs: to recognise his Creator, distinguish right from wrong, and seek His pleasure — a being who, when he rises to this, "can attain more elevated rank than the angels". So the human faculties of understanding, hearing and seeing "should essentially be distinct" from those of the animals. A person who uses them only for material life has not lost his senses; he has demoted them. The Qurʼān itself confirms this reading elsewhere: "They know the outward aspect of this worldly life, but of the Hereafter they are heedless" (30:7), and of the destroyed peoples of ʿĀd and Thamūd, "While they could see clearly." (29:38). Maʿārif presses the point into our own century: a civilisation may conquer space and tame the natural forces to serve its varied needs, yet if all of it serves only physical and material life, it "does not make him distinct from the animal in technicality".

## "Like cattle — no, further astray"

Why does the verse choose cattle (*al-anʿām*), then push past the comparison with *bal hum aḍall* — "nay even more astray"? Ibn Kathir gives two reasons the cattle actually come out ahead. First, cattle at least respond to their shepherd's call, even without understanding his words (he cites 2:171, the shepherd shouting to a flock that hears "nothing but calls and cries") — whereas these people do not respond at all. Second, and more devastating: cattle "fulfill the purpose and service they were created for", while the disbeliever "was created to worship Allah alone in Tawhid" — to single Him out in worship — "but he disbelieved in Allah and associated others in His worship". A creature that fulfils its purpose ranks above one that betrays it; hence Ibn Kathir's striking conclusion that those who obey Allah are more honourable than some angels, while cattle are better than those who disbelieve in Him. Maʿārif adds the dimension of accountability: animals are not bound by the Sharīʿah and have no reward or punishment for their acts — they are required only to serve their physical needs, which they are efficiently doing. A human being who lives only for bodily desires does the same work as the animal, but under an accounting the animal never faces. That is what "nay even more astray" means.

The verse's closing word names the disease: *al-ghāfilūn* — **the heedless ones**. Not the incapable, not the deprived: the inattentive.

## Ayah 180 — the remedy: His Most Beautiful Names

Against this heedlessness, ayah 180 opens a door: *"Allah has the Most Beautiful Names. So call upon Him by them"* — in Arabic, *al-Asmāʼ al-Ḥusnā*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why these names belong to Allah alone: they denote attributes at "the highest degree of perfection", and no created being possesses perfection of that kind — over every "perfect" human there is always someone higher, as the Qurʼān says: "And above every man of knowledge there is someone more knowledgeable." (12:76). Because He alone owns these attributes, He alone is worthy of being called upon — and *duʿāʼ* (calling upon Allah) carries both senses at once: praising, purifying and remembering Allah, and calling Him for help in times of need or difficulty. The verse even supplies the vocabulary: we are not capable of choosing words proper to His glorious being, so He has given us His own.

Ibn Kathir opens with the famous hadith of Abu Hurayrah, collected in the **Two Sahihs**: "Verily, Allah has ninety-nine Names, a hundred less one; whoever counts (and preserves) them, will enter Paradise. Allah is Witr (One) and loves Al-Witr (the odd numbered things)." Then he adds an important caution: Allah's Names are *not restricted* to ninety-nine. His proof is the hadith recorded by **Imam Ahmad in his Musnad** from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿūd — the supplication taught for the person overcome by sadness or grief: "O Allah! I am Your servant, son of Your female servant. My forelock is in Your Hand... I invoke You by every Name that You have and that You called Yourself by, sent down in Your Book, taught to any of Your creatures, or kept with You in the knowledge of the Unseen that is with You. Make the Glorious Qur'an the spring of my heart, the light of my chest, the remover of my grief and the dissipater of my concern." Allah has Names He has never revealed at all. And when the Prophet ﷺ was asked, "O Messenger of Allah! Should we learn these words?" he answered: "Yes. It is an obligation on all those who hear this supplication to learn it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns the verse fully practical. Allah has promised, "Call me and I will answer you" (40:60); the Prophet ﷺ said in a Tradition, "Invoking Allah is the quintessence of worship" — so duʿāʼ is never wasted: it is itself an act of worship whose reward is included in the sheet of one's deeds, and it is granted either with the very thing asked for or, when that thing is untimely or unsuitable for the asker in Allah's knowledge, exchanged with something more proper or beneficial. Maʿārif notes that Tirmidhi and Hakim have enumerated the ninety-nine names in detail, and that invocations made by reciting these names are generally granted. The commentary then hands the reader two prescriptions from the Sunnah. For difficulty and distress, the words reported by **Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Tirmidhi and Nasa'i** through authentic sources: "There is no god but Allah, the Greatest, the Most forbearing, There is no god but Allah, the Lord of the great Throne. There is no god but Allah, the Lord of the Heavens, and the earth and the Lord of the Glorious Throne." And the morning-and-evening invocation the Prophet ﷺ urged upon his own daughter Fāṭimah, reported by **Hakim in his Mustadrak** from Anas — beginning *Yā Ḥayy, Yā Qayyūm*: "O The Alive, The All-Sustaining, I call for help by Your Mercy. Set right every situation that I am in, and do not leave me at the mercy of my inner-self for even a wink of an eye." Notice how directly this last duʿāʼ answers ayah 179: the heedless are precisely those left at the mercy of their inner selves.

## "And leave those who deviate in (the matter of) His names" — ilhad

The verse's second half commands the Prophet ﷺ to keep away from those who distort the prescribed names of Allah. The Arabic word is **ilhad**. Ibn Kathir explains that ilhad here means "deviation, wickedness, injustice and straying", and he notes the related word *lahd*, the hole in the grave — so called "because it is a hole within a hole", turned towards the Qiblah (the direction of prayer). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that ilhad "signifies to decline from the centre", and that in Qurʼanic terminology it is used for deviating from the correct interpretation of the Qurʼanic words or distorting the meanings of the Qurʼanic message. The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites locate its original, pagan form: Ibn ʿAbbās (through al-ʿAwfi) said that belying Allah's Names includes saying that the idol-name *al-Lāt* derived from Allah's Name; Mujahid (through Ibn Jurayj) added that *al-ʿUzzā* was derived from *al-ʿAzīz*, the All-Mighty; Qatadah defined ilhad as associating others with Allah in His Names. The idolaters, in other words, took the divine Names and reassigned them to their idols.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān maps out three forms this deviation takes for us. **First**, calling Allah by names not specified in the Qurʼān and Sunnah — the scholars of the Ummah are unanimous that we may not invent names for Him. He may be called *Nūr* (Light) but not "white"; *Karīm* (generous) but not the synonym *Sakhī*; *Shāfī* (the One who provides cure from disease) but not *Ṭabīb* (doctor) — even where the meaning overlaps, the name must be revealed, not chosen. **Second**, abandoning any of His Names because one thinks it inappropriate in certain situations — a quiet disrespect towards His glorious names. **Third**, applying His Names to created beings. Here Maʿārif distinguishes carefully: names the Qurʼān and Sunnah themselves use for human beings — Raḥīm, Rashīd, ʿAlī, Karīm, ʿAzīz — may be shared; but names denoting Allah's exclusive attributes — Raḥmān, Razzāq, Subḥān, Khāliq, Quddūs, Ghaffār — may never be given to anyone else. To do so out of a false belief that the person owns that attribute is an act of infidelity; to do so heedlessly, from lack of knowledge, is not infidelity but a major sin. Maʿārif then presses on a habit still common: shortening ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ("servant of the Most Merciful") to "Raḥmān", ʿAbd al-Razzāq to "Razzāq" — clipping off the very word "servant" and addressing a human by an exclusive Name of Allah, a major sin committed every time one calls the name, and committed "for no gain" at all, out of sheer thoughtlessness. The verse's warning covers it: "They shall soon be recompensed for what they have been doing."

## Ayah 181 — the community that guides with truth

The passage does not end in the dark. *"And of those whom We have created, there is a community who guides (others) with the truth, and establishes justice therewith."* Ibn Kathir unfolds the two verbs: this is a community "that stands in truth, in words and action" — they proclaim the truth and call to it (*yahdūna bil-ḥaqq*), and they adhere to it themselves and judge by it (*bihi yaʿdilūn*). It was reported that this ayah refers to the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, and Ibn Kathir seals it with the hadith of Muʿawiyah bin Abi Sufyan recorded in the **Two Sahihs**: "There will always be a group of my Ummah who are apparent on the Truth, unabated by those who fail or oppose them, until the (Last) Hour commences" — with other narrations reading "Until Allah's command (the Last Hour) comes while they are still like this" and "And they will dwell in Ash-Sham (Greater Syria)." The verse is thus also a promise: heedlessness will always be widespread ("many" of the jinn and mankind), but truth will never be orphaned.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two reports: through Ibn Jarir, that the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and said, "The people referred to in this verse are my people who shall decide their controversies according to justice and truth and observe justice in all their dealings"; and through ʿAbd ibn Humaid, that he ﷺ said, addressing his Companions, "This verse has been revealed in your favour and prior to you there has been a group of people bearing the same attributes" — then recited the earlier verse of this very surah about the people of Mūsā: "And among the community of Musa there are people who guide with truth and do justice thereby." (7:159). Guiding by truth and judging with justice is, across the nations, the distinct feature of Allah's faithful servants.

## Living the passage

The three ayat leave the believer with a clear programme. From ayah 179: audit the faculties — am I using heart, eyes and ears for what they were uniquely given to me for, or only for what an animal's senses achieve? Maʿārif names the identifying mark of the people of Hell precisely so we can check ourselves against it. From ayah 180: the cure for heedlessness is not willpower alone but duʿāʼ and remembrance — calling on Allah by His revealed Names, which Maʿārif calls the food for one's faith (*īmān*), magnifying the love, respect and awareness of Allah until the hardships of this world grow worthless in one's eyes; and guarding those Names from every distortion, down to how we shorten our children's names. From ayah 181: truth is meant to be lived communally — proclaimed to others and applied to oneself, especially in judgment, "even for their enemies". Maʿārif closes with a sober diagnosis of Muslim decline: from the day the Ummah began to disregard these two features — guiding to truth, judging with justice — an evident regression showed itself in every sphere of its life; and the only way back to "the path of progress and prosperity" is the way of truth and justice this verse describes.

passages.title: Gradual ruin of deniers; their warner is sane
passages.tafsir:
This passage answers two questions at once. The first is a believer's question, and Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān opens by naming it as one that "bothers the minds of many Muslims": if prosperity and progress can only be achieved by following the way of truth and justice, why are the nations far from the truth more prosperous, more advanced, more powerful? The second is a denier's slander — the Quraysh's claim that the man warning them ﷺ was mad. The passage answers both, and the two answers share a root. The deniers misread their own ease as proof that they are on the right path, and misread their warner as a madman, and both misreadings come from the same failure: they will not stop and think. Twice in these five ayat the Qur'an presses that failure as a question — *"Do they not reflect?"* and *"Have they not looked...?"*

Ayah 182 gives the answer to the believer's question: *"As for those who belie our signs, we shall let them be drawn gradually towards (their punishment) from where they do not know."* Allah does not punish those who reject His signs immediately for their sins. Out of His wisdom and mercy, He lets them enjoy their worldly life for a while, then draws them so gradually to their ignominious end that they never know they are being led to it. Their present prosperity is not something propitious for them; it is a respite, a temporary period of relief before the execution of their punishment — which, as Maʿārif notes, is in Qur'anic terminology called **istidrāj**, the gradual drawing of a person toward ruin. Ibn Kathir explains the mechanism plainly: for such people "the doors of provisions will be opened for them and also the means of livelihood, in this life. They will be deceived by all this and think that they are on the correct path."

Both commentaries anchor this in a parallel ayah from Surah al-Anʿām: "So, when they forgot what they were required to remember, We opened to them the gates of everything, until, when they were rejoicing in what they were given, We seized them suddenly, and then they were confounded in despair" (6:44). Notice the sequence the verse itself lays out: forgetting, then open gates, then rejoicing, then sudden seizure.

Maʿārif dissects why this is, in its words, "a more powerful punishment in disguise." Its most essential element is delay: the person is not punished for his evil deeds immediately. Instead, the more he increases in evil, the more he is increased in prosperity and worldly possessions — and it is precisely this prosperity that prevents him from feeling any guilt or taking warning against his crimes. So it quietly deprives him of the one thing that could save him from everlasting punishment: turning to Allah in repentance. Maʿārif captures the resulting state of mind in a devastating image — it "makes one take illness as health and poison as remedy." He is left to go on with his perverted life until death overtakes him and draws him to the eternal chastisement.

Ayah 183 continues the same theme, the wording now turning to the first person: *"And I give them respite. Surely, My plan is firm."* The disbelievers are left to enjoy their worldly life just for a while; then they shall be caught by punishment. Ibn Kathir glosses the respite as Allah prolonging "what they are in," and describes the plan as strong "and perfect." The word rendered "firm" and "strong" is **matīn** — the delay is not neglect; it is design. Two warnings follow from all this, and Maʿārif states both. First, the present prosperity and progress of the non-Muslims should not deceive people: worldly success is simply not evidence of standing with Allah. Second, and more uncomfortably, istidrāj "is not limited to disbelievers only. The iniquitous among Muslims are also dealt with this kind of punishment." It was for this reason, Maʿārif records, that our elders used to fear Allah precisely when He favoured them with prosperity and comforts — they feared lest their prosperity should be a sign of istidrāj.

The same people who misread their ease also misread the man calling them away from it. Ibn Kathir relates the background from Qatadah bin Diʿamah, who said: "We were informed" that the Prophet of Allah once was on Mount as-Safa and called the Quraysh, subtribe by subtribe — "O Children of so-and-so, O Children of so-and-so!" — warning them against Allah's might and what He has done, such as His revenge from His enemies. Some of them commented: "This companion of yours (Prophet Muhammad) is mad; he kept shouting until the morning?" And Allah sent down the ayah: *"Do they not reflect? There is no madness in their companion. He is but a plain warner."*

The ayah's opening word is its argument: **"Do they not reflect?"** The charge of madness (the Arabic word is **jinnah**) collapses the moment anyone actually thinks. The Qur'an calls him **ṣāḥib** — "their companion"; Ibn Kathir identifies him, Muhammad ﷺ, and links the wording to the parallel ayah, "And (O people) your companion is not a madman" (81:22). Maʿārif presses the argument home: a little reflection on their part is enough to prove that he ﷺ was neither of unsound mind nor under any influence of jinn, because "his matchless wisdom and knowledge is an obvious feature of his personality" — those with any claim to wisdom and knowledge are astoundingly bewildered that a man of such extraordinary insight and sagacity could be blamed with madness. Its verdict: "Blaming him with madness, in fact, is madness itself." He is exactly what the ayah says — **nadhīr mubīn**, a plain warner: only an elucidator of realities and a warner against the punishment from Allah.

Ibn Kathir adds a remarkable parallel, ayah 34:46, where Allah prescribes the very method that would settle the question: "Say: 'I exhort you to one (thing) only, that you stand up for Allah's sake in pairs and singly, and reflect, there is no madness in your companion. He is only a warner to you in face of a severe torment.'" Meaning, Ibn Kathir explains: stand for Allah in sincerity, "without stubbornness or bias," as individuals and in groups, and reflect about this man who brought the Message from Allah — is he mad? Whoever does this, "it will become clear to you that he is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in truth and justice." The barrier, in other words, was never the evidence; it was the refusal to reflect without stubbornness or bias.

Ayah 185 then points to where honest reflection should look: *"Have they not looked into the kingdoms of the heavens and the earth, and into things Allah has created, and into the fact that their time may possibly have drawn near."* Maʿārif notes that the Arabic word **malakūt** signifies kingdom in a superlative degree — "the great Kingdom." The verse, it says, invites mankind to practice two important things. First, thoughtful observation of the creation of Allah — the heavens, the earth, and the things existing between them. It does not require a genius: "A little amount of serious thought is enough to make one see that everything, rather every particle of this world, is singing the praise of its Creator," and anyone applying his intellect in conscious observation of things "cannot avoid natural demand of faith in Allah, the One." Ibn Kathir draws the same line: contemplating the kingdom of the heavens and earth and what was created in them leads to certainty that He Who has all this "has no equal or rival," that He Alone deserves the worship and sincere religion — and from there to faith in His Messenger ﷺ, turning to Allah's obedience and rejecting any rivals and idols.

Second, to be mindful of the uncertain period of one's own life. Maʿārif observes that "all crimes and evil deeds are activated by disregard to one's death," while those who are conscious of their indefinite period of life mostly avoid involving themselves in unwanted activities. It cites the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Frequently remember the thing which eliminates the pleasures — the death." The danger the ayah warns of is concrete: life may come to an end any moment, depriving a person of all the chances of accepting the truth and repenting to Allah for his evil deeds.

The ayah closes with a question that shuts every escape route: *"In what message after this will they then believe?"* Ibn Kathir paraphrases: what more warnings and discouragements could compel them to believe, if the warnings and threats that Muhammad ﷺ brought them from Allah in His Book do not? Maʿārif: Allah has provided them with "transparent signs, both internal and external," of the right path and of the true faith — and for those who neglect signs this clear, "there is nothing in the world to guide them to the right path."

The passage ends on the verdict: *"Whomsoever Allah sends astray, none can guide him; and He lets them wander blindly in their transgressions."* Ibn Kathir explains that none can lead such people to guidance — even their best efforts to gain it will not avail them — and pairs the verse with two parallels: "And whomsoever Allah wants to put in Fitnah (error, because of his rejecting of Faith, or trial), you can do nothing for him against Allah" (5:41), and "neither Ayat nor warners benefit those who believe not" (10:101).

Yet Maʿārif reveals the tenderness inside this severe verse. The obstinate ignorance of the disbelievers, despite all the clear signs given to them, could be a source of grief to the Prophet ﷺ, for he was highly considerate and the greatest well-wisher of mankind. Ayah 186 provides him with a consolation: whomsoever Allah leaves wandering in his ignorance and lets go on with his evil deeds can never be guided by anyone, and Allah leaves him "at the mercy of his abject desires." The Prophet ﷺ had done his duty by conveying the message of Allah as explicitly as was possible, and their rejection of the true faith was not for any fault of his.

Maʿārif closes by observing that among the themes of this surah (al-Aʿrāf), three topics are of great importance: the unity of Allah (Tawhid), Prophethood (Risalah), and the life in the Hereafter. These three principles are, in fact, the mainstay of the whole edifice of Islam — and the exposition of the first two, Tawhid and Risalah, has been provided in the foregoing verses.

passages.title: The Hour's timing and the Prophet's human limits
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat close a long passage of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf by answering the question the Makkans loved to throw at the Prophet ﷺ — *when is this Hour you keep warning us about?* — and by drawing from that answer a truth about the Messenger ﷺ himself. Ayah 187 establishes that the timing of the Hour is Allah's alone; ayah 188 widens the lesson: the Prophet ﷺ, for all his rank, is a human being who owns no knowledge of the unseen and no power even over his own benefit and harm except what Allah wills. Together they draw the line between what belongs to Allah alone and what even the chief of the Messengers ﷺ was given.

## Who was asking, and how

Ibn Kathir notes that some said this ayah was revealed about the Jews, but he judges it was about the Quraysh, since the ayah is Makkan — and the Quraysh used to ask about the Hour precisely because they denied it and discounted its coming, as in their taunt elsewhere: "When will be this promise, if you speak the truth?" (10:48). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same occasion from Ibn Jarir and ʿAbd ibn Humaid on the authority of Qatadah: the Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ **by way of mockery** when this doom he kept warning them of would arrive. So the question was not a seeker's question; it was a scoffer's. And there is a striking report behind the ayah's opening words: Tariq bin Shihab said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept mentioning the Last Hour — for people kept asking about it — until this very ayah came down. An-Nasaʼi collected this hadith, which has a strong chain.

## The words of ayah 187

**"Ayyāna mursāhā" — "When will be its appointed time?"** *Mursā*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, signifies to stop or to stay. ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reports from Ibn ʿAbbas that the question refers to the Hour's commencement: they asked about its appointed term and when the end of this world will begin.

**"Al-Sāʿah"** in ordinary Arabic means a short stretch of time; in the Qurʼān's usage it is the name for the Day when all created beings cease to exist, and equally for the Day when all creation is revived and presented before its Lord (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān).

**"Heavy is its burden through the heavens and the earth."** The early commentators read this weightiness in complementary ways, and Ibn Kathir lays them side by side. Qatadah and As-Suddi took the *knowledge* of it to be what is heavy: it presses on the residents of the heavens and the earth because it is hidden from them — none, not even a close angel or a sent Messenger, has knowledge of its appointed time. Al-Hasan and Ibn ʿAbbas took the *event* to be heavy: when the Last Hour comes, it will be heavy on the residents of the heavens and earth, and, in Ibn ʿAbbas's words, "All creatures will suffer its heaviness on the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Jurayj spelled out that heaviness in cosmic terms: the heavens torn, the stars scattered, the sun wound round and losing its light, the mountains made to pass away. Both readings serve the ayah's point — a thing too heavy for creation to carry cannot be a thing creation is told about in advance.

**"It shall not come upon you except baghtatan" — all of a sudden.** Qatadah said Allah has decided this: the Hour arrives without warning, while people are unaware.

**"They ask you as if you were ḥafiyy of it."** *Ḥafiyy*, Ibn ʿAbbas explains, is a scholar or knowledgeable person — the word is generally used for one who invests his effort and employs all his resources to ascertain something (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). Two explanations of the phrase are reported. Al-ʿAwfi relates from Ibn ʿAbbas: "As if you have good relations and friendship with them!" — the pagans of Quraysh asked as though Muhammad ﷺ were their friend who would surely let them in on the secret. Mujahid's explanation, which Ibn Kathir declares the correct one, is: "as if you had asked about its time and so its knowledge is with you." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the psychology behind it: they thought the Prophet ﷺ had somehow secured the knowledge of the exact time and was not disclosing it for some purpose, so they insisted he disclose it. The ayah answers both suspicions at once: "Its knowledge is only with Allah, but most of the people do not know."

## The suddenness, from the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir gathers the hadith that paint this *baghtatan* in unforgettable, everyday colors. Al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the Hour will not commence until the sun rises from the west — and when people see it, all will believe, but at that point faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe beforehand. Then: the Hour will commence while two men have spread a garment between them, and they will have time neither to conclude the transaction nor to fold the garment; after a man has milked his animal, before he can drink the milk; while a man is making his watering hole, before he can make use of the pool; while a man has raised a bite to his mouth, before he can eat it.

And in the hadith of the Night Journey recorded by Imam Ahmad from Ibn Masʿud (Ibn Majah also collected a similar hadith), the Prophet ﷺ related that Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa mentioned the matter of the Last Hour among themselves. Ibrahim said, "I do not have knowledge of it." Musa said, "I have no knowledge of it." ʿIsa said that as for *when* it occurs, only Allah, the Exalted and Most Honored, knows that — but he described what his Lord had conveyed to him of its signs: the Dajjal (the False Messiah) will appear, and Allah will destroy him when he sees ʿIsa; then Gog and Magog will swarm from every mound, and Allah will bring death to all of them by the blessing of his supplication — and when all this has happened, the Hour will be like a pregnant woman whose term is full: her family does not know when she will surprise them and give birth, whether by night or by day. Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion sharply: these are the greatest of the Messengers, yet they did not have knowledge of the Hour's appointed term; ʿIsa spoke only of its signs, since he will descend in the last generations of this Ummah.

The famous hadith of Jibril belongs here too. When Jibril came in the shape of a bedouin to teach the people matters of their religion, he asked the Messenger ﷺ about Islam, then Iman, then Ihsan, and finally, "When will the Hour start?" The Prophet ﷺ answered: "He who is asked about it has no more knowledge of it than the questioner" — that is, as Ibn Kathir explains, "I have no more knowledge in it than you (O Jibril), nor does anyone have more knowledge in it than anyone else" — and he recited "Verily, Allah, with Him (Alone) is the knowledge of the Hour" (31:34). In another narration he said, "Five, their knowledge is only with Allah," then recited the same ayah. Neither the noblest angel nor the Seal of the Messengers ﷺ holds the date.

Similarly Imam Ahmad recorded that Hudhayfah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the Hour and replied: "Its knowledge is with my Lord, the Exalted and Most Honored, none can reveal its time except Him. However, I will tell you about its portents and the signs that precede it. Before it commences, there will be Fitnah (trials) and Harj." Asked what harj is, he said, "It means killing, in the Language of the Ethiopians," and added, "Isolation and loneliness will be common between people, and therefore, almost no one will be able to recognize any other." This is the consistent prophetic pattern: the *when* is refused; the *signs* are taught.

## Near — yet its moment unknown

Ibn Kathir dwells on a paradox that deepens the ayah. This same Prophet ﷺ said — as collected in the Sahih from Anas and Sahl bin Saʿd — "My sending and the Hour are like this," joining his index and middle fingers (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the like of it from Tirmidhi: his appearance and the Day of Qiyamah are as close to each other as two fingers of a hand). He is the unlettered Prophet ﷺ, the chief of the Messengers and their Seal — al-ʿĀqib, who came after many Prophets; al-Muqaffī, the last of a succession; al-Ḥāshir, below whom all people will be gathered on the Day of Gathering. Yet even he was commanded, whenever asked, to defer knowledge of the Last Hour to Allah.

What of the hadiths where he seems to give a time? Muslim recorded from ʿAʼishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that when the bedouins used to ask him about the Hour, he would answer while pointing at the youngest person among them: "If this young man lives, he will not become old before your Hour starts" — and Ibn Kathir explains that he meant the end of their own lives, which introduces them to the life of the Barzakh, the realm between this life and the Hereafter. Each person's death is, in that sense, his own "hour." Likewise Jabir bin ʿAbdullah heard him say, one month before he died: "You keep asking me about the Hour, when its knowledge is with Allah. I swear by Allah that there is no living soul on the face of the earth now [that] will be alive a hundred years from now" (Muslim; a similar hadith is in the Two Sahihs from Ibn ʿUmar, who commented that he meant his generation would have reached its appointed term by then). Not one of these reports breaches the secret; they redirect the questioner from a date he can never have to a death he certainly will.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a caution about calculations: the reports circulating in some Islamic books that give the world a total age of seven thousand years are borrowed from Israelite literature and have no basis in the Qurʼān or the Sunnah — while modern geological estimates of the earth's vast age contradict no ayah or authentic hadith. Ibn Hazm concluded that the world's exact age cannot be assessed by anyone; its translator observes the neat logic of that: an exact age would yield an exact end, and this ayah has sealed that knowledge away.

## Ayah 188: "I possess no power over benefit or harm to myself"

Having closed the door on the Hour's date, Allah commands His Prophet ﷺ to declare something larger about himself: "I possess no power over benefit or harm to myself except as Allah wills. If I had the knowledge of the Ghayb (Unseen), I should have secured for myself an abundance of wealth, and no evil should have touched me. I am but a warner, and a bringer of glad tidings unto people who believe."

The argument is disarmingly practical, and the early commentators unfold it concretely. Ibn ʿAbbas, in the report of Ad-Dahhak, said the "abundance" here refers to money — and in another narration: "I would have knowledge of how much profit I would make with what I buy, and I would always sell what I would make profit from... and poverty would never touch me." Others, Ibn Jarir relates, said it means: had he known the Unseen, he would have prepared during the prosperous years for the years of famine, and prepared ahead for times of high cost. ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said of "and no evil should have touched me": "I would have avoided and saved myself from any type of harm before it comes." The Prophet's ﷺ actual life is the proof, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to two moments: at Hudaybiyah he and his Companions travelled all the way to Makkah in order to perform ʿUmrah, and despite all their desire and effort were turned back to Madinah without it; at Uhud he was himself wounded and the Muslims faced a temporary defeat. Perhaps, Maʿārif suggests, such events were allowed to happen precisely to demonstrate in practical terms that the prophets — with due regard to their being closest to Allah and the best of all human beings — did not possess divine power or all-encompassing knowledge. They were human like other human beings.

This is where the ayah becomes creed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly: all-encompassing knowledge is an exclusive attribute of Allah which cannot be ascribed to any created being, and ascribing these exclusive attributes to anyone other than Allah is the greatest transgression — tantamount to associating partners with Him, when the very purpose of the Qurʼān's revelation and the Prophet's ﷺ advent was to establish the purest unity of Allah. The Christians fell prey to exactly this error when they ascribed the divine attributes of Allah to their Prophet. At the same time, the balance must be kept: Allah invested His prophets with knowledge and power no other human being has ever acquired, and the Prophet ﷺ was favoured above all other prophets — he informed the Muslims of many things which were to happen in the future, and all his foretellings were seen to happen exactly as he had foretold. But this Allah-given knowledge is, in the Qurʼān's own terminology, not "knowledge of the ghayb"; so we are not allowed to call the Prophet ﷺ *ʿĀlim al-Ghayb*, "Knower of the Unseen," for the Knower of the Unseen is none other than Allah — "(He Alone is) the All-Knower of the Ghayb (Unseen), and He reveals to none His Ghayb" (72:26). What Allah discloses to a Messenger is a gift; what remains is His alone. And the lack of such reserved knowledge on a prophet's part is no argument against his prophethood — the knowledge of a prophet can never be equal to the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah.

The ayah ends by naming what the Prophet ﷺ *is*: "I am but a warner and a harbinger of good for people who believe" — warning the evildoers against the punishment of Allah and giving the righteous the good tidings of great reward, as in the parallel ayah: "So We have made this (the Qurʼān) easy on your tongue, only that you may give glad tidings to the pious, and warn with it the most quarrelsome of people" (19:97). Not a fortune-teller, not a keeper of dates — a Messenger.

## Living with a sealed date

Why did Allah, in His wisdom, seal it? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Al-Bukhari and Muslim report on the authority of Abu Hurairah that the Prophet ﷺ spoke of the sudden occurrence of the Qiyamah as something that has been made a close secret — and Maʿārif draws out the mercies in that concealment. Had the definite time of death been known to people, living life peacefully would have been impossible. Had the deniers known the remotely long period before its occurrence, they would only have made more mockery of it. And the undefined dread of a Day that could break in *baghtatan* — mid-meal, mid-sale, mid-milking — is itself an effective restraint against crime and corrupt practices that no announced date could ever be.

And the passage quietly re-aims the question. Once you believe the Day is inevitably coming, that every created being will be presented before the Lord of all creation and called to account for every minor and major deed, then *when* it comes becomes immaterial. The Quraysh's question was a product of their ignorance; wisdom demands the opposite of it — not wasting the precious time of one's life in futile discussions about the timing of the end, but spending every moment of its uncertain span preparing for the great Day itself. The Hour's date is Allah's secret; your readiness for it is entirely your own affair.

passages.title: From one soul to idols that create nothing
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a single sustained argument about gratitude and worship. It opens with the most intimate of Allah's gifts — a spouse to find comfort in, a child growing in the womb, a desperate prayer answered — and shows how human beings take that very gift and credit it to others besides Allah. Then, in ayat 191–195, the Qur'an turns on those "others" and cross-examines them: can they create? help? walk? hold? see? hear? The unit moves from the One who created you from a single soul to the nothings that create nothing — and by the end, the case for shirk (associating partners with Allah) has collapsed under its own weight.

## One soul, and a mate to find comfort in

Ayah 189 begins, in the rendering of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "He is the One who has created you from a single soul and from him created his wife, so that he may find comfort in her." Ibn Kathir explains that Allah created all mankind from Adam, peace be upon him, and from Adam created his wife Hawwa', and from the two of them people spread across the earth — the same truth stated in 4:1 and 49:13.

The key phrase is **li-yaskuna ilayha**, which Ibn Kathir renders "in order that he might enjoy the pleasure of living with her" and explains as meaning that the husband is intimate and compassionate with his wife. He links it to 30:21, where Allah makes spouses "that you may find repose in them, and He has put between you affection and mercy." Then Ibn Kathir adds a striking observation: there is no intimacy between two souls like that between spouses — which is why the Qur'an mentions the sorcerer trying to separate a man from his wife; in normal circumstances that bond is hard to break. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same lesson: man and woman were created of one species precisely so there would be natural affinity and understanding between them, and the rights and duties of marriage aim at a peaceful home.

## The prayer of expectant parents

The ayah then follows a pregnancy stage by stage, in language of great delicacy. "When he covered her" — *taghashshaha*, a modest veil of a word which Ibn Kathir explains as marital intimacy — "she carried a light burden and moved about with it."

The **"light burden"** (*hamlan khafifan*) is early pregnancy, when the mother feels no pain: Ibn Kathir notes that the fetus at this stage is just a *nutfah* (the mixture of the male and female discharge), then becomes an *ʿalaqah* (a piece of thick coagulated blood) and then a *mudghah* (a small lump of flesh). The early authorities lingered over the phrase **fa-marrat bihi** ("she carried it about"): Mujahid said it means she continued the pregnancy, and al-Hasan, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi and al-Suddi are reported to have said similarly — al-Hasan told a questioner, "Had you been an Arab, you would know what it means!" — while Qatadah said it means it became clear that she was pregnant, and Ibn ʿAbbas (in al-ʿAwfi's report) said she was at first unsure whether she was pregnant at all. Different angles, one picture: the almost unnoticed beginning of a life.

"Then when she grew heavy" — when the child could no longer be ignored — "they both invoked Allah, their Lord: *If You give us a Salih child, we shall indeed be among the grateful.*" Ibn Kathir glosses **Salih** as "good in every aspect" — a child, as he puts it, "born human in every respect." The commentators felt the parents' anxiety vividly: ad-Dahhak reports Ibn ʿAbbas saying they feared the child might be born in the shape of an animal; Abu al-Bakhtari and Abu Malik said they feared it might not be human at all; al-Hasan al-Basri read the prayer simply as "If You give us a boy"; and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it in plainer terms — parents fear the child may not be normal, or may be deaf, dumb or blind. In that fear, they bargain with Allah: give us a healthy child and we will be thankful.

Ayah 190 delivers the bitter turn: "But when He gave them a Salih child, they ascribed partners to Him *in that which He had given them*." The prayer was to Allah alone; the child came; and the thanks went elsewhere. The ayah closes by clearing Allah of the whole affair: "High be Allah, Exalted above all that they ascribe as partners to Him."

## Who ascribed the partners? Not Adam and Hawwa'

The pronouns in 189–190 are dual — "they both prayed… they both ascribed partners" — and since the ayah opened with Adam and his wife, a reader might think the shirk is theirs. Both of our commentaries firmly reject this.

Ibn Kathir relies on **al-Hasan al-Basri**, whose explanations here, he notes, come through authentic chains: "This occurred by followers of some religion, not from Adam" — the ayah refers to those among the *offspring* of Adam who fell into shirk. Qatadah adds that al-Hasan applied it to the Jews and Christians: Allah gave them children, and they turned those children into Jews and Christians. Ibn Kathir calls this one of the best interpretations and explains the grammar of it: the Qur'an mentions the individual first (Adam and Hawwa', from whom mankind came) and then slides to the species (mankind, many of whom committed shirk). He compares 67:5, where the "lamps" adorning the sky and the missiles hurled at devils are not the same stars — the Qur'an often moves from one referent to a related one within a single breath.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adopts the same reading on the authority of **Ibn ʿAbbas**, as reported by Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim in Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur: the opening of the ayah holds up Adam and Hawwa' as the model of gratitude their children were meant to follow; the rest of the ayah describes the descendants who betrayed it. It also notes, with scholarly honesty, that a story related by Tirmidhi and Hakim about Adam and Hawwa' being deceived by Shaytan exists: some scholars dismissed it as an unreliable Israelite report, while many hadith scholars confirmed it — but either way, the interpretation above removes any doubt: the Prophet Adam and Hawwa', peace be upon them both, have nothing to do with shirk.

## How shirk creeps into the nursery

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then shows how this ayah plays out in real families, and its examples are uncomfortably contemporary. Shirk enters in a variety of ways. Sometimes parents are misled by the false belief that the newborn is the gift of some holy or godly person rather than of Allah; sometimes they devote the child to a living or dead person and make offerings in that person's name; some take their children to such figures and bow their foreheads before them; and sometimes they fall into shirk through the very **names** they give — names that assign the child to other than Allah: ʿAbd al-ʿUzza ("slave of ʿUzza"), ʿAbd Shams ("slave of the Sun"), ʿAbdullat, Bandah ʿAli. Maʿārif is explicit that such names are prohibited *even if the parents do not really mean the servitude* — the words themselves assign the child to a false lord, and this is a great sin. The grateful alternative: names built on the good names of Allah, like ʿAbd al-Rahman and ʿAbdullah, which the Prophet ﷺ recommended. The commentary laments how casually Muslims now drift into fashionable names and initials that erase this mark of who their children belong to.

## The cross-examination of the idols (191–195)

Having shown the crime — thanking created things for the Creator's gift — the passage now puts the "partners" themselves on trial, and every question is rhetorical because the answer is obvious.

**Ayah 191:** "Do they associate as partners things that create nothing, and are themselves created?" Ibn Kathir's comment cuts to the core absurdity: these idols and images were themselves made by Allah — or carved by human hands, as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, taunted his people: "Do you worship what you yourselves carve?" (37:95). Ibn Kathir brings the Qur'an's own devastating illustration from 22:73–74: if every false god combined its strength, they could not create a single fly — and if the fly snatched something from them, they could not get it back. "So weak are both the seeker and the sought."

**Ayat 192–193:** They can give their worshippers no help, "nor can they help themselves" — Ibrahim smashed his people's idols to pieces (21:58) and nothing stopped him. And if you call them to guidance, they do not follow; "it is the same for you whether you call them or keep silent." A god you cannot even talk to, says ayah 193, is functionally identical to no god at all — exactly Ibrahim's question to his father: "Why do you worship what hears not, sees not, and cannot avail you in anything?" (19:42).

**Ayah 194** lands the deepest blow: "Those you call upon besides Allah are **servants like you**" — *ʿibadun amthalukum*. These worshipped objects are themselves created things — fellow servants, not lords. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paraphrases the Prophet's ﷺ instruction here: tell them their false gods are slaves like themselves, lacking the very faculties of moving, seeing, hearing and speaking — unable to help themselves, let alone rescue you in your need. And then the dare: "So call upon them, and let them answer you, if you are truthful."

**Ayah 195** presses the dare into four questions: "Have they feet to walk with? Or hands to hold with? Or eyes to see with? Or ears to hear with?" Ibn Kathir observes that the worshippers are actually *better* than what they worship — a human being can hear, see, and act with strength of his own; the idol can do none of it. The ayah ends with the Prophet ﷺ commanded to throw down the gauntlet: "Call your partners, then plot against me, and give me no respite." Ibn Kathir hears in this the voice of the earlier prophets — Hud, who told his people, "Plot against me, all of you, and give me no respite; I put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord" (11:54–56), and Ibrahim, who declared himself free of everything they worshipped besides the One who created him (26:75–78, 43:26–28). A man standing alone with Allah fears nothing that an army of false gods can muster.

## The idol on the end of a rope

Ibn Kathir preserves a story from the early days of Islam in Madinah that turns this whole passage into flesh and blood. Two young converts — Muʿadh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Jamuh and Muʿadh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with them both — took to attacking the idols of the idolaters by night, breaking and disfiguring them, even using them as fuel for needy widows, to make their people aware of their error. ʿAmr ibn al-Jamuh, one of the chiefs of his people, had an idol he used to worship and perfume. The two young men would go to that idol, turn it on its head and tarnish it with animal waste; each time, ʿAmr would clean it, perfume it, and finally left a sword beside it, saying, "Defend yourself." At last they tied the idol to a dead dog and threw it into a well on a rope. When ʿAmr saw it, the truth of ayat 191–195 struck him all at once: "By Allah! Had you been a god who has might, you would not end up tied to a dog on a rope!" He embraced Islam, was strong in his Islam, and was martyred at Uhud — may Allah be pleased with him and grant him Paradise. An old man's entire religion was refuted by a rope, a well, and a god that could not climb out.

## Living it

The passage asks two things of a believer. First, **watch what you do with answered prayers**. The parents of ayah 189 prayed sincerely while afraid; the test came when the prayer was granted. Gratitude means attributing the gift to the Giver — in your heart, your speech, and even in the names you give your children, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats as the everyday battlefield of this ayah. Second, **apply the four questions of ayah 195 to whatever you lean on besides Allah**. Anything other than Allah that you treat as the real source of rescue is, in the end, a fellow servant — it did not create you, cannot help itself, and will not answer. "So far beyond is Allah than what they associate with Him" (ayah 190) is not only a doctrine; it is the standing verdict of this trial.

passages.title: Allah the Protector versus blind, deaf idols
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat set a single, stark contrast before the reader — the theme that binds them together: on one side, the living Lord who reveals the Book, protects, and takes charge of His righteous servants; on the other, objects that cannot help their worshippers, cannot help themselves, and stare out at the world through drawn-on eyes that see nothing. The Prophet ﷺ is made to declare where his own security lies — *my Protector is Allah* — and then the idolaters' gods are weighed and found to be nothing at all.

## "My Protector is Allah, Who has revealed the Book"

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 196 as the answer to the challenge in the words immediately before it, where the Prophet ﷺ is told to say: "Call your (so-called) partners (of Allah) and then plot against me, and give me no respite" — that is, invoke your idols for aid against me, give it your best effort, and do not grant me even an instant's reprieve. Ayah 196 is why he can say this without a trace of fear: "Indeed, my Protector is Allah, Who has revealed the Book, and He protects the righteous."

Ibn Kathir paraphrases the inner state behind these words: Allah's support is sufficient; He will suffice me; He is my Supporter; I trust in Him and take refuge with Him. He is my protector in this life and in the Hereafter — and the protector of every righteous believer after me.

Ibn Kathir shows that this fearless stance is the inherited language of the prophets. When the people of Hūd told him, "some of our gods have seized you with evil (madness)," Hūd replied: "So plot against me, all of you, and give me no respite. I put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord! There is not a moving (living) creature but He has the grasp of its forelock" (11:54–56). And Ibrāhīm declared to his people that everything they worshipped was an enemy to him "save the Lord of all that exists, Who has created me, and it is He Who guides me" (26:75–78), and made that disavowal "a legacy lasting among his offspring" (43:26–28). The Prophet ﷺ in ayah 196 stands exactly where Hūd and Ibrāhīm stood: alone before a hostile people, entirely unafraid, because his security rests on Allah.

**Walī.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Arabic word *walī*, rendered "protector," also means *helper* — and it translates the closing phrase of the ayah accordingly: "He helps and protects the righteous." The two senses belong together: the One who shields His servant is the same One who actively comes to his aid.

**Why "Who has revealed the Book"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on this choice. Out of all the divine attributes of Allah, the verse spoke specially of His revelation to the Prophet ﷺ. The reason, Maʿārif explains, is that the Qur'an was the whole point of the conflict: the only reason for the idolaters' hostility to the Prophet ﷺ was his invitation to the message of the Book. So the very thing that provoked their enmity is presented as the guarantee of his safety. He was sure to be helped and protected by the One who had charged him with this Book.

**Who are "the righteous" (al-ṣāliḥīn)?** According to Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records, the righteous here are all those who take no one as equal to Allah — the prophets and the faithful Muslims alike. This turns the second half of the ayah into a general rule and a standing promise: Allah's protection is not a special privilege reserved for His messengers. He helps and protects every Muslim who acts righteously.

## The other side of the ledger: ayat 197–198

Having stated whom *he* relies on, the Prophet ﷺ is made to turn the light back on the idolaters' gods. Ayah 197: "And those whom you call upon besides Him cannot help you, nor can they help themselves." Ibn Kathir points out that this reiterates what was said of the idols earlier in the passage, but now Allah uses **direct speech** — no longer talking *about* the idolaters but *to* them: they cannot help *you*. The argument stops being a description and becomes a confrontation.

And what an argument it is. Ibn Kathir gathers the Qur'an's own evidence: these objects were themselves created and carved — "Worship you that which you (yourselves) carve?" (37:95). If all the false gods combined their strength they could not create a single fly; and if the fly snatched something from them, they could not get it back — "so weak are (both) the seeker and the sought" (22:73–74). If something is this weak, Ibn Kathir asks, how can it be worshipped and invoked for provisions and aid? Indeed, the worshippers are *better* than what they worship: a human being can hear, see, and act, while the idol can do none of these. And the idols cannot even defend themselves against those who would harm them — Ibrāhīm, Allah's Khalīl ("intimate friend"), broke his people's idols, striking them with his own right hand (37:93), and "broke them to pieces, (all) except the biggest of them" (21:58), and they lay there, unable to answer.

**Ayah 198** delivers the final, almost haunting image: "And if you call them to guidance, they hear not; and you will see them looking at you, yet they see not." Ibn Kathir links this to a similar ayah — "If you invoke (or call upon) them, they hear not your call" (35:14) — and then explains the unforgettable detail of the staring eyes: the idols have eyes that stare as if they see, although they are solid. Ibn Kathir even notes the wording: the ayah says *tarāhum* rather than *tarāhā*, treating the idols as if they had minds, since they are made in the shape of humans with eyes drawn on them. The wording itself mimics the illusion the idolaters fell for: a thing that looks alive and is utterly dead.

## The idol on the rope: a story Ibn Kathir tells

Ibn Kathir illustrates the idols' helplessness with a story from the early days of Islam in Madinah. Two young men — Muʿādh bin ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ and Muʿādh bin Jabal, may Allah be pleased with them both — embraced Islam after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived, and took to attacking the idols of the idolaters at night: breaking them, disfiguring them, even using them as fuel for needy widows, all to shake their people awake to their error.

ʿAmr bin al-Jamūḥ, one of the chiefs of his people, had an idol he used to worship and perfume. Again and again the two Muʿādhs would turn it on its head and tarnish it with animal waste; each time, ʿAmr would clean it, perfume it again — and finally left a sword beside it, telling it, "Defend yourself." Then one night the young men tied the idol to a dead dog and threw it into a well on a rope. When ʿAmr found it, the truth broke through: "By Allah! Had you been a god who has might, you would not end up tied to a dog on a rope!" He embraced Islam, was strong in it, and later died a martyr at Uḥud — may Allah be pleased with him and grant him Paradise.

The story is ayah 197 acted out in the streets of Madinah. A god that needs its worshipper to wash it, guard it, and avenge it is no god at all — "nor can they help themselves."

## Living under this ayah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what ayah 196 means for an ordinary believer, and it is worth taking to heart. Since Allah protects *all* who act righteously, the opposition or hostility of anyone cannot truly harm a true Muslim. Most often, Allah grants the righteous believer victory over his enemies in this very world. But Maʿārif goes a step further, into the harder case: what if, for some good reason, the believer is apparently defeated? Even then, nothing essential has been lost — because the real objective of his life was never worldly triumph but Allah's pleasure and obedience to Him in everything he does. An apparent failure that comes from Allah actually draws him *nearer* to that objective. In the truest accounting, his "failure" is success.

That is the quiet confidence this passage plants in the heart. The believer's security is not in the absence of enemies but in the identity of his Protector. On one side of the ledger stand the idols — unable to help their worshippers, unable to help themselves, staring without seeing. On the other stands the declaration the Prophet ﷺ was given, and every righteous believer after him inherits: "Indeed, my Protector is Allah, Who has revealed the Book, and He protects the righteous."

passages.title: Graciousness, pardon, and refuge from Satan's whispers
passages.tafsir:
As Sūrah al-Aʿrāf draws toward its close — after long descriptions of the obstinate ignorance and immoral behaviour of the adversaries of Islam — Allah turns to His Messenger ﷺ and gives him, in a single compact verse, a perfect code of moral conduct, and then teaches him what to do at the exact moment when living by that code becomes hardest. That is what binds ayat 199–202 into one unit: ayah 199 lays down how to deal with people at their worst; ayah 200 deals with the enemy who exploits precisely those moments, Shayṭān; and ayat 201–202 contrast the two kinds of hearts his whisper reaches — the heart mindful of Allah that snaps awake, and the heedless heart that is dragged ever deeper. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān calls ayah 199 the ideal manifesto of Qurʼanic ethics: the discipline through which the Prophet ﷺ was trained until he was conferred with the title *ṣāḥib khuluq ʿaẓīm* — which Maʿārif renders "the manifestation of all moral excellences" — unique to him out of the whole of mankind.

## Three commands, one character (ayah 199)

Ayah 199 contains three short commands: *khudh al-ʿafw* — take to forbearance, show forgiveness; *waʼmur bil-ʿurf* — enjoin al-ʿurf, what is good; *wa aʿriḍ ʿan al-jāhilīn* — and turn away from the ignorant.

**"Take the ʿafw."** The word *ʿafw* carries more than one meaning, and the early authorities read it in two complementary ways.

The first: *ʿafw* is **what people can do easily**. On this reading the Prophet ﷺ is told to accept from people the level of obedience they can reach without hardship, rather than demanding the highest standard. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān illustrates it with ṣalāh: in its true sense the prayer means standing before one's Lord in perfect veneration, with the *khushūʿ* (humbleness and submission) that only a few fortunate worshippers attain — and the Prophet ﷺ was told not to demand that summit from everyone, but to accept what degree of perfection people could achieve easily. This interpretation is reported in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī on the authority of ʿAbdullāh ibn az-Zubayr — that the ayah "was only revealed about the peoples [bad] character" — with similar narrations from Ibn ʿUmar and ʿĀʼishah, and it is the meaning confirmed by Mujāhid. Maʿārif also cites a report, via Ibn Kathīr, that at the ayah's revelation the Prophet ﷺ said he had been commanded to accept common, unexceptional obedience from people in their worship and behaviour, and had decided to do so as long as he was in their company.

The second: *ʿafw* is **pardon**. Ibn Marduwayh reports from Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah that the verse came down after Uḥud, when Ḥamzah was martyred and parts of his body were savagely cut off. Seeing him in that condition, the Prophet ﷺ said he would behave to seventy of their people the way they had behaved with Ḥamzah — and this verse was revealed: such retaliation did not suit his dignified position; he should pardon and forgive. And he lived that pardon to the end: at the conquest of Makkah, with his sworn enemies at his mercy, he set them all free, saying that far from seeking revenge, he would not even blame them for what had happened between them in the past.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān observes that these two meanings pour into one essence: do not demand perfection from people, do not avenge their wrongs, and be generous to them expecting nothing in return. One early authority, ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam, added a historical frame: Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to show forgiveness and turn away from the idolaters for ten years; afterwards He ordered him to be harsh with them.

The most beautiful unpacking of the verse comes from the Prophet ﷺ himself. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim record that when the ayah was revealed he asked, **"What does it mean, O Jibrīl?"** and Jibrīl answered: *Allah commands you to forgive those who wronged you, give to those who deprived you, and keep relations with those who cut theirs with you.* Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān relates this report from Imam Ibn Jarir al-Tabari with a further detail: the Archangel gave his answer after confirming the meaning from Allah. Each clause of the answer reverses the natural instinct. The same teaching appears in the Prophet's ﷺ own instruction reported by Imām Aḥmad from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, and Bayhaqī reports from ʿAlī that the Prophet ﷺ called it manners "better than the manners of all the early and the later people."

**"Enjoin al-ʿurf."** *ʿUrf* literally means "the recognized" — everything done in a way that is good and praiseworthy; al-Bukhārī glossed it simply as righteousness. The point, as Maʿārif draws out, is that forgiveness alone is not the ceiling. The Prophet ﷺ was to forgo revenge *and* keep actively calling his wrongdoers to what is good and beneficial — repaying evil not merely with justice, but with a higher degree of favour and grace: *iḥsān*.

**"Turn away from the ignorant."** Some ignorant diehards will not be moved even by this gentleness; they answer this gentle moral response with more ignorance and harshness. The command is not to be affected by their heart-rending comments and rustic challenges, and not to reply in their terms. Ibn Kathīr — as Maʿārif notes — is careful about what "turning away" means: it means not repaying evil with evil; it does *not* mean abandoning good advice to them, which would not befit the standing mission a prophet and messenger of Allah is charged with. Some scholars summarised the whole ayah by saying people are of two kinds: the good-doer — accept his good and neither ask of him more than he can bear nor what causes him hardship; and the one who falls into shortcomings — enjoin righteousness on him, and if he insists on evil, turn away, for your very ignoring of him may avert his evil and bring him round when he realises his error.

## The verse that stopped ʿUmar

Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī records, from Ibn ʿAbbās, the incident that shows this ayah working as a living rein on power. ʿUyaynah bin Ḥiṣn came to Madinah and, through his nephew al-Ḥurr bin Qays — one of the Qurʼān-reciters ʿUmar loved to keep near him and listen to, young or old — obtained an audience with the Khalīfah. Once inside, he said: "O Ibn al-Khaṭṭāb! You neither give to us sufficiently nor rule with justice between us." ʿUmar became so angry he almost punished him. Then al-Ḥurr spoke: "O Chief of the Faithful! Allah, the Exalted, said to His Prophet ﷺ, *Show forgiveness, enjoin al-ʿUrf, and turn away from the foolish* — verily this man is one of the fools!" By Allah, ʿUmar did not do anything after he heard that ayah being recited — and indeed, as the narration notes, he was one who adhered to the Book of Allah, the Exalted and Most Honored. Maʿārif adds the well-known line said of him: he readily mellowed before the commandments of the Book of Allah, the Mighty, the Exalted. One verse, quoted at the right moment, was enough.

## When the whisper comes (ayah 200)

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains why ayah 200 must follow ayah 199: forgiving the unjust and refusing to answer evil with evil is *heavy duty* — most irksome and hard on human temperament. And it is precisely at such moments that Shayṭān arrives to coax an otherwise calm person into anger and get him "all set to fight." So the Qurʼān gives the standard treatment: when you feel anger flaring where your patience is being tested, recognise at once that the instigation is coming from Shayṭān — and seek refuge with Allah.

The word for his attack is *nazgh* — rendered "an evil whisper" by Ibn Kathīr and "a strike" in Maʿārif: the sudden inner prick of incitement. Ibn Jarīr pinpoints exactly what it is here: "If the devil lures you to get angry, thus directing you away from forgiving the ignorant and towards punishing him — then seek refuge with Allah."

Ibn Kathīr then draws the crucial distinction that structures the whole passage. With a human enemy, leniency works: it might deter him from persistence in his evil, Allah willing — as Allah says elsewhere, "he between whom and you there was enmity will become as though he was a close friend" (41:34). But leniency is useless against the devil, "because he seeks your destruction and total demise"; he is an open enemy to you, O mankind, just as he was for your father before you. Hence two enemies, two weapons: graciousness for people, *istiʿādhah* — seeking refuge with Allah — for Shayṭān.

The ayah seals this with two of Allah's names: *innahu Samīʿun ʿAlīm* — He is All-Hearer, All-Knower. Ibn Jarīr explains: Allah hears the ignorance the fools subject you to and hears your seeking refuge with Him; nothing of His creation's speech escapes His knowledge, and He knows what drives the devil's lures away from you.

**A pattern Ibn Kathīr noticed.** Maʿārif relays, under the heading of "an unusual coincidence," Ibn Kathīr's observation that exactly three verses in the Qurʼān appear as an embodiment of this high moral teaching of repelling evil with what is better — this verse of al-Aʿrāf, 23:96–98 in al-Muʼminūn, and 41:34–36 in Ḥā Mīm as-Sajdah (Fuṣṣilat) — and *all three* conclude with the need to seek refuge from Shayṭān. The inference: Shayṭān takes special interest in human quarrels. Wherever a quarrel is on, the devils converge on it as their favourite hunting ground, and no matter how sedate and forbearing a person is, they will try to incite him past the limits.

And the remedy demonstrably works. Maʿārif cites a hadith that two men were quarrelling before the Prophet ﷺ, one getting out of control in his fit of anger. The Prophet ﷺ said, "I know some words which, if this person were to say, his rage will go away" — *aʿūdhu billāhi min ash-shayṭān ir-rajīm*, I seek refuge with Allah from Shayṭān, the Accursed. The man said it after him, and suddenly his anger was all gone.

## Two hearts, two endings (ayat 201–202)

Ayah 201 describes the people of *taqwā* — those mindful of Allah, who, in Ibn Kathīr's framing, obey His orders and avoid what He forbade. Even the righteous are not out of the whisper's reach; a *ṭāʼif* from Shayṭān comes to them too. Ibn Kathīr glosses it broadly: an evil thought, anger, a whisper of Shayṭān crossing the mind, an intention to err, or even an actual error committed. What distinguishes the people of taqwā is what happens next: *tadhakkarū* — they remember. They remember Allah's punishment and His tremendous reward, His promises and His threats; they repent, return to Him, seek refuge with Him and ask forgiveness before death overtakes them. *Fa-idhā hum mubṣirūn* — "and behold, they then see aright." As Ibn Kathīr puts it, they become aright and aware of the error of their ways.

Ayah 202 turns to the other camp: "their brothers" — meaning, Ibn Kathīr explains, the devils' brothers among mankind, those who listen to the shayāṭīn and obey their orders, just as Allah says "the spendthrifts are brothers of the devils" (17:27).
