Them the devils *yamuddūnahum fī al-ghayy* — plunge deeper into error, helping them commit sins by making the path easy and appealing. *Thumma lā yuqṣirūn* — "then they never stop short." Ibn ʿAbbās (as reported by ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah) read a grim reciprocity in it: "Neither mankind stop short of the evil that they are doing nor the devils stop short of luring them." Ibn Kathīr refers the phrase to the devils, who never cease inciting mankind to commit errors — as Allah says of the devils sent against the disbelievers, pushing them persistently to evil (19:83).

So the passage ends on a stark contrast. For the person of taqwā, Shayṭān's whisper is a passing thing, broken the instant remembrance returns. For his "brothers," it is a partnership that neither side ever breaks off — an ever-deepening spiral, because the one does not stop short of the evil he is doing and the other does not stop short of luring him.

## Living it

The passage asks three concrete things of a believer. With people: accept what they can genuinely give, pardon their errors, keep urging good, and step back from provocation rather than trade in it — forgive those who wrong you, give to those who deprive you, keep relations with those who cut theirs with you. With yourself: treat flaring anger as a diagnostic — Maʿārif says that when a person sees his anger getting out of control, he should know Shayṭān is winning against his better self — and answer it immediately with the istiʿādhah, as the Prophet ﷺ taught the quarrelling man. And underneath both: keep remembrance close, because ayah 201 shows that when the people of taqwā remember Allah, they become aright and aware of the error of their ways. This, Maʿārif concludes, is how noble traits of character flourish at their best.

passages.title: Listening to the Qur'an and humble remembrance
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close Sūrah al-Aʿrāf, and they form its final movement: from the deniers' demand for a made-to-order miracle, to the miracle already in their hands — the Qur'an itself — to how a believer should receive that Qur'an (in attentive silence), and finally to how a believer should live with its Lord (in quiet, humble, constant remembrance). The thread running through all four is *how the Word of Allah is to be met*: the deniers meet it with hostile demands and noise; the believers meet it with listening, lowered voices, and — in the sūrah's very last breath — a prostration.

## Ayah 203: the demand for a custom miracle

The pagans of Makkah had a habit this sūrah has already described: despite the many miracles already shown, they kept demanding ever-new miracles of their own choosing, and when the sign they specified did not come, they turned that into an accusation — "Why have you not brought it?" Ibn Kathir records the early explanations of the phrase *lawlā ijtabaytahā*: Ibn ʿAbbās said it means "Why have you not received a miracle?" — or "Why have you not initiated or made it?" — while Mujāhid read it as "Produce a miracle of your own," a reading Qatādah, al-Suddī, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Jarīr all endorsed. Either way, the demand assumes the Prophet ﷺ manufactures signs on request.

The answer he is told to give dismantles that assumption: "I but follow what is revealed to me from my Lord." Ibn Kathir draws out its meaning: I do not ask such things of my Lord; if Allah sends a miracle I accept it, and otherwise I do not demand one unless He allows me — for Allah is Most Wise, All-Knowing. Signs belong to Allah, not to the messenger's initiative; Ibn Kathir sets alongside this Allah's words in 26:4, that if He willed He could send down from heaven a sign to which their necks would bend in humility.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān exposes what was really wrong with the demand, using a courtroom analogy. A plaintiff's claim stands proven by trustworthy evidence which the other party has not even challenged. No court on earth would then allow that party to say: we will accept the claim only if you produce evidence from witnesses of *our* choosing. The Prophet ﷺ had already been given miracles more numerous and clearer than those of past prophets — so many that scholars wrote separate books about them, such as al-Suyūṭī's two-volume *al-Khaṣāʾiṣ al-Kubrā*. Having seen those, demanding a custom-ordered sign was not honest inquiry but "an exercise in hostility that is not worth noticing."

And yet the ayah does not end on refusal. It turns their attention to the sign already before them: *hādhā baṣāʾiru min rabbikum* — "This is (a Book of) insights from your Lord." Maʿārif explains: this Qur'an has come from your Lord as "a compendium of many proofs and miracles." Ibn Kathir calls it "the most powerful miracle, clearest evidence and most true proof." Maʿārif adds the standing challenge: the whole world was dared to produce even a small sūrah like it, and failed — an open sign that the Qur'an is no human word but the inimitable Word of Allah. Then the careful ending: it is "a guidance and a mercy *for a people who believe*." The proof stands for everyone; the guidance and mercy are unlocked only by faith — whoever deliberates on it honestly, says Maʿārif, cannot part with it without knowing it is from Allah.

## Ayah 204: how to receive the Word — listen, and be silent

If the Qur'an is mercy, ayah 204 gives the condition for receiving that mercy: "When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it attentively and be silent, so that you may be shown mercy." Ibn Kathir sets this against the deliberate tactic of the Quraysh recorded in 41:26 — "Listen not to this Qur'an, and make noise in the midst of its recitation." The believer's posture is the exact opposite of the denier's: silence where they made noise, listening where they urged one another not to listen.

Ibn Jarīr reports an occasion from Ibn Masʿūd: "We would give Salāms to each other during Ṣalāh. So the ayah was revealed: 'When the Qur'an is recited, then listen to it.'" Even greeting one another — a good act in itself — had to give way before the recited Word.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses, citing Qurṭubī and others, that "lending ears" to the Qur'an is more than hearing: it includes obeying the Qur'an and striving to act on its injunctions. And the closing phrase — "so that you may be shown mercy" — hints plainly that the Qur'an's mercy is tied to observing this etiquette; whoever flouts it and shows the Qur'an disrespect invites the opposite.

**Where does the ruling apply?** The commentators differed over whether the verse concerns recitation in Ṣalāh, in the Friday Khuṭbah, or absolutely. The majority, says Maʿārif, hold that since the wording is general, the rule is general — with some detail:

- **In Ṣalāh:** the Hanafi school takes this verse as proof that those praying behind an Imam should not recite; even jurists who direct the follower to recite al-Fātiḥah say, in light of this verse, that he should do so in an interval when the Imam is silent.
- **In the Khuṭbah:** silence is obligatory (wājib). The Prophet ﷺ said that when the Imam comes out for the Khuṭbah, there is no Ṣalāh and no conversation; it is reported that not even a verbal reminder to another person to be quiet is allowed — a hand gesture must suffice. ʿAllāmah Ibn al-Humām even wrote that when the Imam or Khaṭīb is reciting about Paradise or Hell, one may not audibly pray for Paradise or seek refuge from the Fire at that moment — because the verse's promise of mercy is for the one who stays silent. (A voiceless supplication after such verses in one's own nafl prayer — voluntary prayer beyond the obligatory ones — is a different matter: that is established Sunnah and rewarded.) Jurists extend the Khuṭbah rule to the Khuṭbahs of the two ʿEids and of Nikāḥ.
- **Outside Ṣalāh and Khuṭbah:** here the jurists genuinely differed. Some held listening and remaining silent to be wājib in all cases, and acting against it a sin — for this reason they ruled it impermissible to recite the Qur'an loudly where people are busy working or resting, and held that whoever does so sins, as recorded in Khulāṣat al-Fatāwā and other juristic works. Others distinguished: listening is wājib only where the Qur'an is recited *for the purpose of being listened to*, as in Ṣalāh and Khuṭbah. Their evidence: sound aḥādīth show the Prophet ﷺ recited audibly in his night prayers while his wives slept, and a hadith in al-Bukhārī and Muslim records him saying, on a journey, that he recognized his Ashʿarite companions by the voices of their night recitation and could locate their tents by it — yet he never asked them why they recited aloud, nor woke the sleepers to listen. So there is leeway outside Ṣalāh — but all agree it is better and preferable to fall silent and listen whenever recitation is heard.

From this Maʿārif draws pointedly practical conclusions: blasting Qur'anic recitation from a radio at full volume in gatherings where no one is actually listening is an error, and relaying recitation over mosque loudspeakers late at night so that it disturbs the sleeping and the working "is not correct." Reverence for the Qur'an is shown by *how it is heard*, not by sheer volume.

## Ayah 205: the quiet remembrance

Having taught how to receive Allah's Word, the passage turns to how to speak to Him: "Remember your Lord within yourself, humbly (*taḍarruʿan*) and with fear (*khīfatan*), and without loudness of words, in the mornings and the evenings — and do not be among the heedless."

Ibn ʿAbbās held that "remembrance" (*dhikr*) here means the Qur'an itself, so the etiquette concerns recitation; the majority read it as remembrance in the absolute sense, which includes recitation. Maʿārif notes this makes little practical difference: by consensus the same etiquette governs both.

**Three methods of dhikr.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distills three modes from the verse's wording. (1) Dhikr of the heart alone — pondering Allah and His attributes with the tongue still. (2) Dhikr of heart and tongue together, the voice too low for others to hear. Both of these fall under "remember your Lord *within yourself*." (3) Voiced dhikr — but "without loudness of words": an average voice, never rising toward shouting. The best form is to understand what one is saying, keep the heart fixed on it, and let the tongue join in — heart and tongue synchronized. The lowest degree is words on the tongue with a heedless heart. Here Maʿārif quotes the sage Rūmī's couplet: glorification on the tongue while "cow and donkey" occupy the heart — what remembrance is that? Yet, crucially, Maʿārif does not let this become an excuse to quit: even a distracted verbal dhikr carries reward, and constant utterance of the tongue often becomes the very channel through which the heart eventually wakes. Those who feel no presence in their dhikr should not abandon it as useless, but continue and keep striving for attentiveness.

**Why the low voice?** Two reasons emerge from the sources. First, reverence: Maʿārif observes that one naturally cannot shout in the presence of someone one deeply reveres — excessive loudness in dhikr betrays a deficit of awe. The Qur'an says the same of recitation in 17:110: neither too loud nor too soft, but a middle way. Second — and this is the theological heart of it — *Allah is near*. Ibn Kathir relates that the Companions asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Is our Lord close, so that we call Him in secret, or far, so that we raise our voices?" and Allah sent down 2:186: "I am indeed near (to them by My knowledge). I respond to the invocations of the supplicant when he calls on Me (without any mediator or intercessor)." And in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī reports that when people raised their voices in duʿā while travelling, the Prophet ﷺ said: "O people! Take it easy on yourselves, for He Whom you are calling is not deaf or absent. Verily, He Whom you are calling is the All-Hearer, close (by His knowledge), closer to one of you than the neck of his animal." Notice how both texts themselves qualify the nearness — "by My knowledge," "by His knowledge": nothing you whisper escapes Him, and no mediator is needed to carry it. That is why the quiet voice is not a mere technique; it is theology enacted. You whisper to One Who hears.

**Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.** Maʿārif relates the hadith in Abū Dāwūd: the Prophet ﷺ went out late one night and found Abū Bakr praying with a lowered voice and ʿUmar reciting aloud. In the morning he asked each. Abū Bakr said: "The One I was reciting for has heard it — that is sufficient." ʿUmar said: "I intended to drive away sleep and Shayṭān." The Prophet ﷺ told Abū Bakr to raise his voice a little, and ʿUmar to lower his somewhat. And in Tirmidhī, ʿĀʾishah was asked whether the Prophet ﷺ recited loudly or softly; she answered: both, at different times. So the verse does not forbid the voiced dhikr; Imam Abū Ḥanīfah said the reciter has the choice — on two unanimously agreed conditions: no showing off, and no disturbance to others' prayer, work, or rest. Which is more meritorious, loud or low, varies by person, time, and circumstance.

**Humility and fear.** *Taḍarruʿ* is the humbleness born of realizing Allah's greatness while keeping the meaning of one's words in view. The fear the verse names, Maʿārif explains, is the fear of falling short — of failing to do justice to the great task of worshipping Allah — joined to consciousness of one's sins, fear of His punishment, and fear of one's unknown end. Dhikr is to be made in the manner of a person subdued by an aura of awe and fear. Maʿārif notes the pairing echoes 7:55 earlier in this same sūrah — "Supplicate to your Lord humbly and secretly" — where secrecy itself appears as an etiquette of calling on Him.

**Mornings and evenings — or always?** Ibn Kathir notes this ayah was revealed in Makkah before the night of Isrāʾ, when the five daily prayers were ordained, commanding that Allah be worshipped at these two times — comparing 50:39. Maʿārif offers two readings: at minimum, remember Allah twice daily, morning and evening; or — as saying "East and West" means the whole world — "mornings and evenings" means all times, so that one remains committed to dhikr always. ʿĀʾishah said the Prophet ﷺ was devoted to the remembrance of Allah at all times and in all conditions. The verse then closes with its warning: "and do not be among the heedless (*al-ghāfilīn*)" — abandoning remembrance and joining the heedless is, as Maʿārif puts it, a great loss.

## Ayah 206: the angels — and the sūrah ends in sajdah

The final ayah lifts the eyes upward: "Surely those who are with your Lord are never too proud to worship Him; they glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate." Ibn Kathir explains: Allah praises the angels who glorify Him night and day without tiring, and reminds His servants of this so that they *imitate the angels* in tireless worship. Maʿārif widens "those with your Lord": being "with" Allah means being among those He has approved and accepted — the angels, the prophets, and the most righteous of this Ummah. Their mark is that they never assume airs about worship, never think themselves too big for it; they see themselves as weak and needy before Allah and express their ultimate humility by falling in prostration. And Maʿārif draws the beautiful converse: whoever is blessed with constant worship and remembrance carries the very sign of being "with" Allah, in His company.

This ayah is an āyah of sajdah — by the agreement of the scholars, Ibn Kathir notes, it is the first place in the Qur'an where prostration is sanctioned for the reciter and the listener. The sources gather the merits of this act. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, a man asked Thawbān for a deed that would bring him to Paradise; Thawbān answered that he had asked the Prophet ﷺ the same, who told him to make sajdah repeatedly — for every sajdah you make, Allah increases you a rank and forgives you a sin. (Imam Abū Ḥanīfah understood abundant sajdah to mean abundant nafl prayer, since sajdah by itself is not a standalone act of worship but a unit of Ṣalāh.) Also in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah: a servant of Allah is closest to his Lord when in sajdah — so, when in sajdah, pray most ardently, for it is strongly hoped it will be answered; a note in Maʿārif (from Muhammad Taqi Usmani) adds that supplication within the sajdah of prayer belongs in nafl Ṣalāh, using the Arabic supplications of the Qur'an and Sunnah, while in a sajdah made purely for supplication one may pray in any language. And in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah: when the son of Ādam recites a verse of sajdah and prostrates, Shayṭān runs away crying, saying: man was commanded to prostrate and obeyed, so Paradise became his home; I was commanded to prostrate and disobeyed, so Hell became mine.

That is how Sūrah al-Aʿrāf chooses to end: not with an argument, but with a forehead on the ground. The deniers demanded spectacles; the believers were given a Book, taught to fall silent before it, to whisper to a Lord Who is close — by His knowledge, closer to a rider than the neck of his own animal — and to join the angels in the worship that pride refuses and humility performs.
